bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing

bivy.name: Libby Lake

bivy.name: Upper Eagle Lake and Horsehead Pass
bivy.notes: The hub of the southern Sawtooth and the practical base for Switchback Mountain, with Hoodoo and Raven Ridge also within reach along the crest. Access is the Gold Creek side, not the Twisp River: turn off the highway onto the North Fork Gold Creek road, then a signed spur for several miles to the Eagle Lakes trailhead at about 4,760 ft. bivy.name: Boiling Lake basin

From the road it is reached over Horsehead Pass from Upper Eagle Lake in a short day. bivy.name: Prince Creek Campground - boat-in
bivy.notes: The lake-side gateway to Star, Courtney and the southern crest. Most parties land in the afternoon, camp here, and start the climb at first light. The other useful boat stop is Moore Point, about ten miles further up-lake and five and a half below Stehekin, a smaller camp with a dock, a picnic shelter, food storage and a toilet, from which the Fish Creek trail climbs to Round Lake and the Oval Lakes country - that is the water-side way to Oval Peak. The Lakeshore trail connecting the two took heavy damage in the storms of December 2025, with debris flows and washouts between Prince Creek and Moore Point, and Moore Point has also been closed at times for post-fire flood risk, so confirm both the camp and the trail are open before committing to an itinerary that depends on walking between them. bivy.name: Boiling Lake basin

bivy.name: Scatter Lake basin

bivy.name: Bird Creek Camp, Devore Creek trail
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Devore Peak and Tupshin Peak, and it is worth being clear that these two are not a Sawtooth trip. They stand west of Lake Chelan on the long ridge dividing Company Creek and Hilgard Creek from Devore Creek, and everything about them - the wilderness, the permit system, the transport - is different from the Twisp River peaks. The usual way in is a ferry to the Stehekin landing, then the Company Creek road, with the Devore Creek trail reached from Weaver Point on the far side of the head of the lake; Bird Creek Camp sits about four miles up that trail at around 4,200 ft. From here Tupshin's South Ridge and Devore's Southeast Ridge are both reachable, and parties commonly climb both from the same base, either from this camp or from a higher bivouac around 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek basin. Both are steep, brushy and loose by reputation and neither is a walk-up. The season is roughly late July into early October; the approach is low, hot and overgrown early, and the upper slopes hold snow. This is the least forgiving logistics in the zone - a party that misses a boat or a bus loses a day at each end - so build slack into the itinerary and carry more food than the schedule strictly needs.
bivy.water: Bird Creek is immediately past the camp; the site sits about a hundred feet short of the crossing. Below here, Devore Creek is the last dependable water on the climb, so fill there if you are unsure. Parties going higher can camp near 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek drainage, where there is water in early and mid-season but which can dry out late.

Peak-season demand is high enough that an early-access lottery governs the best dates and the odds are poor; plan around it rather than hoping. Open fires are banned at several camps in this unit and restricted to established pits elsewhere, and a total ban is normal by late summer. The ferry and the Stehekin shuttle are the other half of the planning: the boat must be booked, the shuttle up the valley runs a limited seasonal schedule, and the Company Creek road trailhead is several miles from the landing, so missing a bus costs you a half day on foot.
bivy.capacity: Three small tent openings and a fire ring - room for perhaps four small tents. Very small, and there is no overflow.

bivy.name: Mackinaw Shelter camp, North Fork Sauk
bivy.notes: This is the first night for a Glacier Peak climb by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, which is the route most parties use now that the western approaches have gone. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at the road end. bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites in the trees on a river bench, comfortably two or three parties, and the only organised camping in the valley bottom

bivy.name: White Pass and the Foam Creek benches under White Mountain
bivy.notes: White Pass at about 5,900 feet is the second night for a Glacier Peak climb, or the first if a strong party pushes the whole eight and a half miles and three thousand feet from the road in one go. It is the point where the North Fork Sauk trail meets the long-distance crest trail and where the climbing approach turns east. From here a boot path runs east-northeast under the southeast side of White Mountain for a bit over a mile toward a high shoulder, then the Foam Creek path traverses on toward an eastern col at around 6,600 feet for the first view of the mountain. Parties who want to break the approach differently camp somewhere along that traverse rather than at the pass itself, which trades a sheltered established site for wind and a shorter summit day. It is exposed ground once you leave the pass, with nothing to hide behind in a thunderstorm, and the traverse is genuinely confusing in fog.

bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person party limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Camp on the existing bare sites — this is fragile subalpine meadow that recovers slowly and is heavily used. Carry a stove; open flame is inappropriate here and is usually prohibited outright under summer restrictions.
bivy.capacity: Several established sites just south of the pass, plus scattered ground on the benches east of it; a popular crossroads with a long-distance trail running through it, so expect other parties in July and August

bivy.name: Glacier Gap
bivy.notes: This is the high camp for Glacier Peak by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, and the single most-used climbing camp on the mountain. bivy.water: Meltwater streams off the surrounding snowfields, running through most of the climbing season but silty; late in a hot summer it can be reduced to a drip from the base of a snow patch, so scout it on arrival rather than at dinner time
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. No fires — this is bare rock, pumice and alpine ground above treeline with no wood and nothing that recovers. Twelve-person party limit. Human waste needs carrying out or burying properly well away from the meltwater, which everybody camped here is drinking.
bivy.capacity: A large basin with many bivouac sites and rock-walled platforms — it takes a lot of parties without feeling crowded, and there is always room to build another windbreak

bivy.name: Kennedy Ridge and the Glacier Creek camps, Suiattle side
bivy.notes: This is the base for Glacier Peak's Kennedy Glacier and for the Frostbite Ridge line above it, and since the White Chuck approach died it is the only practical way at the mountain's north and west sides. The walk in is long even when the road is open — the Suiattle River trail runs about seven miles to the river bridge and the crest trail then carries you south toward Kennedy Ridge, so this is a full day before the climbing camp is even in sight. Kennedy Creek has no bridge and will not get one; the standard tactic is to camp short of it and cross in the morning when the flow is at its lowest, using whatever logs are currently in place rather than wading the main channel. With the road washed out the trailhead is still reachable on foot or by bike from the closure point, which adds roughly nine miles each way to an approach that was already the longest on the mountain.

Check the road order before driving: the Suiattle River road washed out about four and a half miles in during the December 2025 storms, temporary bridge work was scheduled across the middle of the 2026 season, and the campgrounds and trailheads up that road were shut for the season while it stood.
bivy.capacity: Forested sites in ones and twos scattered along the crest trail near the creek crossings, plus rougher bivouac ground higher on the ridge; nothing organised, and no single site takes a large party

bivy.name: Boulder Basin above Sitkum Creek — and the White Chuck situation

The approach that made it popular no longer exists, and the story is worth getting right rather than repeating old published mileage. In October 2003 a storm put a record flood down the White Chuck, a debris flow off the mountain buried Kennedy Hot Springs under about five feet of material, and the river rebuilt its own valley floor. Anything you read describing five and a half easy miles to the hot springs and a steep climbers' path to the basin is describing an approach that has not been available for twenty years. Parties wanting the north and west sides of the mountain now go in from the Suiattle instead.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams through the basin, dependable through the climbing season and thinning late
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit and a twelve-person limit still apply in theory. In practice the binding constraint is the road: the White Chuck road is closed from a little under four miles in all the way to its far end, and the trail beyond it is not maintained and not going to be. Treat any plan that relies on this basin as needing a specific check with the district first.
bivy.capacity: Open basin ground with room for several tents; historically the busiest camp on the mountain, and now one of the emptiest

bivy.name: Buck Creek Pass and the High Pass camps
bivy.notes: Buck Creek Pass at about 5,800 feet is the base for three peaks in this zone that have nothing to do with Glacier Peak's own approaches. Helmet Butte sits half a mile northeast of the pass and is the shortest objective from here. Buck Mountain rises directly south across the valley and is normally taken by leaving the Buck Creek trail lower down for the east ridge of Cleator and the Buck–Berge col, which also gives Mount Berge. From the pass a way trail continues north over Flower Dome to High Pass, which is both a fine high camp in its own right and the link over into the Napeequa, tying this side of the zone to Clark and Luahna. Getting here is around ten miles and three thousand feet of steady forest walking up Buck Creek from Trinity, so it is a full first day. It is a scenic and genuinely popular pass, which for a climbing party means arriving early enough to get a site. When the Chiwawa road is shut at Atkinson Flat the trailhead itself is roughly eleven road miles further on, which turns a two-day trip into a four-day one or a long bike shuttle.
bivy.water: A stream at the pass is the main supply and is reliable through the season; the higher camps toward High Pass run on snowmelt only and can be dry by September
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Trinity trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Fires are prohibited where posted and the meadow ground here is exactly the kind of place that gets posted — carry a stove. Camp on the bare established sites rather than in the heather. The road is the real permit question: the Chiwawa River road is closed from Atkinson Flat north to Trinity under a storm order running through the end of 2027, with no reopening estimate, and a large 2026 fire closure covered the same road on top of it.
bivy.capacity: Several established forested and meadow-edge sites at the pass itself, enough for a few parties, with rougher and more exposed ground higher toward Flower Dome and High Pass

bivy.name: Napeequa Valley floor near Louis Creek

From the Little Giant trailhead the very first obstacle is fording the Chiwawa itself — the old bridge is gone and its remains are in the brush by the water, so the crossing is a wade and its depth decides the trip. The trail then climbs, drops a couple of hundred feet through the Little Giant Creek drainage and switchbacks up open meadow to Little Giant Pass at about 6,400 feet, roughly four and a half miles in, with Clark Mountain filling the view on the far side. Dropping into the Napeequa costs about two thousand feet, and from the valley floor the standard progression is two miles up-valley to Louis Creek and then a crossing of the Napeequa before climbing out toward Butterfly Butte. This valley camp is what a party uses on the way in when the day runs out at the bottom of the descent, or on the way out with the pass still to reclimb. Crossing the Napeequa is a real decision rather than a formality: it is glacier-fed, it runs high through early summer and it peaks in the afternoon, so cross in the morning and be willing to walk the bank looking for something better.
bivy.water: The Napeequa runs the length of the valley and is heavy with glacial silt off Clark and Luahna, so it needs settling as well as filtering; Louis Creek and the side streams run clearer
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Little Giant trailhead, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove rather than fire in the meadow. Both closures that matter land on this approach: the Chiwawa River road is shut above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year storm order, and the 2026 fire closure named the Little Giant trail itself along with the Napeequa trails and the roads either side, running from mid-August to the end of October.
bivy.capacity: Informal ground on the valley flats and in the timber edge — no developed sites, room for a couple of parties, and rarely anybody else there

bivy.name: Butterfly Butte and the Pilz Glacier basin camps
bivy.notes: This is the climbing camp for Luahna Peak and Chalangin Peak and the Napeequa-side base for Clark Mountain, roughly eleven hundred feet above the Napeequa floor after the river crossing near Louis Creek. The benches around Butterfly Butte at about 5,850 feet are the comfortable choice and look straight across at Clark; a broad basin below the Pilz Glacier headwall around 6,200 feet is the higher option and shortens summit day meaningfully. Parties pushing for a very early start use bivouac ground higher again on the northeast ridge, at roughly 6,800 and 7,200 feet, where there is no water and no shelter. Luahna is reached over the Pilz Glacier, so an ice axe, crampons and glacier gear belong on any list here. Chalangin sits half a mile northwest of Luahna and is more often taken by its own north side, bypassing the glacier, than by traversing the connecting ridge from Luahna — the traverse is long and the direct approach is the better plan. These are lightly visited summits and the register entries are years apart, so assume no boot track, no other party and no help.
bivy.water: A stream serves the benches around 5,850 to 6,200 feet and is the practical water for this camp; there is a pond at about 6,500 feet below the glacier, and above that it is snowmelt or nothing
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at the Little Giant trailhead. No fires this high — carry a stove. Camp on bare ground and rock rather than the heather benches. Subject to the same Chiwawa road closure and 2026 fire closure as the valley below it.
bivy.capacity: Small flat clearings on the benches around the butte for one or two parties, and higher up a broad basin under the glacier headwall with room for several; everything above is genuine bivouac ground rather than campsites

bivy.name: Boulder Pass and Thunder Basin, White River
bivy.notes: This is the standard base for Clark Mountain and the reason Clark is a White River peak rather than a Little Giant one. From the trailhead at about 2,300 feet the White River trail runs flat for four miles, then the Boulder Creek trail turns east and climbs for another seven, crossing Boulder Creek at around 4,000 feet — a wade or a log, and high water there turns parties round early in the season. Good camps exist in a large open basin at about 4,900 feet and again just below the pass around 6,000 feet, with the pass itself at about 6,200 feet holding dry ground even when there is snow about. From the pass the Walrus Glacier route traverses the basin east of the ridge point, crosses the northeast ridge around 6,700 feet and gains the glacier for the east side of the mountain; the whole thing runs to about twenty-five miles round trip and six and a half thousand feet of gain. Tenpeak is a technical summit with a north couloir and a milder-looking southeast face, it sees very few ascents, and most parties want a third day to climb it properly from a basin camp rather than pushing it in one.

bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the White River trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove only up here. The White River road was inside the 2026 fire closure that ran from mid-August to the end of October along with the Chiwawa side, so this approach and the Little Giant one were shut at the same time by the same order — do not assume that losing one leaves the other.
bivy.capacity: Open ground at the pass with plenty of dry spots for several tents, a good basin camp about a mile below it, and separate rough ground over in Thunder Basin for one or two parties

bivy.name: Kennedy Ridge and the Glacier Creek camps, Suiattle side

bivy.name: Mackinaw Shelter camp, North Fork Sauk

bivy.capacity: Several established sites just south of the pass, plus scattered ground on the benches east of it; a popular crossroads with a long-distance trail running through it, so expect other parties in July and August

bivy.capacity: Several established sites just south of the pass, plus scattered ground on the benches east of it; a popular crossroads with a long-distance trail running through it, so expect other parties in July and August

It sits at about 7,300 feet at the head of the basin, reached by crossing what is left of the White Chuck Glacier northeast from the White Pass area — and what is left is the point, because that glacier has retreated faster than almost anything else in the range and the crossing is now largely bare rock, pumice and meltwater ponds rather than ice. From camp the route works up the ridge to about 8,400 feet, traverses onto the upper Suiattle Glacier, gains the upper Cool Glacier around 9,200 feet and climbs it westward to regain the ridge for the summit. Summit day from here runs long by any measure and thirteen hours camp to camp is normal rather than slow. Being a gap it funnels wind, so build or use the rock walls. Most parties take three days from the North Fork Sauk road and a fourth is worth having for weather.
bivy.water: Meltwater streams off the surrounding snowfields, running through most of the climbing season but silty; late in a hot summer it can be reduced to a drip from the base of a snow patch, so scout it on arrival rather than at dinner time
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. No fires — this is bare rock, pumice and alpine ground above treeline with no wood and nothing that recovers. Twelve-person party limit. Human waste needs carrying out or burying properly well away from the meltwater, which everybody camped here is drinking.
bivy.capacity: A large basin with many bivouac sites and rock-walled platforms — it takes a lot of parties without feeling crowded, and there is always room to build another windbreak

bivy.name: Kennedy Ridge and the Glacier Creek camps, Suiattle side
bivy.notes: This is the base for Glacier Peak's Kennedy Glacier and for the Frostbite Ridge line above it, and since the White Chuck approach died it is the only practical way at the mountain's north and west sides. The walk in is long even when the road is open — the Suiattle River trail runs about seven miles to the river bridge and the crest trail then carries you south toward Kennedy Ridge, so this is a full day before the climbing camp is even in sight. Kennedy Creek has no bridge and will not get one; the standard tactic is to camp short of it and cross in the morning when the flow is at its lowest, using whatever logs are currently in place rather than wading the main channel. Above the forest the route climbs the ridge and the glacier toward the saddle between the Kennedy and Vista glaciers at around 8,000 feet, where bivouac sites exist for parties willing to sleep on snow and rock with no shelter and no clean water. With the road washed out the trailhead is still reachable on foot or by bike from the closure point, which adds roughly nine miles each way to an approach that was already the longest on the mountain.
bivy.water: Glacier Creek and Kennedy Creek are both right there and both silty with glacial flour — let it settle or filter accordingly. Higher on the ridge water disappears entirely by late season and has to be carried or melted.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Suiattle road end. Stove only above the forest. Check the road order before driving: the Suiattle River road washed out about four and a half miles in during the December 2025 storms, temporary bridge work was scheduled across the middle of the 2026 season, and the campgrounds and trailheads up that road were shut for the season while it stood.
bivy.capacity: Forested sites in ones and twos scattered along the crest trail near the creek crossings, plus rougher bivouac ground higher on the ridge; nothing organised, and no single site takes a large party

bivy.name: Boulder Basin above Sitkum Creek — and the White Chuck situation
bivy.notes: Boulder Basin sits somewhere around 5,500 to 6,000 feet on a rib south of Sitkum Creek and is the historic high camp for the Sitkum Glacier, once the shortest and most popular route up Glacier Peak. The approach that made it popular no longer exists, and the story is worth getting right rather than repeating old published mileage. In October 2003 a storm put a record flood down the White Chuck, a debris flow off the mountain buried Kennedy Hot Springs under about five feet of material, and the river rebuilt its own valley floor. The hot springs are gone — not damaged, gone, and not being rebuilt. By 2006 less than a third of the White Chuck River trail survived and there are no plans to repair it. The road reopened partway in 2011 to a point near the old trailhead area, which for a while allowed a long road walk and a rough approach up what remained, but it is closed again from under four miles in and the surviving trail is a treacherous bushwhack rather than a route. Anything you read describing five and a half easy miles to the hot springs and a steep climbers' path to the basin is describing an approach that has not been available for twenty years. Parties wanting the north and west sides of the mountain now go in from the Suiattle instead.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams through the basin, dependable through the climbing season and thinning late
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit and a twelve-person limit still apply in theory. In practice the binding constraint is the road: the White Chuck road is closed from a little under four miles in all the way to its far end, and the trail beyond it is not maintained and not going to be. Treat any plan that relies on this basin as needing a specific check with the district first.
bivy.capacity: Open basin ground with room for several tents; historically the busiest camp on the mountain, and now one of the emptiest

bivy.name: Buck Creek Pass and the High Pass camps
bivy.notes: Buck Creek Pass at about 5,800 feet is the base for three peaks in this zone that have nothing to do with Glacier Peak's own approaches. Helmet Butte sits half a mile northeast of the pass and is the shortest objective from here. Buck Mountain rises directly south across the valley and is normally taken by leaving the Buck Creek trail lower down for the east ridge of Cleator and the Buck–Berge col, which also gives Mount Berge. From the pass a way trail continues north over Flower Dome to High Pass, which is both a fine high camp in its own right and the link over into the Napeequa, tying this side of the zone to Clark and Luahna. Getting here is around ten miles and three thousand feet of steady forest walking up Buck Creek from Trinity, so it is a full first day. It is a scenic and genuinely popular pass, which for a climbing party means arriving early enough to get a site. When the Chiwawa road is shut at Atkinson Flat the trailhead itself is roughly eleven road miles further on, which turns a two-day trip into a four-day one or a long bike shuttle.
bivy.water: A stream at the pass is the main supply and is reliable through the season; the higher camps toward High Pass run on snowmelt only and can be dry by September
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Trinity trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Fires are prohibited where posted and the meadow ground here is exactly the kind of place that gets posted — carry a stove. Camp on the bare established sites rather than in the heather. The road is the real permit question: the Chiwawa River road is closed from Atkinson Flat north to Trinity under a storm order running through the end of 2027, with no reopening estimate, and a large 2026 fire closure covered the same road on top of it.
bivy.capacity: Several established forested and meadow-edge sites at the pass itself, enough for a few parties, with rougher and more exposed ground higher toward Flower Dome and High Pass

bivy.name: Napeequa Valley floor near Louis Creek
bivy.notes: This is the way into the Napeequa for Luahna Peak, Chalangin Peak, the Napeequa side of Clark, and Tenpeak's east end. From the Little Giant trailhead the very first obstacle is fording the Chiwawa itself — the old bridge is gone and its remains are in the brush by the water, so the crossing is a wade and its depth decides the trip. The trail then climbs, drops a couple of hundred feet through the Little Giant Creek drainage and switchbacks up open meadow to Little Giant Pass at about 6,400 feet, roughly four and a half miles in, with Clark Mountain filling the view on the far side. Dropping into the Napeequa costs about two thousand feet, and from the valley floor the standard progression is two miles up-valley to Louis Creek and then a crossing of the Napeequa before climbing out toward Butterfly Butte. This valley camp is what a party uses on the way in when the day runs out at the bottom of the descent, or on the way out with the pass still to reclimb. Crossing the Napeequa is a real decision rather than a formality: it is glacier-fed, it runs high through early summer and it peaks in the afternoon, so cross in the morning and be willing to walk the bank looking for something better.
bivy.water: The Napeequa runs the length of the valley and is heavy with glacial silt off Clark and Luahna, so it needs settling as well as filtering; Louis Creek and the side streams run clearer
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Little Giant trailhead, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove rather than fire in the meadow. Both closures that matter land on this approach: the Chiwawa River road is shut above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year storm order, and the 2026 fire closure named the Little Giant trail itself along with the Napeequa trails and the roads either side, running from mid-August to the end of October.
bivy.capacity: Informal ground on the valley flats and in the timber edge — no developed sites, room for a couple of parties, and rarely anybody else there

bivy.name: Butterfly Butte and the Pilz Glacier basin camps
bivy.notes: This is the climbing camp for Luahna Peak and Chalangin Peak and the Napeequa-side base for Clark Mountain, roughly eleven hundred feet above the Napeequa floor after the river crossing near Louis Creek. The benches around Butterfly Butte at about 5,850 feet are the comfortable choice and look straight across at Clark; a broad basin below the Pilz Glacier headwall around 6,200 feet is the higher option and shortens summit day meaningfully. Parties pushing for a very early start use bivouac ground higher again on the northeast ridge, at roughly 6,800 and 7,200 feet, where there is no water and no shelter. Luahna is reached over the Pilz Glacier, so an ice axe, crampons and glacier gear belong on any list here. Chalangin sits half a mile northwest of Luahna and is more often taken by its own north side, bypassing the glacier, than by traversing the connecting ridge from Luahna — the traverse is long and the direct approach is the better plan. These are lightly visited summits and the register entries are years apart, so assume no boot track, no other party and no help.
bivy.water: A stream serves the benches around 5,850 to 6,200 feet and is the practical water for this camp; there is a pond at about 6,500 feet below the glacier, and above that it is snowmelt or nothing
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at the Little Giant trailhead. No fires this high — carry a stove. Camp on bare ground and rock rather than the heather benches. Subject to the same Chiwawa road closure and 2026 fire closure as the valley below it.
bivy.capacity: Small flat clearings on the benches around the butte for one or two parties, and higher up a broad basin under the glacier headwall with room for several; everything above is genuine bivouac ground rather than campsites

bivy.name: Boulder Pass and Thunder Basin, White River
bivy.notes: This is the standard base for Clark Mountain and the reason Clark is a White River peak rather than a Little Giant one. From the trailhead at about 2,300 feet the White River trail runs flat for four miles, then the Boulder Creek trail turns east and climbs for another seven, crossing Boulder Creek at around 4,000 feet — a wade or a log, and high water there turns parties round early in the season. Good camps exist in a large open basin at about 4,900 feet and again just below the pass around 6,000 feet, with the pass itself at about 6,200 feet holding dry ground even when there is snow about. From the pass the Walrus Glacier route traverses the basin east of the ridge point, crosses the northeast ridge around 6,700 feet and gains the glacier for the east side of the mountain; the whole thing runs to about twenty-five miles round trip and six and a half thousand feet of gain. Tenpeak Mountain is served from the same trailhead by a different drainage — six miles up the White River, then an old unmaintained sheep path toward Thunder Creek and Thunder Basin, with dense slide alder between roughly 4,200 and 5,000 feet that is the hardest part of the day. Tenpeak is a technical summit with a north couloir and a milder-looking southeast face, it sees very few ascents, and most parties want a third day to climb it properly from a basin camp rather than pushing it in one.

bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the White River trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove only up here. The White River road was inside the 2026 fire closure that ran from mid-August to the end of October along with the Chiwawa side, so this approach and the Little Giant one were shut at the same time by the same order — do not assume that losing one leaves the other.
bivy.capacity: Open ground at the pass with plenty of dry spots for several tents, a good basin camp about a mile below it, and separate rough ground over in Thunder Basin for one or two parties

bivy.name: Mackinaw Shelter camp, North Fork Sauk
bivy.notes: This is the first night for a Glacier Peak climb by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, which is the route most parties use now that the western approaches have gone. It sits about five flat miles up the North Fork Sauk trail through genuinely large old-growth, and the walk in is easy enough that a party arriving late in the day can still reach it. The shelter the camp is named for collapsed years ago and there is no roof here — treat the name as a map label rather than a promise. Camping here rather than pushing on matters because the next three miles gain three thousand feet in relentless switchbacks with no reliable water on them, so this is the place to drink, fill everything you carry, and start that climb cool. Coming out, most parties pass straight through. Access is the problem rather than the camp: the December 2025 storms damaged roads and trails across this side of the wilderness and reaching the North Fork Sauk trailhead at all should be confirmed before the drive, not assumed.
bivy.water: Excellent and year-round — the North Fork Sauk runs right past the camp, and this is the last dependable water before White Pass
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in and deposited at the trailhead box. Party size is capped at twelve, counting people and stock together. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at the road end. Fires are not banned outright at this elevation but summer forest-wide restrictions routinely prohibit all open flame from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites in the trees on a river bench, comfortably two or three parties, and the only organised camping in the valley bottom

bivy.name: White Pass and the Foam Creek benches under White Mountain
bivy.notes: White Pass at about 5,900 feet is the second night for a Glacier Peak climb, or the first if a strong party pushes the whole eight and a half miles and three thousand feet from the road in one go. It is the point where the North Fork Sauk trail meets the long-distance crest trail and where the climbing approach turns east. From here a boot path runs east-northeast under the southeast side of White Mountain for a bit over a mile toward a high shoulder, then the Foam Creek path traverses on toward an eastern col at around 6,600 feet for the first view of the mountain. Parties who want to break the approach differently camp somewhere along that traverse rather than at the pass itself, which trades a sheltered established site for wind and a shorter summit day. It is exposed ground once you leave the pass, with nothing to hide behind in a thunderstorm, and the traverse is genuinely confusing in fog.
bivy.water: A small spring and snowmelt at the pass, dependable early but often down to a trickle by late season; the benches toward Foam Creek hold snowmelt into midsummer and then dry out
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person party limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Camp on the existing bare sites — this is fragile subalpine meadow that recovers slowly and is heavily used. Carry a stove; open flame is inappropriate here and is usually prohibited outright under summer restrictions.
bivy.capacity: Several established sites just south of the pass, plus scattered ground on the benches east of it; a popular crossroads with a long-distance trail running through it, so expect other parties in July and August

bivy.name: White Pass and the Foam Creek benches under White Mountain
bivy.notes: White Pass at about 5,900 feet is the second night for a Glacier Peak climb, or the first if a strong party pushes the whole eight and a half miles and three thousand feet from the road in one go. It is the point where the North Fork Sauk trail meets the long-distance crest trail and where the climbing approach turns east. From here a boot path runs east-northeast under the southeast side of White Mountain for a bit over a mile toward a high shoulder, then the Foam Creek path traverses on toward an eastern col at around 6,600 feet for the first view of the mountain. Parties who want to break the approach differently camp somewhere along that traverse rather than at the pass itself, which trades a sheltered established site for wind and a shorter summit day. It is exposed ground once you leave the pass, with nothing to hide behind in a thunderstorm, and the traverse is genuinely confusing in fog.
bivy.water: A small spring and snowmelt at the pass, dependable early but often down to a trickle by late season; the benches toward Foam Creek hold snowmelt into midsummer and then dry out
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person party limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Camp on the existing bare sites — this is fragile subalpine meadow that recovers slowly and is heavily used. Carry a stove; open flame is inappropriate here and is usually prohibited outright under summer restrictions.
bivy.capacity: Several established sites just south of the pass, plus scattered ground on the benches east of it; a popular crossroads with a long-distance trail running through it, so expect other parties in July and August

bivy.name: Glacier Gap
bivy.notes: This is the high camp for Glacier Peak by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, and the single most-used climbing camp on the mountain. It sits at about 7,300 feet at the head of the basin, reached by crossing what is left of the White Chuck Glacier northeast from the White Pass area — and what is left is the point, because that glacier has retreated faster than almost anything else in the range and the crossing is now largely bare rock, pumice and meltwater ponds rather than ice. From camp the route works up the ridge to about 8,400 feet, traverses onto the upper Suiattle Glacier, gains the upper Cool Glacier around 9,200 feet and climbs it westward to regain the ridge for the summit. Summit day from here runs long by any measure and thirteen hours camp to camp is normal rather than slow. Being a gap it funnels wind, so build or use the rock walls. Most parties take three days from the North Fork Sauk road and a fourth is worth having for weather.
bivy.water: Meltwater streams off the surrounding snowfields, running through most of the climbing season but silty; late in a hot summer it can be reduced to a drip from the base of a snow patch, so scout it on arrival rather than at dinner time
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. No fires — this is bare rock, pumice and alpine ground above treeline with no wood and nothing that recovers. Twelve-person party limit. Human waste needs carrying out or burying properly well away from the meltwater, which everybody camped here is drinking.
bivy.capacity: A large basin with many bivouac sites and rock-walled platforms — it takes a lot of parties without feeling crowded, and there is always room to build another windbreak

bivy.name: Kennedy Ridge and the Glacier Creek camps, Suiattle side
bivy.notes: This is the base for Glacier Peak's Kennedy Glacier and for the Frostbite Ridge line above it, and since the White Chuck approach died it is the only practical way at the mountain's north and west sides. The walk in is long even when the road is open — the Suiattle River trail runs about seven miles to the river bridge and the crest trail then carries you south toward Kennedy Ridge, so this is a full day before the climbing camp is even in sight. Kennedy Creek has no bridge and will not get one; the standard tactic is to camp short of it and cross in the morning when the flow is at its lowest, using whatever logs are currently in place rather than wading the main channel. Above the forest the route climbs the ridge and the glacier toward the saddle between the Kennedy and Vista glaciers at around 8,000 feet, where bivouac sites exist for parties willing to sleep on snow and rock with no shelter and no clean water. With the road washed out the trailhead is still reachable on foot or by bike from the closure point, which adds roughly nine miles each way to an approach that was already the longest on the mountain.
bivy.water: Glacier Creek and Kennedy Creek are both right there and both silty with glacial flour — let it settle or filter accordingly. Higher on the ridge water disappears entirely by late season and has to be carried or melted.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Suiattle road end. Stove only above the forest. Check the road order before driving: the Suiattle River road washed out about four and a half miles in during the December 2025 storms, temporary bridge work was scheduled across the middle of the 2026 season, and the campgrounds and trailheads up that road were shut for the season while it stood.
bivy.capacity: Forested sites in ones and twos scattered along the crest trail near the creek crossings, plus rougher bivouac ground higher on the ridge; nothing organised, and no single site takes a large party

bivy.name: Boulder Basin above Sitkum Creek — and the White Chuck situation
bivy.notes: Boulder Basin sits somewhere around 5,500 to 6,000 feet on a rib south of Sitkum Creek and is the historic high camp for the Sitkum Glacier, once the shortest and most popular route up Glacier Peak. The approach that made it popular no longer exists, and the story is worth getting right rather than repeating old published mileage. In October 2003 a storm put a record flood down the White Chuck, a debris flow off the mountain buried Kennedy Hot Springs under about five feet of material, and the river rebuilt its own valley floor. The hot springs are gone — not damaged, gone, and not being rebuilt. By 2006 less than a third of the White Chuck River trail survived and there are no plans to repair it. The road reopened partway in 2011 to a point near the old trailhead area, which for a while allowed a long road walk and a rough approach up what remained, but it is closed again from under four miles in and the surviving trail is a treacherous bushwhack rather than a route. Anything you read describing five and a half easy miles to the hot springs and a steep climbers' path to the basin is describing an approach that has not been available for twenty years. Parties wanting the north and west sides of the mountain now go in from the Suiattle instead.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams through the basin, dependable through the climbing season and thinning late
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit and a twelve-person limit still apply in theory. In practice the binding constraint is the road: the White Chuck road is closed from a little under four miles in all the way to its far end, and the trail beyond it is not maintained and not going to be. Treat any plan that relies on this basin as needing a specific check with the district first.
bivy.capacity: Open basin ground with room for several tents; historically the busiest camp on the mountain, and now one of the emptiest

bivy.name: Buck Creek Pass and the High Pass camps
bivy.notes: Buck Creek Pass at about 5,800 feet is the base for three peaks in this zone that have nothing to do with Glacier Peak's own approaches. Helmet Butte sits half a mile northeast of the pass and is the shortest objective from here. Buck Mountain rises directly south across the valley and is normally taken by leaving the Buck Creek trail lower down for the east ridge of Cleator and the Buck–Berge col, which also gives Mount Berge. From the pass a way trail continues north over Flower Dome to High Pass, which is both a fine high camp in its own right and the link over into the Napeequa, tying this side of the zone to Clark and Luahna. Getting here is around ten miles and three thousand feet of steady forest walking up Buck Creek from Trinity, so it is a full first day. It is a scenic and genuinely popular pass, which for a climbing party means arriving early enough to get a site. When the Chiwawa road is shut at Atkinson Flat the trailhead itself is roughly eleven road miles further on, which turns a two-day trip into a four-day one or a long bike shuttle.
bivy.water: A stream at the pass is the main supply and is reliable through the season; the higher camps toward High Pass run on snowmelt only and can be dry by September
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Trinity trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Fires are prohibited where posted and the meadow ground here is exactly the kind of place that gets posted — carry a stove. Camp on the bare established sites rather than in the heather. The road is the real permit question: the Chiwawa River road is closed from Atkinson Flat north to Trinity under a storm order running through the end of 2027, with no reopening estimate, and a large 2026 fire closure covered the same road on top of it.
bivy.capacity: Several established forested and meadow-edge sites at the pass itself, enough for a few parties, with rougher and more exposed ground higher toward Flower Dome and High Pass

bivy.name: Napeequa Valley floor near Louis Creek
bivy.notes: This is the way into the Napeequa for Luahna Peak, Chalangin Peak, the Napeequa side of Clark, and Tenpeak's east end. From the Little Giant trailhead the very first obstacle is fording the Chiwawa itself — the old bridge is gone and its remains are in the brush by the water, so the crossing is a wade and its depth decides the trip. The trail then climbs, drops a couple of hundred feet through the Little Giant Creek drainage and switchbacks up open meadow to Little Giant Pass at about 6,400 feet, roughly four and a half miles in, with Clark Mountain filling the view on the far side. Dropping into the Napeequa costs about two thousand feet, and from the valley floor the standard progression is two miles up-valley to Louis Creek and then a crossing of the Napeequa before climbing out toward Butterfly Butte. This valley camp is what a party uses on the way in when the day runs out at the bottom of the descent, or on the way out with the pass still to reclimb. Crossing the Napeequa is a real decision rather than a formality: it is glacier-fed, it runs high through early summer and it peaks in the afternoon, so cross in the morning and be willing to walk the bank looking for something better.
bivy.water: The Napeequa runs the length of the valley and is heavy with glacial silt off Clark and Luahna, so it needs settling as well as filtering; Louis Creek and the side streams run clearer
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Little Giant trailhead, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove rather than fire in the meadow. Both closures that matter land on this approach: the Chiwawa River road is shut above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year storm order, and the 2026 fire closure named the Little Giant trail itself along with the Napeequa trails and the roads either side, running from mid-August to the end of October.
bivy.capacity: Informal ground on the valley flats and in the timber edge — no developed sites, room for a couple of parties, and rarely anybody else there

bivy.name: Butterfly Butte and the Pilz Glacier basin camps
bivy.notes: This is the climbing camp for Luahna Peak and Chalangin Peak and the Napeequa-side base for Clark Mountain, roughly eleven hundred feet above the Napeequa floor after the river crossing near Louis Creek. The benches around Butterfly Butte at about 5,850 feet are the comfortable choice and look straight across at Clark; a broad basin below the Pilz Glacier headwall around 6,200 feet is the higher option and shortens summit day meaningfully. Parties pushing for a very early start use bivouac ground higher again on the northeast ridge, at roughly 6,800 and 7,200 feet, where there is no water and no shelter. Luahna is reached over the Pilz Glacier, so an ice axe, crampons and glacier gear belong on any list here. Chalangin sits half a mile northwest of Luahna and is more often taken by its own north side, bypassing the glacier, than by traversing the connecting ridge from Luahna — the traverse is long and the direct approach is the better plan. These are lightly visited summits and the register entries are years apart, so assume no boot track, no other party and no help.
bivy.water: A stream serves the benches around 5,850 to 6,200 feet and is the practical water for this camp; there is a pond at about 6,500 feet below the glacier, and above that it is snowmelt or nothing
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at the Little Giant trailhead. No fires this high — carry a stove. Camp on bare ground and rock rather than the heather benches. Subject to the same Chiwawa road closure and 2026 fire closure as the valley below it.
bivy.capacity: Small flat clearings on the benches around the butte for one or two parties, and higher up a broad basin under the glacier headwall with room for several; everything above is genuine bivouac ground rather than campsites

bivy.name: Boulder Pass and Thunder Basin, White River
bivy.notes: This is the standard base for Clark Mountain and the reason Clark is a White River peak rather than a Little Giant one. From the trailhead at about 2,300 feet the White River trail runs flat for four miles, then the Boulder Creek trail turns east and climbs for another seven, crossing Boulder Creek at around 4,000 feet — a wade or a log, and high water there turns parties round early in the season. Good camps exist in a large open basin at about 4,900 feet and again just below the pass around 6,000 feet, with the pass itself at about 6,200 feet holding dry ground even when there is snow about. From the pass the Walrus Glacier route traverses the basin east of the ridge point, crosses the northeast ridge around 6,700 feet and gains the glacier for the east side of the mountain; the whole thing runs to about twenty-five miles round trip and six and a half thousand feet of gain. Tenpeak Mountain is served from the same trailhead by a different drainage — six miles up the White River, then an old unmaintained sheep path toward Thunder Creek and Thunder Basin, with dense slide alder between roughly 4,200 and 5,000 feet that is the hardest part of the day. Tenpeak is a technical summit with a north couloir and a milder-looking southeast face, it sees very few ascents, and most parties want a third day to climb it properly from a basin camp rather than pushing it in one.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and streams through the basin below the pass and at the pass itself well into the season; Thunder Basin runs on creeks that are dependable in summer. The lower Boulder Creek crossing is the water hazard rather than the water supply.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the White River trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove only up here. The White River road was inside the 2026 fire closure that ran from mid-August to the end of October along with the Chiwawa side, so this approach and the Little Giant one were shut at the same time by the same order — do not assume that losing one leaves the other.
bivy.capacity: Open ground at the pass with plenty of dry spots for several tents, a good basin camp about a mile below it, and separate rough ground over in Thunder Basin for one or two parties

bivy.name: Kool-Aid Lake
bivy.notes: The first camp on the traverse coming from Cascade Pass, reached by climbing to Cache Col and dropping a short but awkward distance southwest to the tarn. It is where the permit regime changes, which is the practical reason to know it exists even if you are only passing through. Published elevations vary by a couple of hundred feet, with figures around 6,300 the most common and one outlier several hundred feet higher, so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. From here the day ahead crosses the Red Ledge and the Middle Cascade Glacier toward Old Guard Peak and Sentinel, and there are further ridge bivouacs at around 6,300 ft just past the Red Ledge if the lake is full or the hour is late. Early season this is a snow camp with easy water everywhere; late season it is bare heather and rock and the tarn is the only source.
bivy.water: The tarn itself plus snowmelt runnels feeding it. Reliable in July and through most of August, but it is a shallow pool with a small catchment and it can drop to a warm, silty puddle by September in a light snow year. Cache Col just above has no water at all, so parties camping high on the shoulder have to carry from here or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Once you cross Cache Col you are out of North Cascades National Park and into Glacier Peak Wilderness, so no park permit covers this camp. Sign the free self-issue wilderness register instead. If you spend a night on the park side, including at Cascade Pass or on the shoulder below the Cache Glacier, that night does need an NPS wilderness permit collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Campfires have no place at this elevation; carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small heather and gravel platforms around a tiny tarn, comfortable for two or three parties and crowded beyond that. No facilities, no toilet, nothing built.

bivy.name: Yang Yang Lakes
bivy.notes: The second camp for most north-to-south parties, sitting in a shallow bowl below Le Conte Mountain after the drop off the Middle Cascade Glacier. It is the natural base for Old Guard Peak, whose summit is reached from the Le Conte Glacier above by a class 2 to 3 snow couloir and short scramble on the west side, or by two to three pitches of easy to moderate fifth class on the east ridge. Sentinel Peak is the other objective from here and the two are usually taken together. The descent into and climb out of this basin is steep on both sides, so parties running late often push instead to Le Conte Pass above and accept the thinner water. Snow lingers in the bowl well into July, which is when the camping is easiest and the heather is protected.
bivy.water: Two lakes, which makes this the most dependable water on the northern half of the traverse. Nothing above it is reliable: the ridge camps toward Formidable and the ground up at Le Conte Pass are snowmelt-only late in the season, though the pass usually holds tarns into midsummer.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit at the trailhead register. Camp at least 100 feet back from the lakeshores. No campfires; the ground here is thin alpine heather that does not recover.
bivy.capacity: Several unimproved sites in the heather between the two small lakes, enough for two or three parties. No toilet and no established platforms.

bivy.name: White Rock Lakes
bivy.notes: The third camp and the one most parties remember, reached from Yang Yang across the Le Conte Glacier and the Le Conte-Sentinel col, then down a long traverse under Sentinel and Old Guard. It looks straight across at Dome Peak and the Dana Glacier, which is the day that follows. Sinister Peak is not climbed from here directly, but this is the last camp with easy water before the ground gets serious: the Chickamin and Dome glaciers are the way to Sinister and to the Gunsight Range, and everything from here east is snow, ice and rock with no running water. It is a windy basin and the good sites are the sheltered ones near the outlet. Snow can cover the lakes into early July, which some parties prefer because it makes the camping flat and the water trivially available.
bivy.water: The lakes, fed by the snowfields and the Le Conte and Dana ice above them. Normally good all season, though the outlet stream can be reduced to a trickle late in a dry summer and the smaller pools go stagnant.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Keep camps 100 feet from the water. Stoves only.
bivy.capacity: Open benches near the outlet of the larger lake and scattered spots around the basin, wind-exposed but roomy enough for several parties. Unimproved, no toilet.

bivy.name: Itswoot Ridge
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the southern peaks and the camp most parties coming in from Downey Creek actually use. Camps are quoted anywhere between roughly 5,900 and 6,400 ft depending on which bench you take, so the number here describes the lower, wetter end of the ridge rather than a single spot. From the benches it is moderate snow of about thirty degrees, or a scree-and-heather line on the left in late season, up to Spire Col at 7,760 ft, and from the col a short descending traverse onto the upper Dana Glacier puts you under the southeast and southwest faces of Spire Point. Dome Peak is the other objective, reached over the Dana Glacier and the Dome Glacier above. Reaching this ridge from the car is a full day with a heavy pack, so plan on arriving late and going nowhere else that evening.
bivy.water: Small running creeks below the lower benches, fed by snowfields on the north side of the ridge, and generally dependable through the normal climbing season. The higher benches toward the col dry out first, so drop back down for water rather than assuming it is there.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.
bivy.capacity: A string of flat heather benches along the ridge rather than one site, so several parties can spread out without crowding each other. No toilet, no built platforms.

bivy.name: Cub Lake
bivy.notes: Roughly 12 miles and about 3,900 ft of gain from the Downey Creek trailhead, reached by a steep switchbacking descent off the Bachelor Creek meadows and a walk around the north shore. Parties report anywhere from six hours to eleven getting here, which is a fair measure of how much the brush and the pack weight vary. It is the south-end hub: from the lake the trail climbs to Itswoot Ridge for Spire Point and Dome Peak, and everything on the Chickamin side including Sinister Peak and the Gunsight summits starts from the same ground. Because it is the established camp it also takes the impact, and there is a reasonable argument for camping on the ridge above instead where the ground is less worn, at the cost of carrying water. Coming out, this is where the traverse ends and the brush begins.
bivy.water: The lake, reliable all season. This is the last certain water for anyone heading up onto the ridge and glaciers, and the first on the way out.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Downey Creek trailhead. Camp 100 feet back from the shore. Practically speaking no fires, and the site is heavily enough used that the surrounding wood is already gone.
bivy.capacity: A well established camp at the lake with room for a few parties, plus meadow sites nearby. It is the most used ground in the southern half of the zone and it shows.

bivy.name: Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
bivy.notes: This exists because of the brush, and the brush is the single most important thing to understand about the south end. From the Downey Creek trailhead at 1,440 ft the Downey Creek trail runs about six easy forested miles to Sixmile Camp; after that the abandoned Bachelor Creek trail deteriorates badly. The first two miles are tolerable, then it crosses to the south side and turns into slide alder and avalanche deadfall, with reports of sixty or more trees over the trail and long sections where following it is closer to bushwhacking than hiking. Parties routinely take nine to eleven hours from the car to Cub Lake and a slow group with heavy packs can lose the trail entirely. Splitting the approach with a night around the 4,500 ft meadows near the head of the creek is the honest answer for anyone who is not fast, and it is why some parties choose to enter from Cascade Pass and exit here rather than the other way round, so the brush is done downhill and with lighter packs. There is a north-side line through open forest paralleling the creek that some report as better than the trail itself. Everything about this approach is currently harder than the above suggests: the Suiattle River Road is closed to vehicles at about milepost 4 after flood damage, under an order running to the start of 2028 unless lifted sooner, which leaves roughly sixteen extra road miles each way to a trailhead at mile 20. The road also spent about a decade closed before reopening in 2014, so a long closure here is the normal state of affairs rather than a surprise. Confirm the road before committing to this end.
bivy.water: Bachelor Creek runs the whole way and is never the problem. The creek crossing itself can be, in high water or early season.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at Downey Creek. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but the ground is wet forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
bivy.capacity: Rough forest sites and a meadow flat near the head of the creek, party-sized only. Nothing established, no toilet.

bivy.name: Spire Col bivouac
bivy.notes: The col at 7,760 ft between Itswoot Ridge and the upper Dana Glacier, and the highest useful bivouac for Spire Point. Taking it saves an hour or more off summit morning on the Southwest Face and puts you above the section of snow that softens in the afternoon. It is fully exposed, cold, and windy, which is the trade. Parties heading on to Dome Peak sometimes use it too, though the Dome Glacier camps further east are better placed for that. Treat this as a fair-weather option: there is no shelter, and retreating from here in bad weather means downclimbing snow you came up in daylight.
bivy.water: None. Melt snow, or carry from the creeks below Itswoot Ridge. In late season the snow near the col can be gone entirely and then there is nothing at all.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere on this side of the zone.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on the col itself, with further spots scattered along the ridge below it. Rock and snow, nothing flat and nothing built.

bivy.name: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
bivy.notes: These are the camps that put the eastern peaks in range, and they are the reason parties carry a full glacier kit past Itswoot Ridge. The col between the Dana and Dome glaciers holds a couple of rock rings around 7,470 ft, and further east the Dome-Chickamin col is a genuine high camp with figures around 8,000 ft and above quoted for it. From that eastern col the Chickamin Glacier is the highway to Sinister Peak, whose North Face and Southwest Route are both reached across it, and on to the three Gunsight Range summits beyond, which are granite spires ringed by the Chickamin and Blue glaciers and among the most remote objectives in the state. Parties on the Gunsight peaks routinely cross the Chickamin twice in a day from a camp on this ground. Season is short: the glaciers are best covered from July into August, later brings open crevasses and bare ice, and there is no water, no shelter and no quick way down from any of it.
bivy.water: None running. Every drop is melted snow, and on bare ice years even that takes hunting for. Carry what you can from Cub Lake or the Itswoot Ridge creeks and plan the fuel for melting.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek register. Camp on snow, rock or ice. Pack out human waste, which matters more here than anywhere else in the zone because the meltwater below runs straight into the glacier-fed creeks.
bivy.capacity: Rock rings and cleared platforms for one or two parties at a time. At the Dome-Chickamin col there is a flat, large, windy option on the west side and a smaller, harder, calmer one on the east. Nothing else, and no toilet.

bivy.name: Kool-Aid Lake
bivy.notes: The first camp on the traverse coming from Cascade Pass, reached by climbing to Cache Col and dropping a short but awkward distance southwest to the tarn. It is where the permit regime changes, which is the practical reason to know it exists even if you are only passing through. Published elevations vary by a couple of hundred feet, with figures around 6,300 the most common and one outlier several hundred feet higher, so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. From here the day ahead crosses the Red Ledge and the Middle Cascade Glacier toward Old Guard Peak and Sentinel, and there are further ridge bivouacs at around 6,300 ft just past the Red Ledge if the lake is full or the hour is late. Early season this is a snow camp with easy water everywhere; late season it is bare heather and rock and the tarn is the only source.
bivy.water: The tarn itself plus snowmelt runnels feeding it. Reliable in July and through most of August, but it is a shallow pool with a small catchment and it can drop to a warm, silty puddle by September in a light snow year. Cache Col just above has no water at all, so parties camping high on the shoulder have to carry from here or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Once you cross Cache Col you are out of North Cascades National Park and into Glacier Peak Wilderness, so no park permit covers this camp. Sign the free self-issue wilderness register instead. If you spend a night on the park side, including at Cascade Pass or on the shoulder below the Cache Glacier, that night does need an NPS wilderness permit collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Campfires have no place at this elevation; carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small heather and gravel platforms around a tiny tarn, comfortable for two or three parties and crowded beyond that. No facilities, no toilet, nothing built.

bivy.name: Yang Yang Lakes
bivy.notes: The second camp for most north-to-south parties, sitting in a shallow bowl below Le Conte Mountain after the drop off the Middle Cascade Glacier. It is the natural base for Old Guard Peak, whose summit is reached from the Le Conte Glacier above by a class 2 to 3 snow couloir and short scramble on the west side, or by two to three pitches of easy to moderate fifth class on the east ridge. Sentinel Peak is the other objective from here and the two are usually taken together. The descent into and climb out of this basin is steep on both sides, so parties running late often push instead to Le Conte Pass above and accept the thinner water. Snow lingers in the bowl well into July, which is when the camping is easiest and the heather is protected.
bivy.water: Two lakes, which makes this the most dependable water on the northern half of the traverse. Nothing above it is reliable: the ridge camps toward Formidable and the ground up at Le Conte Pass are snowmelt-only late in the season, though the pass usually holds tarns into midsummer.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit at the trailhead register. Camp at least 100 feet back from the lakeshores. No campfires; the ground here is thin alpine heather that does not recover.
bivy.capacity: Several unimproved sites in the heather between the two small lakes, enough for two or three parties. No toilet and no established platforms.

bivy.name: White Rock Lakes
bivy.notes: The third camp and the one most parties remember, reached from Yang Yang across the Le Conte Glacier and the Le Conte-Sentinel col, then down a long traverse under Sentinel and Old Guard. It looks straight across at Dome Peak and the Dana Glacier, which is the day that follows. Sinister Peak is not climbed from here directly, but this is the last camp with easy water before the ground gets serious: the Chickamin and Dome glaciers are the way to Sinister and to the Gunsight Range, and everything from here east is snow, ice and rock with no running water. It is a windy basin and the good sites are the sheltered ones near the outlet. bivy.name: Kool-Aid Lake

These are the highest useful sleeping spots on this part of the crest and the direct bases for Sentinel Peak and for Lizard Mountain, which stands just east of the col that carries the route across to the far side. accounts disagree on the elevations of both saddles by several hundred feet, with Lizard quoted anywhere from the high 6,000s to the mid 7,000s, so no numbers are recorded. A camp here is a fair-weather decision and nothing else: there is no shelter, no water, and the ground on both sides is glaciated, so retreating in cloud means downclimbing snow you only saw once in daylight. Most parties cross both in a day and sleep at a lake; the ones who stop are the ones who came to climb the peaks rather than pass them.
bivy.water: None running. Melt snow, or carry from the lakes below on whichever side you came from. In a late, thin season the snow at the saddles can be gone and then there is nothing at all.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or ice only. Pack out human waste, which matters here because the meltwater below feeds the lakes people are drinking from.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms and small rock benches at each of the two saddles, one party at a time at either. Nothing built, no toilet, nothing sheltered.

bivy.name: Crest bivouacs above the South Cascade and Chickamin glaciers
bivy.notes: SAY IT PLAINLY: THESE ARE NOT SITES, THEY ARE WHEREVER A PARTY GETS TO. Elephant Head is the southernmost peak, standing on the divide above the lakes at the south end of the crest with big cliffs dropping east into the head of the west fork of Agnes Creek, between the ice on either side. It gets a handful of ascents in a decade and there is no established camp for it, so parties climbing it either work out from the lake basin below or level a spot on the divide and accept a dry, exposed night. The same is true of anyone caught out on the South Cascade side by weather or by a slower day than planned. The season is short and matters more here than anywhere else: July into August has the glaciers covered and the bivouac snow usable, while September brings open crevasses, bare ice and no water at all. Anyone planning a night on this ground should carry the fuel to melt snow and treat the whole thing as an unplanned shelter that happens to be foreseeable.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and unreliable after midsummer. The last certain water on this stretch is the lakes below, and everything east of the divide is snow, ice and bare rock.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or ice, never on the heather benches. Pack out human waste. No fires; there is nothing to burn and nothing that would recover.
bivy.capacity: Whatever the party can level. Rock rings, gravel benches and snow platforms for one party at a time, scattered along the divide. No toilet and no established sites of any kind.

bivy.name: Cache Col and the Cache Glacier shoulder
bivy.notes: The col is the gateway to everything here. From the Cascade Pass trail a boot path climbs south along the arm and onto the mellow Cache Glacier, which is corniced at the col early in the season and can need a careful step through. Parties who leave the car in the afternoon and lose the light on the climb sometimes stop here rather than commit to the awkward descending traverse beyond it, and parties coming back north at the end of a trip do the same. It is a fair-weather choice only: it is a high, open saddle with no shelter and no water, and in cloud the ground on both sides is easy to lose. Treat the elevation as approximate, since published figures for the col vary by a couple of hundred feet.
bivy.water: None at the col itself. Early in the season there are melt runnels on the shoulder below it; by August there is usually nothing, and parties either carry up from the Cascade Pass side or melt snow. This is the single most common reason people push on down to the tarn below instead of stopping here.
bivy.permit: THIS IS THE LAST GROUND ON THE PARK SIDE, and the distinction decides which permit you need. A night at or above the col is inside North Cascades National Park and requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, with part of the inventory reservable in advance and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage applies. One step south of the col you are in Glacier Peak Wilderness and a free self-issue register slip is all that is needed. Do not assume the wilderness self-issue covers a night at the col.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms and a few rock benches on the shoulder below and at the col, room for one or two parties. Nothing built, no toilet, no windbreaks worth the name.

bivy.name: Spider-Formidable Col
bivy.notes: THE WORKING BASE CAMP FOR BOTH SPIDER MOUNTAIN AND MOUNT FORMIDABLE, and the reason to know about it is that a party climbing either peak stops here while a party walking the traverse does not. The twin notches of the col divide the two mountains, and it is reached by crossing the upper Middle Cascade Glacier almost due south from the Red Ledge. Spider Mountain is climbed from here by its south gully, stepping onto the buttress to the east and finishing along a corniced east ridge, about nineteen miles round trip from the Cascade Pass trailhead. Formidable is the other direction, and its south scramble is only class 3 but is long, loose, exposed and hard to route-find, with a fatality on record; the same ground is the only practical descent. Estimates of the col's height run from roughly 6,600 to 7,400 feet. The descent off the south side toward Yang Yang can be very steep snow and parties have resorted to a hand line anchored on buried pickets.
bivy.water: Water trickles off the slabs beside the col through most of the climbing season, which is unusual for ground this high and is the main reason the col gets used as a base rather than just crossed. It is meltwater, so it weakens through August and can stop entirely in a light snow year, and there is nothing else until the lakes well below on either side.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit from the register at whichever trailhead you started from. Camp on snow, rock or bare slab rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere south of Cache Col. Stoves only.
bivy.capacity: A small number of party-sized spots split between the west notch of the col and the ground above the east pass, on glacial slabs and snow. Two parties is comfortable, three is crowded, and there is no toilet.

bivy.name: Drop Creek high camp
bivy.notes: THIS IS THE OTHER WAY TO FORMIDABLE AND IT IS NOT THE TRAVERSE. It starts at the South Fork Cascade River trailhead, which is little more than a bend in the Cascade River Road around mile 17 to 18 near the Forest Service 1590 junction, well below the road end at Cascade Pass. The first mile is maintained, then the trail deteriorates into ups, downs and overgrown nettle sections; past the Middle Fork turnoff you cross Drop Creek on a log and turn up into its valley on a climbers' path. That path fades after a few hundred vertical feet, but the forest above about 4,000 feet is open and the bushwhacking is unusually easy for this part of the range, with one short slide alder thicket below 4,600 feet. The camp is the obvious flat ground at around 7,100 feet with water, and from it the ground steepens to class 3 with a permanent snowfield near 7,400 feet and one narrow chasm crossing that is worth protecting. The whole approach avoids glacier travel entirely, which is why it has become the late-season choice, and recent trail work has made it the most pleasant it has been in years. Reckon on roughly twenty-five miles and eight thousand feet for the round trip.
bivy.water: Running water beside the camp for most of the season, fed by the snowfield above, and a second reliable source lower down around 5,600 feet before the steep meadow climb. Late in a dry summer take the lower water seriously, because the high source is a snowfield that is shrinking.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness on Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead register. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is the usual requirement for the vehicle at Forest Service trailheads on this road, unlike the park trailhead at the end of it, so check before leaving the car. No fires at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: Open alpine benches with room for a party or two, on heather and rock. Unimproved, no toilet, no windbreaks.

bivy.name: South Fork Cascade River valley camps
bivy.notes: The fallback first night on the Drop Creek approach to Formidable, for a party that starts late or is not confident of reaching the high camp in one push. It exists because the valley section is slower than its mileage suggests once the maintained tread runs out, with overgrown stretches and repeated small gains and losses. Camping here costs you the high camp's position and its view, and it means carrying the whole climb the next day, so most parties push through; it is recorded because the alternative to knowing it is there is a headlamp bushwhack up Drop Creek. No elevation is given because no confident figure was found for the usual sites.
bivy.water: The South Fork and Drop Creek itself, running all season. Water is never the problem down here; the log crossing in high water can be.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at the Forest Service trailhead. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but it is damp valley forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
bivy.capacity: Rough forest sites along the valley trail and near the Drop Creek crossing, party-sized only. Nothing established.

bivy.name: Le Conte Pass
bivy.notes: The pass sits on the shoulder above the lakes in the basin below Le Conte Mountain, and it is the direct base for Le Conte itself, which is climbed by working up its east slope on talus and blocky rock by the line of least resistance rather than by any single defined route. It is also where parties running late stop instead of dropping into and re-climbing out of the steep basin below, which is the trade that decides most itineraries on this stretch: better position and worse water, against reliable water and a thousand feet of extra work. From the pass the next day crosses the Le Conte Glacier, which is the most broken ice on this part of the crest and has turned parties around outright, so this is a camp to leave early and roped. Published elevations for the pass vary, so treat the figure as approximate.
bivy.water: Small tarns at the pass hold water through midsummer and are the practical source, but they are snowmelt pools with tiny catchments and they can be gone or foul by September. Late in the season this is a dry camp and the lakes below are the honest answer.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Keep camps back from the tarns, camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than on the heather, and pack out human waste. Stoves only.
bivy.capacity: Heather and gravel benches around the pass and its tarns, enough for two or three parties spread out. Unimproved, no toilet.
