bivy.name: Neve Camp
bivy.notes: Under two miles from the Colonial Creek trailhead on flat valley trail, this is the camp that exists to absorb a late arrival rather than to stage a climb. Parties driving over from the west side after work can sleep here and still be at Junction by early afternoon the next day. It is deep forest with no views, and the bugs are heavy through midsummer. Nothing about it is alpine, which is exactly its function on a corridor where the climbing is fifteen or more miles in.
bivy.water: Thunder Creek runs beside the camp and is reliable all season.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required year round. Issued at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, or emailed in advance against a reservation. Roughly 60% of sites are reservable through recreation.gov (spring lottery, then a general on-sale in late April); the rest is held for walk-up and can only be claimed the day before or day of your start.
bivy.capacity: Small forested camp, reported at roughly five tent spots, spread out enough that parties are not on top of each other. Confirm the count and per-site party limit when the permit is issued.

bivy.name: Junction Camp
bivy.notes: About ten miles in, this is where the trail finally gives something back after a long forest walk, with the Boston Glacier visible through a gap in the trees. It is the natural first or second night for parties heading to Mount Logan, and the standard stopping point on the way back out from a high camp. The trail to Fisher Basin and Easy Pass leaves from here, so it also works as a hinge for loop itineraries. The climb up gains roughly a thousand feet in a bit over two miles and is the first real work of the approach.
bivy.water: Thunder Creek is the source and is dependable, but the camp sits on a bench well above it, so water means a descent and a climb back with full bottles. Arrive with enough to cook on if you get in late.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the rest of the corridor. Fire rings and a privy are present here, unlike the cross-country zones higher up — but confirm current fire restrictions on the permit rather than assuming the rings mean fires are legal.
bivy.capacity: Three designated sites, one tucked away and more private than the others. A separate stock camp sits nearby. The quota is small enough that a weekend party without a reservation should have a fallback in mind.

bivy.name: Skagit Queen Camp
bivy.notes: Roughly thirteen miles up the valley, reached after a steep mile of climbing through silver fir, and the last creekside camp before the trail commits to the headwaters. Remains of early twentieth-century mining work sit just beyond the camp. The bridge over Thunder Creek in this stretch was rebuilt in recent years, but high water in the side creeks earlier in the season is still worth asking about at the permit desk.
bivy.water: Directly on Thunder Creek, reliable through the season.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required. The quota applies to the specific camp and night, so an itinerary that slips a day needs the permit amended rather than ignored.
bivy.capacity: Small hiker camp, a handful of sites. Treat capacity as tight and reserve if your schedule cannot flex by a day.

bivy.name: Thunder Basin Hiker Camp
bivy.notes: The staging camp for Booker, Storm King and Buckner from the west, and for parties continuing over the pass toward Stehekin. It sits in meadows and small trees with roughly a thousand feet of climbing still to reach the pass, and it is reliably buggy in warm weather. Because the pass is closed to camping, groups wanting to be higher have to leave the designated system entirely and take a cross-country zone permit instead. Snow lingers in the basin and on the pass well into summer, and how long is the single most variable thing about timing a trip here.
bivy.water: Creek water at the camp, dependable through the normal climbing season. Sources higher toward the pass thin out as the snow goes.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required. CAMPING IS PROHIBITED AT PARK CREEK PASS ITSELF, so this is the last legal designated camp on the west approach. A portable food canister is recommended and black bears are active in the basin; canisters can be borrowed at the permit offices.
bivy.capacity: Small subalpine hiker camp near seventeen miles in; a separate stock camp sits about a mile lower and requires fording Thunder Creek. Sites are few, and this is the most contested camp in the corridor because everyone headed for the pass wants it.

bivy.name: Fremont Glacier moraine high camp
bivy.notes: Reached by leaving the trail in the flat sandy meadows a short distance north of Park Creek Pass and climbing several hundred feet into old moraine, this is the high camp for the Fremont Glacier side of Mount Logan and the only realistic way to get above the pass legally. The ground is flat, sandy and sheltered, which matters on a rib this exposed. Parties also report usable bivy ground higher, near where the climbers' route meets the glacier around eight thousand feet, though water up there is entirely a function of what snow is left. Which option is better is genuinely conditions-dependent and worth asking at the permit desk the morning you pick up.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and glacier runoff, and it is seasonal. Sources near the first stream crossings north of the pass are more dependable; higher moraine camps can go dry late in a hot summer, so carry capacity to melt or haul.
bivy.permit: Requires a CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE permit from Marblemount, not a designated-camp permit. Fires prohibited outright. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, never in meadows or within 100 ft of water. Zone camping legally begins a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail, and out of sight of both. Waste in a cathole, or carried out in a blue bag above treeline or on glaciers.
bivy.capacity: Cross-country zone camping rather than a designated site, so no fixed site count. Most zones cap a party at six. One permit covers the party.

bivy.name: Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail
bivy.notes: The eastern counterpart to Thunder Basin: the last practical night before crossing Park Creek Pass from the Stehekin side, and the staging point for Buckner and Booker approached from the east. The trail above climbs through hanging meadows to the pass with good views of Goode, Buckner and Booker on the way. Coming in from Stehekin turns a very long one-way walk into a shorter approach than the roughly nineteen miles from Colonial Creek, at the cost of a lake crossing and road transport. Which side is faster depends entirely on whether the shuttle is running to the upper valley that season.
bivy.water: Park Creek is immediately adjacent and reliable.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park proper. Permits for an approach started from Stehekin still come through the same park system. Plan around Lake Chelan boat and shuttle schedules, since a missed connection can put you a day off your permitted itinerary.
bivy.capacity: Creekside stock camp on the Park Creek trail. Small; the neighbouring Two Mile camp downvalley was reduced to a single site by past flooding, so do not count on it as overflow.

bivy.name: Twin Lakes Road upper section and the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead pullouts
bivy.notes: This is the road rather than a campsite, because on this approach the road is the variable that decides what the trip is. The first four and a half miles to the Tomyhoi Lake and Yellow Aster Butte trailhead are rough gravel that an ordinary car can manage with patience; the straight section below the switchbacks is the worst of it, with loose rock and deep potholes. The final two miles to Twin Lakes are narrow, unmaintained for passenger cars, short of pullouts, and genuinely want high clearance. Parties turned back at the lower lot are looking at an extra two miles and roughly 1,500 ft of road walking each way before the climb even starts, which turns a comfortable day on Winchester or a two-day Larrabee trip into something much longer, and is a good reason to plan on sleeping out. The road is snowbound well into the season most years and is often not drivable to the upper end until July. Call the ranger station before committing, and if you park low, camping in a pullout the night before is a common and reasonable way to save the morning.
bivy.water: Creeks cross the road in places but there is nothing reliable at the lot itself; carry water up from the valley or plan to filter higher
bivy.permit: A recreation pass must be displayed at the trailhead, and the state parks pass is not accepted here. Fill in the free self-issue wilderness permit at the register where one is provided. Dispersed roadside camping on national forest land outside the wilderness boundary is generally allowed, but never in a way that narrows the road or blocks a pullout.
bivy.capacity: A dozen or so vehicles in the trailhead lot, plus scattered pullouts along the road; it fills on summer weekends and there is nowhere to turn around if you keep going and change your mind

bivy.name: Twin Lakes basin road-end camp
bivy.notes: This is the base for everything on the north side of the zone. An alpine cirque at 5,200 ft with the two lakes, subalpine trees and meadow, vault toilets at both lakes, picnic tables at many sites, and no drinking water. Because you can drive to it in a capable vehicle it is the only place in the zone where a heavy pack costs you nothing, so most parties on Winchester, Mount Larrabee and American Border Peak sleep here and start from the isthmus between the lakes. The Winchester Mountain trail and the High Pass trail both begin there. It does not melt out completely until July in most years, and late-season parties should expect a busy, social camp rather than a quiet one. Everything the lakes hold is heavily used; pick an established site rather than making a new one in the meadow.
bivy.water: The two lakes, right at camp. No treated water; filter or boil.
bivy.permit: Recreation pass or the posted per-vehicle day-use fee for the trailhead. Free self-issue wilderness permit at the register for anyone continuing onto the trails. The lakes basin at the road end sits outside the wilderness and several sites have metal fire rings, but everything above and beyond is wilderness where fires are prohibited outright, and county or forest-wide burn bans routinely close the road-end rings as well. Party size in the wilderness is capped at twelve. Hang or canister your food.
bivy.capacity: Roughly ten to fifteen informal sites spread around the two lakes; first come, first served, and competitive on any decent summer weekend

bivy.name: Winchester Mountain Lookout
bivy.notes: A 1935 lookout on the 6,521 ft summit, kept standing by volunteers from a local hiking club rather than by the agency, and genuinely open for anyone to sleep in on a first-come basis. It is 1.7 miles and about 1,300 ft above the Twin Lakes trailhead, which makes it one of the easiest real summits in the range to reach and a fine advance camp for a light party heading on to Mount Larrabee, though it sits off the direct High Pass line and most climbers heading for American Border Peak carry on past the junction rather than up. Treat the building as borrowed. It survives on people sweeping it out, closing the shutters properly, packing out their rubbish and leaving it drier than they found it; a run of poor behaviour is exactly why the winter season was closed. Always carry a tent or bivy, because it may well be occupied when you arrive and there is only room for two on the bunks. There are patches of ground outside the building flat enough to sleep on. The trail crosses steep, exposed snow slopes that linger into July and sometimes August, and an ice axe is the right call before the traverse is bare.
bivy.water: None at the summit. Carry everything up from Twin Lakes, or melt snow early in the season.
bivy.permit: Free, no reservations, no fee, and no way to book it. Locked from November through May, reopening when conditions allow, and off limits as a shelter in winter beyond stepping inside with the shutters left as they are. Wilderness rules apply on the trail and at the summit: no fires at all, party size twelve, no toilet, so pack out everything including human waste.
bivy.capacity: Two bunks inside and floor space for a couple more at a squeeze; twelve is the legal party limit but the building comfortably holds far fewer

bivy.name: High Pass camp
bivy.notes: High Pass is reached from the Twin Lakes isthmus by way of the Winchester junction, a traverse under an avalanche chute, then Low Pass and a short climb, roughly two and a half miles with a little over a thousand feet of gain. It is directly on the line for both of the big objectives here: the basin north of the pass leads to the south face of Mount Larrabee and its standard south ridge scramble, and the same ground continues around Larrabee's west slope towards American Border Peak. Camping at the pass buys you height and a very short morning, and costs you water and shelter, since it is a windy notch with almost nothing flat. The snow slopes between Twin Lakes and the pass are the crux of the approach for much of the season and can stay steep and firm into August. Parties who want to sleep dry and drink freely usually pass over the top and drop into the mine basin instead.
bivy.water: Nothing running. Snow patches into midsummer are the only source, so most parties carry water from Twin Lakes or drop to the creek at the mine basin below.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Twin Lakes register. Mount Baker Wilderness rules: no fires, party size twelve, camp on durable ground, pack out all waste including human waste. The international boundary runs a little over a mile north of the pass; camp and climb south of it, and see the border note on the mine basin below.
bivy.capacity: A couple of small tent spots on and just below the pass; two or three tents at most, and they are exposed

bivy.name: Gargett Mine basin bivy
bivy.notes: This is the base camp for American Border Peak and for the west side of Mount Larrabee, and it is what turns both from a punishing single push into a sane two-day trip. From High Pass a boot path drops north and west into the basin, reached in well under an hour from the pass and about two and a half hours from the Twin Lakes trailhead. The workings themselves sit on a bench with space for a handful of people lying down, and the friendlier option is to keep descending a few hundred feet to the green basin below, where gravel bars beside the creek take proper tents. From here the American Border Peak approach traverses Larrabee's west slope to a notch around 6,200 ft and on into the moraine bowl below the south saddle, which is the reason parties who try the peak in a day so often run out of daylight. Fill every bottle before you leave the creek. Snow lingers in the bowls above the basin all summer, and the ground is loose scree and gravel that will not hold a stake well.
bivy.water: A creek runs through the basin by the old mine, and it is the last reliable water on the way to either summit; everything beyond is snowmelt or nothing

bivy.name: Yellow Aster Butte tarns (Yellow Aster Meadows)

bivy.name: Tomyhoi Lake

bivy.permit: No camping within one mile of Gold Run Pass, which rules out the whole upper part of the descent; the lake itself is far enough down to be legal. Free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead register, recreation pass on the vehicle, no fires, party size twelve, pack out waste.
bivy.capacity: A handful of rough forested sites at the lake; quiet, and rarely full

bivy.name: Twin Lakes Road upper section and the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead pullouts
bivy.notes: This is the road rather than a campsite, because on this approach the road is the variable that decides what the trip is. The first four and a half miles to the Tomyhoi Lake and Yellow Aster Butte trailhead are rough gravel that an ordinary car can manage with patience; the straight section below the switchbacks is the worst of it, with loose rock and deep potholes. bivy.name: Twin Lakes basin road-end camp

bivy.permit: Recreation pass or the posted per-vehicle day-use fee for the trailhead. Free self-issue wilderness permit at the register for anyone continuing onto the trails. The lakes basin at the road end sits outside the wilderness and several sites have metal fire rings, but everything above and beyond is wilderness where fires are prohibited outright, and county or forest-wide burn bans routinely close the road-end rings as well. Party size in the wilderness is capped at twelve. Hang or canister your food.

bivy.name: Cutthroat Creek trailhead
bivy.notes: The lot sits a mile up the forest road from SR 20 and has a vault toilet but no water. Parties climbing the South Buttress or Southeast Buttress routinely sleep here or in a pullout on the road in before a pre-dawn start, though the lot itself is signed for day use and how strictly that is read varies; dispersed camping in the trees along the forest road below is the uncontroversial option. Access is entirely gated by the SR 20 winter closure, and the road has been shut for construction windows in recent seasons, so confirm before driving out.
bivy.water: None — no potable water at the trailhead. Cutthroat Creek runs below the lot and needs filtering.
bivy.permit: No camping permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day pass covers parking. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, NOT the national park, so there is no backcountry permit system here at all.
bivy.capacity: Large gravel lot, roughly 20-30 vehicles; fills on summer weekends with larch-season hikers

bivy.name: Cutthroat basin climbers' bivy — SOUTH-SIDE routes only
bivy.notes: SERVES THE SOUTH AND SOUTHEAST ROUTES ONLY. The North Ridge is normally approached from the State Creek side, and this bivy does not help that party at all. From the trailhead a way-path leaves the Cutthroat Lake trail, drops to cross the creek and climbs meadows into the bowl under the south and southeast sides, roughly two hours with a pack. The meadows are thin and the basin sees enough traffic to show it.

bivy.capacity: Several scattered one- and two-tent pads in the meadows and among the boulders; no established camp, so parties spread out

bivy.name: Cutthroat Lake basin, outside the quarter-mile closure
bivy.notes: The lake sits about 1.8 miles in with roughly 500 ft of gain, in the basin under the peak's north and east sides. It is a pleasant place to stage, but the quarter-mile closure exists because the shoreline was being loved to death and it is enforced rather than advisory. bivy.capacity: Limited and regulated — the usable ground is set back from the water, so realistically a handful of small parties

bivy.permit: None — dispersed national forest camping, no permit and no quota.
bivy.capacity: A small flat area under the cliff; room for one or two parties at most

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground to the Cutthroat Creek trailhead, a short drive east on SR 20 along Early Winters Creek. Because nothing here can be booked, arriving Friday evening in July or August is a gamble and the fallback is dispersed camping on a spur road. The season runs roughly May or June through September or October, entirely dependent on when the highway opens and when snow returns.
bivy.water: Potable water provided in season, shut off once the campground closes for the year.
bivy.permit: No reservations and no permit — first-come, first-served with a nightly fee. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to camp, only to park at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: 27 sites, tents and small RVs

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby

bivy.capacity: Informal rather than developed — a small amount of workable ground on the shelf near the pass, room for a party or two, with no facilities of any kind

bivy.name: Honeymoon Meadows and Camp Siberia — the West Fork Dosewallips side of LaCrosse Pass
bivy.notes: This is the eastern way to LaCrosse Basin and the one to use when the East Fork Quinault quota is gone. From the road end the trail runs up to Dose Forks at about 7.6 miles, Big Timber at 10.3, Diamond Meadow at 12.7 and Honeymoon Meadows at 15, with the LaCrosse Pass trail branching a little before that and Camp Siberia at around 16 near Anderson Pass. Bicycles help on that stretch. Add the road walk to every figure before deciding this is the short way.
bivy.water: Reliable at all of them — the West Fork Dosewallips runs beside the trail the whole way and the meadows carry side streams into the autumn
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance through the federal recreation booking site. The Dosewallips side is not a quota area and these camps are usually available at short notice, which is a real advantage over the Quinault approach to the same country. Animal-resistant food container required. Honeymoon Meadows sits near the fire line and Camp Siberia above it, so assume no fires at either.
bivy.capacity: Honeymoon Meadows is an open riverside meadow camp with several sites and is the pleasant one; Camp Siberia near Anderson Pass is smaller, higher and colder, with a few spots and an old shelter frame. Diamond Meadow and Big Timber lower down break the walk further.

bivy.name: Sixteen Mile Camp — the base directly under Mount Lawson
bivy.notes: This is the camp for MOUNT LAWSON and effectively the only one. The peak rises about 3,800 ft above the river in a mile and a third, straight out of the drainage the camp sits in, and the climb is a class 2 slog on steep forest and open slope rather than anything technical — the work is the approach, not the summit. The camp is roughly twelve miles up the valley from the North Fork trailhead, past Wolf Bar, Halfway House, Elip Creek and Trapper Shelter, and the walk is gentle until the last few miles where the valley narrows and the trail climbs and drops across steep sidehill. THE FORDS ARE THE WHOLE PLANNING PROBLEM. There are three of them — Wild Rose Creek, Elip Creek and the North Fork itself right at this camp — and the river crossing here is regularly impassable during snowmelt or after heavy rain. Parties have been turned around at it having walked twelve miles. Go in late summer when the river is low, carry poles, and treat a high river as a trip-ending condition rather than something to force. Reach the trailhead by the North Shore Road; the South Shore Road has been washed out and a phone will still try to send you that way.
bivy.water: Reliable. The North Fork Quinault runs at the camp, which is also the reason the camp exists and the reason it can be unreachable; treat everything.
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, reserved in advance through the federal recreation booking site. The North Fork Quinault is not a quota area, so this is one of the easier permits in the park, but nothing here is held back as a same-day walk-up and camps this far in do not always surface in an online search — telephone the wilderness information centre if it will not show. An approved animal-resistant food container is mandatory throughout the park wilderness and free loaners are handed out with permits. This camp sits below the 3,500 ft fire line, so fires are legal in the established rings when no seasonal ban is running, and bans are usual by midsummer.
bivy.capacity: Four established sites on the river flat, and it is rarely contested — almost everyone walking this valley is bound for Low Divide and passes straight through

bivy.name: Elip Creek and the lower North Fork Quinault camps
bivy.notes: These break the walk to Sixteen Mile rather than serving any summit directly, and that matters more than it sounds: the drive to the North Fork trailhead is long, most parties arrive in the afternoon, and twelve miles with a climbing pack on the same day is an unpleasant way to start. Wolf Bar at about two and a half miles is the late-arrival camp, Elip Creek at roughly six and a half is the natural halfway stop, and Trapper Shelter a mile and a half further is the last of them before the valley steepens. Grades are easy to Trapper and then the trail begins working up and down high above the river. Two of the three fords are below Sixteen Mile, so a night here also lets you look at the water level before committing to the upper valley. Deep old-growth forest, heavy shade, mosquitoes in early summer and no views whatsoever — this is shelter and mileage, nothing more.
bivy.water: Reliable at all of them — the river or the named side creek. The lower valley is rainforest and water is never the constraint here.
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance; not a quota area and usually obtainable at short notice. Animal-resistant food container mandatory. All of these sit well below the fire line so established rings are legal outside a burn ban.
bivy.capacity: Elip Creek has four sites, Wolf Bar five and Halfway House two. Trapper Shelter above them holds two small spots and is best treated as day or emergency use only rather than a planned night.

bivy.name: Pyrites Creek — where the Chimney Peak approach leaves the trail
bivy.notes: This is the camp for CHIMNEY PEAK, and the reason it rather than the chalet meadow is that the approach leaves the East Fork Quinault trail at about nine miles, which is where this camp sits. Push on to the chalet and you have walked four miles past your own turning and given yourself them back again in the morning. The peak stands immediately north above the valley with its southeast face rising something like 4,800 ft in less than a mile, streaming waterfalls into the valley below — spectacular from the trail and completely useless as a line of ascent. The climb goes round to the southwest ridge and is class 3 scrambling once you are on it, with the first ascent not made until 1941, which says something about how the ground below it behaves. Expect a long, steep, largely trackless day out of the valley floor. June through September is the workable window. The walk in from Graves Creek is thirteen miles to the chalet with staged camps at Pony Bridge and O'Neil Creek before this one, so most parties take two easy days in rather than one hard one.
bivy.water: Reliable — the East Fork Quinault and the creek the camp is named for both run all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, and THE EAST FORK QUINAULT IS A QUOTA AREA. It has been run under a nightly cap of thirty permits or roughly two hundred people since 2024, so this is a booking to make the day reservations open rather than a fortnight out. The summer season runs mid-May to mid-October and releases in one drop in mid-April at seven in the morning Pacific time. Eight dollars per person per night for anyone sixteen or over plus a six dollar booking fee, or an annual wilderness pass that covers the nightly charge. BEAR CANISTERS ARE SPECIFICALLY REQUIRED IN THIS VALLEY and enforced rather than advised — the Enchanted Valley was closed over bear problems and reopened on that condition. Free loaners at the Quinault and Port Angeles wilderness offices.
bivy.capacity: A modest forested riverside camp with a handful of sites, quieter than the valley above it because most parties push the extra four miles to the chalet meadow

bivy.name: Lake LaCrosse and Hart Lake — the base for Mount La Crosse and White Mountain
bivy.notes: THE camp for both MOUNT LA CROSSE and WHITE MOUNTAIN, which stand less than a mile apart on either side of a small unnamed glacier directly above the basin. Both are scrambles rather than climbs — La Crosse at 6,417 ft goes at class 2 and was first climbed in 1928, White Mountain at 6,378 ft is class 2 as well — so from a camp here the two together are a single long day rather than an expedition. Lake LaCrosse sits at about 4,800 ft, roughly 400 ft higher and a mile and a half further than Marmot Lake, with Hart Lake in between; Marmot is covered in the Staircase file and is a perfectly good camp, but it is further from these two summits and it is the wrong side of the shelf. From the East Fork Quinault you go through Enchanted Valley and over Anderson Pass. From the Duckabush you come up the river and over O'Neil Pass. Every one of those is two days in for most parties carrying gear, which is why these summits see so little traffic. July through September; the basin holds snow late and the passes either side of it later still.

This basin is not itself one of the named quota areas, but the East Fork Quinault approach to it is, so which trailhead you walk in from changes what you have to book — check the whole itinerary rather than just the camp. An animal-resistant food container is required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED, well above the parkwide 3,500 ft line. Elk work this basin heavily and bears are regular visitors.
bivy.capacity: A small number of sites spread between the two lakes, in and above open subalpine basin. Neither holds a crowd and the meadow ground is fragile, so use the established pads rather than making new ones.

bivy.name: O'Neil Pass and the upper Duckabush shelf
bivy.notes: A high, exposed alternative to the lake basin for a party that wants to be moving early on WHITE MOUNTAIN or that is traversing rather than going in and back. The pass sits at roughly 4,900 ft on the long shelf that carries the trail in a slow horseshoe between the Duckabush head and the East Fork Quinault, and Chimney Peak and the Anderson massif are both in view from it — which is the honest reason most people stop here rather than any advantage on climbing day. bivy.capacity: Informal rather than developed — a small amount of workable ground on the shelf near the pass, room for a party or two, with no facilities of any kind

bivy.name: Sunrise Mine road end — the Sperry and Vesper Creek staging point
bivy.notes: This is the working start for SPERRY PEAK, and Sperry is honestly a day objective with no camp of its own — parties leave from here in the dark, ford the South Fork Stillaguamish, grind up through the talus of Wirtz Basin under Morning Star, take the switchbacked chute to Headlee Pass and traverse under Sperry's south side before scrambling the summit blocks. The only established camp on that line lies beyond the pass in the upper Vesper Creek basin, which the earlier upper-loop file already carries, so the realistic choice here is a long day from the car or a night in that basin. Sleeping at the road end is what most parties do and it works: the spur is short, and a pre-dawn start gets you through the chute before the day's rockfall gets going. Three things decide whether the trip happens at all. The FORD half a mile in is the real gate and it is not a formality — it runs hard in snowmelt and log crossings that worked one season are gone the next. The CHUTE below Headlee Pass is loose, narrow and known for rock coming down it, so parties should not stack up in it and helmets belong on well before the base. And SNOW holds in that chute and on the pass long after the valley is bare, which regularly turns a June or early-July attempt around. The spur itself is rough with potholes and encroaching brush; a low car can usually manage it slowly but scrapes are common. There is no cell coverage from the moment you leave the main loop road.
bivy.water: None at the road end. The creek crossings begin half a mile in and the first of them is the difficult one, so load every litre down in the valley rather than planning to draw here.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass to leave a vehicle, and nothing else. This is national forest but NOT designated wilderness, so there is no self-issue permit, no quota and no party-size cap. Overnight parking is allowed. Fires at the road end are governed by whatever seasonal forest-wide restrictions are running, which from midsummer usually means no open flame at all.
bivy.capacity: Car bivy only. A small gravel turnaround at the end of the spur with room for perhaps a dozen vehicles and no sites, tables or pads. It overflows onto the road shoulder on summer weekends and the last cars in walk a fair way back to the trail start.

bivy.name: Lower Gothic Basin — the slab benches and tarns short of Foggy Lake
bivy.notes: The basin lip, where the climbers' trail finally stops climbing and opens out among tarns and slabs, sits about a mile below Foggy Lake and is the quieter alternative to it. For GOTHIC PEAK this costs almost nothing — Gothic's ordinary line goes up from the basin side and the extra mile to the lake buys no advantage — while for DEL CAMPO it does cost you, because Del Campo's southeast ridge is entered from the north side of Foggy Lake and camping short of it adds a mile and several hundred feet to summit day. Choose accordingly: this is the Gothic camp and the bad-weather camp, not the Del Campo one. Getting here means the Weden Creek trail, which is a mining-era path rather than a graded one — steep, direct, rocky, with slabby sections that are genuinely unpleasant when wet and a few spots where hands come out. It gains close to three thousand feet in under five miles after the flat mile of road walking. The basin is bare rock and thin alpine soil with almost nothing to dig in, so waste comes out with you. Snow lies here well into July in an ordinary year and the timing moves by weeks between a heavy and a light winter. Old adits and workings are scattered through the basin and some are open holes in bad light; keep to the used ground.
bivy.water: Melt streams and the tarns run through the basin most of the season and thin out late in a hot August. TREAT THE PROVENANCE OF THIS WATER SERIOUSLY: the whole drainage is old mining ground and metals leached from tailings, arsenic in particular, are documented through this valley system. Filters, tablets and boiling deal with organisms and do nothing whatever about dissolved metals. Draw from snowmelt and small feeder runnels well above any workings rather than from anything draining a spoil heap, and if in doubt carry it in.
bivy.permit: National forest land OUTSIDE designated wilderness, so no camping permit, no quota and no party-size limit. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass to leave a vehicle. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED throughout the basin regardless of season, and there is nothing to burn anyway — carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small parties spread wide. The ground is polished slab, boulder and thin heather with pockets of flat gravel rather than any built-up site, so it takes two or three tents comfortably and rewards walking another five minutes to find your own rather than crowding the first flat spot.

bivy.name: Weden Creek trail junction, one mile up the Monte Cristo road
bivy.notes: This is for the party that runs long rather than the party that plans well. The walk out from Gothic Basin is a steep descent on greasy slab in fading light and it is where people get hurt on this approach, so a known flat spot at the bottom of the climbing — before the last mile of road back to Barlow Pass — is worth recording. It is also a legitimate soft start: a party arriving late can walk the flat mile up the old road, sleep beside the creek, and be climbing at first light with the whole basin ahead of them rather than the drive still in their legs. The first three quarters of a mile of the Weden Creek trail runs almost level along the creek before it turns uphill in earnest, and that stretch is where the usable ground is. Do not confuse this with the Monte Cristo townsite four miles further up the same road, which is a different place serving different peaks. The road from Barlow Pass is gated to vehicles and stays that way, so everything here is on foot. Being valley bottom, it is buggy in early summer and stays cold and damp long into the morning.
bivy.water: Weden Creek runs right there and is the easiest water on the whole approach, but it drains the same mineralised ground as the basin above and carries the same metals question. Treat it as washing and cooking-fire water at best, and carry drinking water in.
bivy.permit: National forest, outside wilderness, so dispersed camping is allowed and needs no permit. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. Fires are a poor idea in a wooded valley bottom under summer restrictions and are usually banned outright from midsummer; assume a stove.
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents at most, on flat forest ground near where the trail leaves the road and follows the creek. This is dispersed camping on undeveloped ground, not a site — no table, no ring, no toilet, nothing signed.

bivy.name: Red Bridge Campground, Mountain Loop Highway
bivy.notes: The nearest developed campground to the Sunrise Mine road, about ten miles below it on the paved section of the loop, and therefore the sensible base for SPERRY when you want a real night rather than a car bivy at a crowded road end. It is markedly closer to the Sunrise Mine spur than the larger campgrounds down at Verlot and much quieter, at the cost of fewer sites and no drinking water. Being on the paved lower loop it stays reachable all year and is entirely unaffected by whether the gravel section beyond Barlow Pass has opened for the season, which matters more here than it looks: that gravel stretch between Barlow Pass and the Bedal gate shuts each winter and typically does not open until somewhere in the second half of May. Barlow Pass itself is reached from this paved western side and normally opens earlier, but a slide anywhere below it closes everything above at a stroke and has done so recently, in which case basing low here and driving in each morning is the way to keep the trip. Sixteen sites go quickly on a fine Friday and none of them are reservable, so arrive early or have a fallback. Two group-only campgrounds sit within a couple of miles further up the same stretch, both reservation-only, and both are worth knowing about for a club climb that needs one site for a large party rather than several small ones. No cell coverage.
bivy.water: No potable supply on site. The South Fork Stillaguamish runs alongside and filters fine here — this is a different drainage from the mineralised Sauk-side ground above Barlow Pass, so the metals problem that dogs Gothic Basin does not apply.

Fires are allowed in the rings when seasonal restrictions permit, and those restrictions routinely shut them from midsummer.
bivy.capacity: Around sixteen developed sites on the river bar, taking tents and small vehicles, with tables, fire rings and vault toilets. Fee campground, first come first served, open roughly late spring through early autumn.

bivy.name: Sunrise Mine road end — the Sperry and Vesper Creek staging point
bivy.notes: This is the working start for SPERRY PEAK, and Sperry is honestly a day objective with no camp of its own — parties leave from here in the dark, ford the South Fork Stillaguamish, grind up through the talus of Wirtz Basin under Morning Star, take the switchbacked chute to Headlee Pass and traverse under Sperry's south side before scrambling the summit blocks. The only established camp on that line lies beyond the pass in the upper Vesper Creek basin, which the earlier upper-loop file already carries, so the realistic choice here is a long day from the car or a night in that basin. Sleeping at the road end is what most parties do and it works: the spur is short, and a pre-dawn start gets you through the chute before the day's rockfall gets going. Three things decide whether the trip happens at all. The FORD half a mile in is the real gate and it is not a formality — it runs hard in snowmelt and log crossings that worked one season are gone the next. The CHUTE below Headlee Pass is loose, narrow and known for rock coming down it, so parties should not stack up in it and helmets belong on well before the base. And SNOW holds in that chute and on the pass long after the valley is bare, which regularly turns a June or early-July attempt around. The spur itself is rough with potholes and encroaching brush; a low car can usually manage it slowly but scrapes are common. There is no cell coverage from the moment you leave the main loop road.
bivy.water: None at the road end. The creek crossings begin half a mile in and the first of them is the difficult one, so load every litre down in the valley rather than planning to draw here.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass to leave a vehicle, and nothing else. This is national forest but NOT designated wilderness, so there is no self-issue permit, no quota and no party-size cap. Overnight parking is allowed. Fires at the road end are governed by whatever seasonal forest-wide restrictions are running, which from midsummer usually means no open flame at all.
bivy.capacity: Car bivy only. A small gravel turnaround at the end of the spur with room for perhaps a dozen vehicles and no sites, tables or pads. It overflows onto the road shoulder on summer weekends and the last cars in walk a fair way back to the trail start.

bivy.name: Lower Gothic Basin — the slab benches and tarns short of Foggy Lake
bivy.notes: The basin lip, where the climbers' trail finally stops climbing and opens out among tarns and slabs, sits about a mile below Foggy Lake and is the quieter alternative to it. For GOTHIC PEAK this costs almost nothing — Gothic's ordinary line goes up from the basin side and the extra mile to the lake buys no advantage — while for DEL CAMPO it does cost you, because Del Campo's southeast ridge is entered from the north side of Foggy Lake and camping short of it adds a mile and several hundred feet to summit day. Choose accordingly: this is the Gothic camp and the bad-weather camp, not the Del Campo one. Getting here means the Weden Creek trail, which is a mining-era path rather than a graded one — steep, direct, rocky, with slabby sections that are genuinely unpleasant when wet and a few spots where hands come out. It gains close to three thousand feet in under five miles after the flat mile of road walking. The basin is bare rock and thin alpine soil with almost nothing to dig in, so waste comes out with you. Snow lies here well into July in an ordinary year and the timing moves by weeks between a heavy and a light winter. Old adits and workings are scattered through the basin and some are open holes in bad light; keep to the used ground.
bivy.water: Melt streams and the tarns run through the basin most of the season and thin out late in a hot August. TREAT THE PROVENANCE OF THIS WATER SERIOUSLY: the whole drainage is old mining ground and metals leached from tailings, arsenic in particular, are documented through this valley system. Filters, tablets and boiling deal with organisms and do nothing whatever about dissolved metals. Draw from snowmelt and small feeder runnels well above any workings rather than from anything draining a spoil heap, and if in doubt carry it in.
bivy.permit: National forest land OUTSIDE designated wilderness, so no camping permit, no quota and no party-size limit. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass to leave a vehicle. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED throughout the basin regardless of season, and there is nothing to burn anyway — carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small parties spread wide. The ground is polished slab, boulder and thin heather with pockets of flat gravel rather than any built-up site, so it takes two or three tents comfortably and rewards walking another five minutes to find your own rather than crowding the first flat spot.

bivy.name: Weden Creek trail junction, one mile up the Monte Cristo road
bivy.notes: This is for the party that runs long rather than the party that plans well. The walk out from Gothic Basin is a steep descent on greasy slab in fading light and it is where people get hurt on this approach, so a known flat spot at the bottom of the climbing — before the last mile of road back to Barlow Pass — is worth recording. It is also a legitimate soft start: a party arriving late can walk the flat mile up the old road, sleep beside the creek, and be climbing at first light with the whole basin ahead of them rather than the drive still in their legs. The first three quarters of a mile of the Weden Creek trail runs almost level along the creek before it turns uphill in earnest, and that stretch is where the usable ground is. Do not confuse this with the Monte Cristo townsite four miles further up the same road, which is a different place serving different peaks. The road from Barlow Pass is gated to vehicles and stays that way, so everything here is on foot. Being valley bottom, it is buggy in early summer and stays cold and damp long into the morning.
bivy.water: Weden Creek runs right there and is the easiest water on the whole approach, but it drains the same mineralised ground as the basin above and carries the same metals question. Treat it as washing and cooking-fire water at best, and carry drinking water in.
bivy.permit: National forest, outside wilderness, so dispersed camping is allowed and needs no permit. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. Fires are a poor idea in a wooded valley bottom under summer restrictions and are usually banned outright from midsummer; assume a stove.
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents at most, on flat forest ground near where the trail leaves the road and follows the creek. This is dispersed camping on undeveloped ground, not a site — no table, no ring, no toilet, nothing signed.

bivy.name: Red Bridge Campground, Mountain Loop Highway
bivy.notes: The nearest developed campground to the Sunrise Mine road, about ten miles below it on the paved section of the loop, and therefore the sensible base for SPERRY when you want a real night rather than a car bivy at a crowded road end. It is markedly closer to the Sunrise Mine spur than the larger campgrounds down at Verlot and much quieter, at the cost of fewer sites and no drinking water. Being on the paved lower loop it stays reachable all year and is entirely unaffected by whether the gravel section beyond Barlow Pass has opened for the season, which matters more here than it looks: that gravel stretch between Barlow Pass and the Bedal gate shuts each winter and typically does not open until somewhere in the second half of May. Barlow Pass itself is reached from this paved western side and normally opens earlier, but a slide anywhere below it closes everything above at a stroke and has done so recently, in which case basing low here and driving in each morning is the way to keep the trip. Sixteen sites go quickly on a fine Friday and none of them are reservable, so arrive early or have a fallback. Two group-only campgrounds sit within a couple of miles further up the same stretch, both reservation-only, and both are worth knowing about for a club climb that needs one site for a large party rather than several small ones. No cell coverage.
bivy.water: No potable supply on site. The South Fork Stillaguamish runs alongside and filters fine here — this is a different drainage from the mineralised Sauk-side ground above Barlow Pass, so the metals problem that dogs Gothic Basin does not apply.
bivy.permit: A developed fee campground on national forest land — the per-night fee is all that is needed and no pass or permit applies to the site itself. Nothing here is inside wilderness. Fires are allowed in the rings when seasonal restrictions permit, and those restrictions routinely shut them from midsummer.
bivy.capacity: Around sixteen developed sites on the river bar, taking tents and small vehicles, with tables, fire rings and vault toilets. Fee campground, first come first served, open roughly late spring through early autumn.

bivy.name: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County
bivy.notes: Sits in old-growth timber near where Squire Creek meets the North Fork Stillaguamish, a few miles west of Darrington on SR 530 — not on the Mountain Loop Highway, and not up the Squire Creek road itself. It is the most comfortable base for a weekend on the Darrington granite, with flush toilets and a swimmable creek, at the cost of a drive back into town each morning. Because it is county-run rather than Forest Service, the fee schedule, season and reservation window are set separately from the national forest campgrounds and should be checked on their own.
bivy.water: Piped drinking water via spigots through the campground; reliable in season
bivy.permit: None — this is a COUNTY park, not Forest Service. Nightly fee, reservations through the Snohomish County Parks system. A Northwest Forest Pass does nothing here.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 30 non-hookup sites, tents and RVs, reservable

bivy.name: Clear Creek Campground
bivy.notes: Small campground on the Sauk River a few miles southeast of Darrington on the Mountain Loop Highway, sitting essentially at the mouth of the Clear Creek road that serves Three O'Clock Rock, Exfoliation Dome and Green Giant Buttress. That position is the whole appeal — you can be at the Eightmile trailhead within twenty minutes of leaving camp. Vault toilets only, no water, and twelve sites go quickly on summer weekends.
bivy.water: No potable water on site — carry your own or treat from the river
bivy.permit: Standard Forest Service nightly fee, bookable through Recreation.gov; typically open May through September. No climbing or wilderness permit needed.
bivy.capacity: 12 single sites, vehicles to about 40 ft

bivy.name: Dispersed roadside camping, Clear Creek Road
bivy.notes: Climbers routinely sleep in a vehicle or throw a tent down at a pullout on the Clear Creek road rather than pay for a site, and the trailhead turnaround at the end of the drivable road is the usual spot. This is dispersed camping in the ordinary national forest sense — no fee, no reservation, no permit — which is the practical difference between here and the North Cascades park zones just up the valley. Campfire bans are common from midsummer onward and are worth confirming before you plan on one. No facilities of any kind, so pack out everything including waste.
bivy.water: Creeks near the road most of the season, but nothing developed — filter or treat everything
bivy.permit: NO camping permit required for dispersed camping on national forest land; general forest rules apply (14-day stay limit, camp within about 150 ft of the road, 100 ft from water). A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is required to PARK at the Eightmile trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Informal pullouts and the trailhead turnaround; a handful of parties at most

bivy.name: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
bivy.notes: The Squire Creek road out of the west end of old Darrington has been cut by a washout well short of its historic end for many years, so the drivable road end is A MOVING TARGET and the walk in to Squire Creek Wall is longer than older descriptions suggest. Parties sleeping in the car or under a tarp at the closure are doing so to get an early start on that extra walking, not because there is anything established there. Confirm the current closure point before committing — how far you can drive has changed repeatedly between seasons, and it is the single biggest variable in a Squire Creek Wall day.
bivy.water: Squire Creek runs close by and is dependable, but needs treating
bivy.permit: None for dispersed camping on forest land; the usual 14-day and setback rules apply.
bivy.capacity: A few parties, informal

bivy.name: Squire Creek Wall on-route ledges
bivy.notes: The long routes on Squire Creek Wall have a couple of usable ledges high on the face, the better-known ones roughly a third and two-thirds of the way up, and parties moving slowly on the full-length lines have used them to split the climb. This is genuine bivouac ground rather than camping — a ledge, a rope, and whatever you hauled. Most parties climbing here do not need it, and it should be treated as a planned option for the biggest routes or as an emergency out, rather than as a reason to carry overnight gear by default.
bivy.water: A rock pocket at the lower ledge holds water through much of the season, but it is a puddle, not a source — assume it may be dry and carry what you need
bivy.permit: None
bivy.capacity: Small ledges, one party

bivy.name: Squire Creek Pass
bivy.notes: Reached by the unmaintained Eightmile trail off the Clear Creek road, this open pass under the Squire Creek walls is the only real high camp on this side of the granite. It is more often a hiking objective than a climbing one, and camping there is genuinely limited, so use the existing sites and plan on a stove rather than a fire. It is a poor choice as a base for Three O'Clock Rock or Exfoliation Dome, which are approached from lower on the same road and climbed from the car.
bivy.water: Seasonal snowmelt and streams below the pass; unreliable late in a dry summer
bivy.permit: No camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass required at the Eightmile trailhead on Clear Creek Road.
bivy.capacity: Limited — a small number of existing sites at and near the pass

bivy.name: Sulphide Glacier camp
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for the most straightforward route on Shuksan and the best launching point for the summit pyramid. The plateau is flat, spacious and well positioned, and a privy has been maintained on the ridgeline here in recent seasons, which is unusual at this elevation. The permit is the binding constraint on the whole trip rather than the terrain, so plan the paperwork before the climb. Snow covers the site into early summer, and late in the season the approach turns to loose ground and heather that is harder work than the mileage suggests.
bivy.water: Usually available — running water is often audible and reachable over the rocks near camp — but this is a snowmelt supply that varies with the year and the week. Bring the means to melt snow and treat found water as likely rather than certain.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry (wilderness) permit required — this is a DIFFERENT authority from the Mt Baker side, and a Forest Service pass does not cover it. Permits come through Recreation.gov, with a spring early-access lottery followed by a general on-sale, and a share held back for walk-ups issued within 24 hours at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Reservation and per-person nightly fees apply — these permits are no longer free. The zone carries a small daily party quota.
bivy.capacity: A broad flat plateau on the ridgeline with room for several parties, though the daily permit quota caps how many can legitimately be there

bivy.name: Shannon Ridge crest camps, below the park boundary
bivy.notes: The fallback for parties who could not get a North Cascades backcountry permit, and honestly worse than the camp above — lower, drier, and leaving a much longer summit day. The trade is administrative rather than scenic, so decide before you drive out whether you would rather chase a walk-up permit at a ranger station. bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, same as the 6,400 ft camp — through Recreation.gov or as a walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, with fees. Confirm that your permit covers camping this high in the zone rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms only, for one or two parties; no established sites

bivy.name: Lake Ann basin
bivy.notes: The usual first night for both the Fisher Chimneys and the North Face, and the jurisdictional line running just past it is the single most useful thing to understand about camping on this side of Shuksan — one night at the lake is a Forest Service matter, the next night up on the route is a national park one. The trailhead sits near 4,700 ft and the trail drops before climbing back to the basin, so the return is uphill at the end of a long day. Access is entirely gated by SR 542, plowed to Artist Point on a seasonal schedule and closed with the first serious snowfall in autumn. Snow can linger in the basin into August in a heavy year.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams through most of the season. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness — the lake sits roughly a mile outside the national park boundary, so no park permit is needed to camp here. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required at the Lake Ann trailhead, camping must be at least two miles from the trailhead between mid-May and mid-November, and the standard 12-person wilderness party limit applies. The permit boundary is signed beyond the lake, and every camp past it needs a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit.
bivy.capacity: Established sites around the lake basin; popular with hikers as well as climbers and busy on summer weekends

bivy.name: Fisher Chimneys camps, White Salmon and above Winnie's Slide
bivy.notes: Camping above the chimneys is what makes Fisher Chimneys a comfortable two- or three-day climb rather than a very long push, and it puts the party above the loose, route-finding-heavy section for summit day. The lower site near the top of the White Salmon is the more common choice and the more scenic; the higher one above Winnie's Slide costs you a steep snow or ice pitch with a full pack. Which is preferable depends on the party and on conditions in the chimneys, and reasonable people disagree. Both are small and exposed, so a party arriving to find them occupied needs a plan.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only in practice. Runoff sometimes appears on the rock below the glaciers in warm conditions, but neither site should be planned around finding liquid water.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required — these camps are inside the park, past the signed boundary above Lake Ann. Reserve through Recreation.gov or take a walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center within 24 hours; fees apply and the zone carries a small daily party quota. A Northwest Forest Pass covers only the parking at the Lake Ann trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Small platforms for one or two parties at each of two levels — around 6,800 ft where the chimneys top out near the White Salmon, and higher near 7,300 ft above Winnie's Slide

bivy.name: North Face bivy, where the rib meets the face
bivy.notes: North Face parties share the early approach with the White Salmon Glacier route through a brushy section before the two diverge, and the usual bivy sits near 5,500 ft where the rib abuts the face, above Price Lake. It is a working bivy chosen for position on a serious route rather than for comfort, and the point of it is an early start onto sustained steep snow and ice. Objective hazard governs everything here: the face is avalanche-prone, particularly early in the season and further left, so timing and a cold night matter more than the site itself. This is a spring-into-early-summer route in most years.
bivy.water: Seasonal melt only. Late in the year expect nothing and carry or melt.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required — the approach leaves Forest Service ground shortly past Lake Ann and the bivy is inside the park. Through Recreation.gov or as a walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; fees apply and the zone quota is small. Do not assume the Lake Ann trailhead pass covers this.
bivy.capacity: One party; rough ground with a couple of usable spots, not a camp

bivy.name: Dana Yelverton Shelter site
bivy.notes: A named point on the crest just below Old Snowy, where a stone shelter once stood and where a hiker died in a summer blizzard in the early 1960s. The shelter is now a scatter of rubble and offers no protection whatsoever, so treat the name as a map label rather than a resource. Its value is position: it is the highest place on this side you can legally sleep, which shortens a summit morning on Old Snowy to almost nothing and puts Ives within an easy pre-dawn traverse. The cost is that it is fully exposed at the high point of the Pacific Crest Trail in Washington, with no water, no wind shelter and no retreat that is not a long descent. The history is the warning: weather arrives here fast and out of season.
bivy.water: None. Snow patches persist nearby into midsummer and can be melted, but from late summer this is a dry camp and water must be carried up from the basin
bivy.permit: Free self-issued Goat Rocks Wilderness permit. CAMPFIRES ARE SPECIFICALLY PROHIBITED at this location by wilderness regulation, and the 100-foot setback from the Pacific Crest Trail applies — the trail passes right through, so a legal pitch here takes some walking.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small tents on the crest at best; there is no shelter left to sleep in and the ground is broken rock

bivy.name: Climbers Bivouac
bivy.notes: The summer roadhead for Monitor Ridge, and effectively the only place to sleep close to that route, since the mountain above 4,800 feet is closed to camping. It is a rough clearing in second-growth timber at the end of a Forest Service road, with tent pads and fire rings but nothing else, and the sites are small and packed in. The value is purely positional: the summit trail leaves from here and a night at the trailhead turns a long day into a manageable one. Plan the permit before the campsite, because the permit is the real constraint — the quota tightens sharply in mid-May, and the whole summer sells on release day. Arrive with your blue bag and use it; there is a composting toilet where the trail meets the tree line, and above that there is nothing at all.
bivy.water: None. There is no water at the trailhead, so carry everything you need for the night and for the climb. Pit toilets are provided
bivy.permit: Camping itself is free, but the parking requires a Northwest Forest Pass, an Interagency pass, or a small day fee. SEPARATELY AND UNAVOIDABLY, a climbing permit is required year round for anyone going above 4,800 feet on the mountain, and camping above 4,800 feet is prohibited outright. From April 1 to October 31 that permit carries a daily quota and a per-climber fee of about twenty dollars: 350 climbers a day from April 1 to May 14, then only 110 a day from May 15 through October 31. Permits are sold first come, first served with no lottery, released a month at a time on the first day of the preceding month at seven in the morning Pacific time, and the summer dates sell out within minutes of release. From November 1 to March 31 the permit is free and self-issued at the trailhead with no quota. Blue bags are mandatory for all human waste above the tree line and are stocked at the trailhead kiosk.
bivy.capacity: Around fourteen small primitive tent sites, close together, first come and first served only; motorhomes and trailers are directed elsewhere

bivy.name: Marble Mountain Sno-Park
bivy.notes: The winter and shoulder-season staging point, and the start of the Worm Flows route when the road to Climbers Bivouac is under snow. It is lower than the summer trailhead, so Worm Flows carries a bigger day at roughly 5,700 feet of gain, which is the main argument for sleeping here rather than driving in the dark. Camping in a plowed parking lot is not scenic and it works: the lots are large, the toilets are open and the warming hut takes the edge off a cold morning. Parties commonly move up to camp on the snow around the Chocolate Falls area on the way, which stays below the 4,800-foot line if you site it carefully — check your altimeter rather than guessing, because that boundary is a legal one. Avalanche conditions on the Worm Flows gullies, not the permit, are the season's real gate.
bivy.water: None liquid in winter — melt snow, and carry water in the shoulder seasons. Two vault toilets are provided, and a warming hut is open through the winter months
bivy.permit: A Washington Sno-Park permit is required from December 1 to March 31, and this is a non-motorised area. The Mount St. Helens climbing permit is still required for anyone above 4,800 feet, but through the winter window it is free, self-issued at the trailhead and unlimited — the single easiest time of year to climb this mountain from a paperwork point of view. The 4,800-foot camping prohibition applies in winter exactly as it does in summer.
bivy.capacity: Two large plowed lots plus adjacent forest; winter parties routinely pitch tents in and beside the lots, so capacity is generous and informal rather than defined

bivy.name: Commonwealth Basin and Red Pond
bivy.notes: This is the natural overnight for Lundin Peak and for Red Mountain, and it is the only site here that sits directly beneath its objectives rather than across a ridge from them. From the pass the PCT runs north about two and a half miles before the Commonwealth Basin trail branches left and climbs the basin; spur paths reach Red Pond at around three and a half to four miles, with Red Pass another half mile above at roughly 5,400 ft. Red Mountain's scramble leaves from near the pass, and Lundin's west ridge is gained by traversing the ridge crest west from the same ground, so a camp at the pond removes the entire approach from the summit day. Be honest about the trade: both peaks are comfortable day climbs car-to-car and most parties do them that way, so this is a way to buy a relaxed morning or to rescue a late finish rather than a necessity. The basin is snowbound and avalanche-prone well into spring, and the old trail below the pond is steep and eroded in places.
bivy.water: The creek through Commonwealth Basin runs all summer and Red Pond holds water into autumn. Treat everything. The upper basin melts out late and can be entirely snow-covered into early July.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the PCT trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to October 31. Party size capped at 12. Unlike Melakwa, Snow and Gravel Lakes, this basin is NOT on the designated-sites-only list, so dispersed camping is legal here — which puts the whole burden on siting well, on durable ground and away from the water. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft, which covers the pond and the upper basin. Parking at the exit 52 trailhead takes a Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass; in winter the lot becomes a Sno-Park and needs the state permit instead. No drones anywhere in the wilderness.
bivy.capacity: Informal established sites scattered through the basin and a small amount of level ground by the pond; a handful of parties rather than a large camp

bivy.name: Melakwa Lake and Upper Melakwa Lake designated sites
bivy.notes: The camp for Kaleetan Peak and Bryant Peak, and the reason both are practical objectives at all. It is about four and a quarter miles and 2,700 ft from the Denny Creek trailhead, over Hemlock Pass at roughly 4,600 ft and down to the lake just below it. Kaleetan's south ridge leaves the far end of the basin and turns immediately into steep talus and loose ridge scrambling; Bryant's southeast slopes rise straight out of the basin on the opposite side. Doing either from the car is a long day with the approach done twice, and this is one of the few places in the zone where camping genuinely changes the character of the climb rather than just the start time. The counterweight is that Denny Creek is one of the busiest trails in the state and the designated sites are few, so arriving on a Saturday afternoon expecting a spot is a poor plan. Snow lingers in the basin into July and the slopes above it hold avalanche hazard much later than the trail suggests.
bivy.water: Both lakes are reliable through the season, as is the outlet stream. Treat it. Frozen and snow-covered in winter and early spring.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Denny Creek trailhead, roughly May 15 to October 31. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Melakwa Lake — this basin is explicitly on the designated-sites-only list and dispersed camping around the shore is not allowed. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the crest, so the whole basin is stove-only. Party size capped at 12. Trailhead parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass, or the state Sno-Park permit in winter.
bivy.capacity: A limited number of established sites split between the two lakes; small, and taken early on summer weekends

bivy.name: Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, PCT beyond Kendall Katwalk
bivy.notes: These sit about seven and a half miles out on the PCT, a mile or so past the Kendall Katwalk. For Kendall Peak itself they are past the objective — the scramble leaves the PCT well before the Katwalk — so this is a contingency rather than a plan for that peak. Their real value is as the only established camp on the crest walk north, which is what makes a PCT approach to Huckleberry Mountain and Chikamin Peak thinkable at all: from here the trail keeps north past Alaska Mountain toward Huckleberry, with Chikamin beyond that. Treat the Katwalk itself as the gate on the season. It is a narrow shelf blasted into a cliff and it is genuinely dangerous with snow on it, so the practical window here is mid-summer to early autumn rather than whenever the road is open. The ridge is exposed to weather with nowhere to retreat below treeline for miles.
bivy.water: Both lakes hold water through summer; treat it. Late-season they drop and the ground around them gets trampled and dusty. No running water on the ridge between here and the pass.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the exit 52 PCT trailhead. Gravel Lake is on the designated-sites-only list, so camp only at established sites within half a mile of it. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this trail, which means the entire segment including both lakes — stoves only. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park; the lot is a Sno-Park in winter.
bivy.capacity: Several established sites split between the two small lakes; exposed, limited, and popular with through-hikers as well as weekend parties

bivy.name: Rachel Lake designated sites
bivy.notes: This is the base for Alta Mountain and for Hibox Mountain, and it belongs to a completely different approach than the Alpental peaks — I-90 exit 62 to Kachess Lake, then Box Canyon Road up to the trailhead at about 2,800 ft. The trail runs an easy few miles up Box Canyon Creek and then climbs hard and rootily to the lake at four and a bit miles. Alta is reached by continuing over the ridge crest above the lake; Hibox leaves the trail lower down, at around 3,300 ft, on a steep boot path onto Box Ridge. Both are day scrambles from the car for a fit party, so a night here is about a civilised start or a plan that ran long. The honest caveat is the state of the basin: it is one of the most hammered lake basins in the wilderness, the parking lot fills by mid-morning in summer, and the designated sites exist because dispersed camping wrecked the shoreline. Snow-free window is roughly July into October.
bivy.water: The lake and Box Canyon Creek are reliable all season. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Rachel Lake trailhead, filled out at the box and carried for the trip. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of Rachel Lake and Rampart Lakes. Campfires are banned outright within half a mile of Rachel Lake and everywhere above 5,000 ft on this side of the crest, so plan on stoves regardless of where you end up. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the trailhead, or a small daily fee. No drones. As of August 2026 the Box Canyon road and this trailhead were inside a wildfire closure order affecting a large part of the eastern Alpine Lakes; confirm the trailhead is actually open before driving to it.
bivy.capacity: Multiple established sites around the lake, but the basin is visibly damaged from decades of overuse and the hardened sites are what is left

bivy.name: Rampart Lakes basin
bivy.notes: A shelf of small lakes on the south side of Alta Mountain, reached by climbing north out of the Rachel Lake basin to the ridge crest at about 5,100 ft and then contouring west for most of a mile. Roughly six miles and 2,500 ft from the trailhead. For Alta Mountain's Rampart Ridge scramble this is better placed than Rachel Lake itself, since the ridge walk to the summit starts from the crest junction just above the basin rather than from the lake below it. Camping high also means camping exposed: the shelf is open, weather arrives with no warning, and there is nothing to shelter behind. Late July through September is the realistic season, and the basin is a well-known destination in its own right, so expect to share it.
bivy.water: The tarns hold water through the season. Treat it. They are shallow and warm late in summer, so draw from the inlets where you can.
bivy.permit: Same free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit as Rachel Lake, from the Rachel Lake trailhead box. Designated sites only within half a mile of the lakes. No campfires anywhere above 5,000 ft on this side, and the whole basin sits above that line — stoves only, without exception. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Subject to the same 2026 wildfire closure of the Box Canyon approach; check before committing.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites spread across the shelf between the tarns; more room than Rachel Lake but correspondingly busier on weekends

bivy.name: Alaska Lake and Joe Lake, Gold Creek
bivy.notes: The direct way into Chikamin Peak and Huckleberry Mountain from the freeway, off Gold Creek Pond on the north shore of Keechelus Lake. Be clear-eyed about what this is: the Gold Creek trail is maintained for about five miles and then stops being a trail. Beyond the junction it is overgrown with vine maple and alder and crosses talus, and the two branches beyond it are steep bootpaths — left a mile to Alaska Lake at about 4,230 ft, right up the valley and then very steeply to Joe Lake at about 4,620 ft. Joe Lake sits under Alaska Mountain with Huckleberry Mountain immediately north across the PCT, which makes it the closest sleeping ground to Huckleberry's west route. Chikamin lies further north again along the crest. Elevation recorded is Alaska Lake, the lower of the two. This is a route-finding exercise in brush, not a hike, and it is at its worst in high summer when the vegetation is up. Parties who want a trail instead should take the PCT and sleep at Ridge and Gravel Lakes.
bivy.water: Both lakes are reliable, as is Gold Creek the whole way up the valley. Treat it. Water is not the problem here — the approach is.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Neither lake is on the designated-sites-only list, so dispersed camping is legal, which makes careful siting on durable ground your responsibility. Campfires prohibited above 4,000 ft, so both lakes are stove-only. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the Gold Creek Pond parking. As of August 2026 the PCT above this valley was inside a large wildfire closure; check current status before planning anything on this side of the crest.
bivy.capacity: Rough informal sites at both lakes; small, unimproved, and reached by boot paths rather than maintained trail

bivy.name: Park Lakes basin
bivy.notes: The standard camp for Chikamin Peak's southeast slopes, and the reason Chikamin is the peak in this group least honestly described as a Snoqualmie Pass objective. Most parties reach it from Mineral Creek on the far eastern side, walking up from a trailhead at around 2,375 ft — an approach that begins nowhere near I-90 exit 52. From the pass it is reachable instead by the PCT north over Chikamin Pass, which is a long day in itself. Upper Park Lake sits at about 4,700 ft in open meadow and rolling ground with roomy sites, and a short side trail drops around 550 ft to Glacier Lake where there are more sites on the north shore among boulders and heather. From the basin the southeast slopes rise directly toward the summit. Note the campfire ban is specific to this basin rather than an elevation rule, and it is enforced — the meadows are fragile and the ground here recovers slowly.
bivy.water: The lakes and the basin outlets run all season. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at whichever trailhead you start from. Campfires are prohibited in the Park Lakes basin outright, and above 5,000 ft generally on this side of the crest. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. The eastern approaches were inside the 2026 wildfire closure area; confirm before driving out.
bivy.capacity: Large established sites among trees and meadow at Upper Park Lake, comfortable for a group; more sites at Glacier Lake below

bivy.name: Kachess Campground, I-90 exit 62
bivy.notes: The drive-in answer for the eastern half of this zone, and the one you pass on the way to Box Canyon Road, so it is the sensible place to sleep the night before an Alta Mountain or Hibox Mountain day rather than driving over the pass at four in the morning. It is a lakeside family campground rather than anything resembling a climbers' camp, and it fills on summer weekends, so book rather than arrive hopeful. It sits low, on the shore of Kachess Lake, well below the trailhead. If it is full there is unreserved dispersed camping along the logging road toward the Rachel Lake trailhead, which is rough and unimproved but free and closer to the walk-in.
bivy.water: Drinking water is provided during the operating season.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, most sites reservable in advance and the remainder first-come. No wilderness permit required to sleep here and no trailhead pass needed for the campground itself. Seasonal operation only — it closes outside the summer months, so it is not a winter option. As of August 2026 this campground was among those closed by the wildfire order covering the north end of Kachess Lake; check it is open before relying on it.
bivy.capacity: Large developed Forest Service campground of roughly 150 tent and RV sites plus a group site; a mix of reservable and first-come, and very busy in summer

bivy.capacity: A limited number of established sites split between the two lakes; small, and taken early on summer weekends
