Campfires prohibited above 4,000 ft, so both lakes are stove-only. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the Gold Creek Pond parking. As of August 2026 the PCT above this valley was inside a large wildfire closure; check current status before planning anything on this side of the crest.
bivy.capacity: Rough informal sites at both lakes; small, unimproved, and reached by boot paths rather than maintained trail

bivy.name: Park Lakes basin
bivy.notes: The standard camp for Chikamin Peak's southeast slopes, and the reason Chikamin is the peak in this group least honestly described as a Snoqualmie Pass objective. Most parties reach it from Mineral Creek on the far eastern side, walking up from a trailhead at around 2,375 ft — an approach that begins nowhere near I-90 exit 52. From the pass it is reachable instead by the PCT north over Chikamin Pass, which is a long day in itself. Upper Park Lake sits at about 4,700 ft in open meadow and rolling ground with roomy sites, and a short side trail drops around 550 ft to Glacier Lake where there are more sites on the north shore among boulders and heather. From the basin the southeast slopes rise directly toward the summit. Note the campfire ban is specific to this basin rather than an elevation rule, and it is enforced — the meadows are fragile and the ground here recovers slowly.
bivy.water: The lakes and the basin outlets run all season. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at whichever trailhead you start from. Campfires are prohibited in the Park Lakes basin outright, and above 5,000 ft generally on this side of the crest. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. The eastern approaches were inside the 2026 wildfire closure area; confirm before driving out.
bivy.capacity: Large established sites among trees and meadow at Upper Park Lake, comfortable for a group; more sites at Glacier Lake below

bivy.name: Kachess Campground, I-90 exit 62
bivy.notes: The drive-in answer for the eastern half of this zone, and the one you pass on the way to Box Canyon Road, so it is the sensible place to sleep the night before an Alta Mountain or Hibox Mountain day rather than driving over the pass at four in the morning. It is a lakeside family campground rather than anything resembling a climbers' camp, and it fills on summer weekends, so book rather than arrive hopeful. It sits low, on the shore of Kachess Lake, well below the trailhead. If it is full there is unreserved dispersed camping along the logging road toward the Rachel Lake trailhead, which is rough and unimproved but free and closer to the walk-in.
bivy.water: Drinking water is provided during the operating season.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, most sites reservable in advance and the remainder first-come. No wilderness permit required to sleep here and no trailhead pass needed for the campground itself. Seasonal operation only — it closes outside the summer months, so it is not a winter option. As of August 2026 this campground was among those closed by the wildfire order covering the north end of Kachess Lake; check it is open before relying on it.
bivy.capacity: Large developed Forest Service campground of roughly 150 tent and RV sites plus a group site; a mix of reservable and first-come, and very busy in summer

bivy.name: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps
bivy.notes: The workhorse camp of the entire western half of this zone. From the trailhead at the north end of Cooper Lake the trail runs about four gentle miles along the Cooper River to Pete Lake, and roughly two and a half more to the Lemah Meadows area and the Pacific Crest Trail junction. Parties bound for Lemah Mountain and Lemah Two leave the trail here and follow a climbers' path up the north side of Lemah Creek past waterfalls to the meadow at about 3,600 ft, where the creek spreads into shallow ponds; camp at the far end, and expect a thicket of slide alder that is best turned in the timber to the north rather than fought through. Parties bound for Chimney Rock also pass through, but leave the PCT further north — see the Chimney Glacier basin entry. Pete Lake itself is low, forested and mosquito-ridden in early summer, and it is a long way from any summit, so it works as a first-night camp or a bail-out rather than a climbing base. Season is roughly July into October; the valley clears early but the basins above hold snow well into July. The Cooper River road is paved then gravel and passenger-car friendly. Honest caveat for 2026: the Pete Lake trail was inside a large wildfire closure on the Cle Elum Ranger District through late summer, with the closure scheduled to run to the end of October and subject to change — confirm the trail is open before driving out.
bivy.water: Reliable all season — the lake itself, the Cooper River along the trail, and Lemah Creek and its north fork above the meadows
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead board, filled out and carried. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve including stock. Campfires are legal at these elevations but the lakeshore is heavily used and a stove is the better manners; no fires above 5,000 ft anywhere in this wilderness.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites around Pete Lake, enough for a dozen or more parties on a summer weekend; the meadow camps beyond are informal and hold two or three tents each

bivy.name: Chimney Glacier hanging basin — the big boulder bivy
bivy.notes: THIS IS CHIMNEY ROCK'S REAL BASE, and it is the reason parties take the Cle Elum side rather than the Middle Fork. From Pete Lake continue to the PCT, turn north, and at the second switchback where the trail starts up toward Waptus Pass leave it westward through open forest, dropping slightly to the North Fork of Lemah Creek at around 3,380 ft. Cross on a log — the crossing is the crux of the approach in high water — and find the boot path on the far side, marked by a large cairn with faded flagging for the first couple of hundred feet. It climbs steeply, roughly 1,400 ft, into the hanging basin below the Chimney Glacier. Aim for the huge boulder near the creek in the middle of the basin. Round trip from the car is on the order of thirty miles for the peak, so this is a two- or three-night trip for most parties, and it puts the East Face and East Face Direct within a reasonable summit day. The same basin serves the standard West Face and South Summit line by way of the glacier and the notch. Best from mid-July to mid-September: earlier and the glacier crossing is straightforward but the approach is a snow slog, later and the ice is bare and crevassed. Expect no company. The alternative from the Middle Fork is described under the Dutch Miller Gap entry and is longer, rougher and more committing for the same summit — the Pete Lake side is the right answer unless the Cle Elum roads are closed.
bivy.water: Meltwater creek running through the basin, dependable while the glacier is melting; late in a dry September it can shrink and want a walk uphill
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Pete Lake trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited — this is well above 5,000 ft in a fragile basin with no wood to spare. Camp on rock or snow, not on the heather.
bivy.capacity: Small. Three or so flat spots around one enormous boulder, including two single-person rectangles tucked under its overhung south side; comfortably two to four climbers, tight beyond that

bivy.name: Escondido Ridge tarns
bivy.notes: The high camp on the Pacific Crest Trail between Lemah Meadows and Waptus Pass, reached by the long string of switchbacks up onto Escondido Ridge. It is the camp for Little Big Chief Mountain from the south and west, and for the string of Chief summits along that crest. Escondido Lake itself sits below the trail and is invisible from it — the name means hidden and it is earned — so most parties camp on the ridge bench rather than dropping to the lake. That view is the reason to be here, and it is also a warning — this is an exposed ridge camp with no shelter in a thunderstorm and no water you can count on. From here Little Big Chief is a long traversing day rather than a short one; parties who want a shorter summit day come at it from Chief Creek on the Waptus side instead. Snow lingers on the switchbacks into July. Honest caveat for 2026: this stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail and its eastern access trails were inside the summer fire closure — verify before committing.
bivy.water: Small tarns and seasonal snowmelt only. They are shallow, they warm up and they can dry out by late September — treat everything and carry a reserve late in the year.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Pete Lake trailhead. Group limit twelve. Above 5,000 ft, so campfires are prohibited outright; the bench is exposed and there is nothing to burn anyway.
bivy.capacity: A broad open bench with several flat tent sites and small tarns scattered nearby; four or five parties could spread out without crowding each other

bivy.name: Waptus Lake, with Spade Lake above it
bivy.notes: Waptus is roughly nine miles of easy river trail from Salmon la Sac with only about 800 ft of gain, which makes it the least strenuous long approach in the zone and a genuinely pleasant first night. For climbers here it is the eastern gateway to LITTLE BIG CHIEF MOUNTAIN, which sits immediately southwest of Dutch Miller Gap. The useful camps for that peak are not at the lake but a couple of miles further up the valley, near the bridge over the Waptus River above the lake and near the ford of Chief Creek — call it twelve miles in — and from there the climb is a straight 4,000 ft of off-trail work to the northeast face scramble. Spade Lake is the other well-known destination above Waptus and it is worth being clear about what it is and is not: the spur trail gains nearly 3,000 ft in about three miles of steep, downed-timber forest with scrambly and overgrown sections, and it lands in a rocky cirque on the flank of Mount Daniel. It is a superb, lonely camp and it is NOT a base for Chimney Rock, which lies across the valley on the other side of the crest. Snow lingers in the Spade cirque into July. Honest caveat for 2026: the Waptus and Spade trails were both inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer — check the status of the closure order before driving to Salmon la Sac.
bivy.water: Waptus Lake, the Waptus River and Chief Creek at the lower camps; the lake and small inlet streams at Spade
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Salmon la Sac trailhead. Group limit twelve including stock — this is horse country and the trail is shared. Campfires are permitted at Waptus but banned at Spade and everywhere else above 5,000 ft. Camp at least a hundred feet back from water and off the meadows.
bivy.capacity: Large — Waptus has upwards of two dozen established sites strung along the shore and near the outlet, first come first served. Spade Lake above is the opposite: scattered bluff sites for a party or two.

bivy.name: Park Lakes Basin
bivy.notes: The base for THREE QUEENS, and the reason that peak sits in this zone at all — it shares the Cooper River road with Pete Lake and nothing else. Drive the Cooper River road past Cooper Lake and over Cooper Pass to the Mineral Creek trailhead at around 2,375 ft, then follow the Mineral Creek trail roughly four and a half miles and 2,300 ft up to the basin. The trail crosses Mineral Creek several times on logs and rocks, and in high water those crossings are the hardest part of the day — early season parties should expect at least one that is genuinely unpleasant. From the basin the standard scramble goes up loose slabs, talus and heather to the ridge, and the middle peak's south face and south chimney and the west peak's west ridge are reached from the same camp with a traverse. The rock is loose and the notch below the summit block is exposed with no obvious easy line, so this is a scramble that repays a rope more often than its grade suggests. Many parties skip the camp entirely and do Three Queens as a long day from the car, which is honest and reasonable in good conditions — the basin is worth a night mainly if you want two of the three summits. Best late July through September. Honest caveat for 2026: the Mineral Creek trail was closed by the summer wildfire that took its name from this very peak, along with the Spectacle Lake access and a long stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail; the closure ran into autumn and must be confirmed before any trip.
bivy.water: The lakes and their connecting streams, plus Glacier Lake just above — reliable through the season
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Mineral Creek trailhead. Group limit twelve. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED IN PARK LAKES BASIN specifically, in addition to the general ban above 5,000 ft. Stay off the meadow edges.
bivy.capacity: Several established sites among the trees, meadows and rolling knolls of the basin; three or four parties fit without being on top of each other

bivy.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
bivy.notes: The staging camp for the whole Middle Fork half of this zone, and the answer to the question of what to do with a seven-mile road walk. Forest Road 56 is rough — potholes, ruts and washed river-rock sections that want high clearance — and it is GATED AT DINGFORD CREEK, so the last roughly seven miles to the horse camp are closed road with about 1,300 ft of gain. That stretch is legal and pleasant to bike and most parties do, then walk from here; a mountain bike is the right tool, a gravel bike is survivable. The camp itself is low, forested and buggy, but it is quiet and it sits at the foot of everything. BURNT BOOT PEAK is climbed from here by fording the Middle Fork — cold and thigh-deep at ordinary summer flows, and not to be attempted in high water — and then working up the northwest side to the gully system and the northeast gully at around 5,800 ft. The boot path to Hardscrabble Lakes leaves the old road about half a mile below the camp, marked by a large broken log lying across the road; it is easy to walk past. Continuing up-valley on foot the trail runs about six more miles to the old Camp Pedro area and on toward Dutch Miller Gap. Season is May into October at this elevation, but the peaks above hold snow until July.
bivy.water: The Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Hardscrabble Creek, both right at camp and both reliable
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the gate. Group limit twelve including stock. Fires are legal at this elevation and the camp has established rings, but wood is picked over and summer burn bans are common on this district.
bivy.capacity: Large — an old horse camp with a broad clearing and riverside sites near Hardscrabble Creek; several parties, stock included

bivy.name: Upper Hardscrabble Lake
bivy.notes: The high camp for BIG SNOW MOUNTAIN's east ridge, which is the easier and much less confusing of that peak's two routes. From the boot path junction on the old road the trail climbs steeply and roughly to lower Hardscrabble Lake at about 4,060 ft, and the upper lake is another half mile and 500 ft above it. The path is a climbers' track, not a maintained trail, and the section between the lakes is slabby, brushy and locally class 3 or 4 — this is the hardest walking on the route. From the upper lake the east ridge route goes over a pass at roughly 5,760 ft and then along to the summit at 6,680 ft, with a final few hundred feet that often want microspikes well into summer. The alternative north slope route from Dingford Creek is shorter on paper and involves serious route-finding and bushwhacking whose difficulty depends entirely on how much snow is still lying; parties who have done both generally recommend the east ridge unless the north side is still filled in. The same camp is the natural start for the high traverse west toward IRON CAP MOUNTAIN. Season is essentially August and September; earlier and the slabs below the lakes are running with meltwater. Unlike the Cle Elum-side camps in this zone, the Middle Fork approach was outside the 2026 fire closure — which is the one situation in which the western approach to this range is the correct choice.
bivy.water: The lake, plus snowmelt runnels early in the season
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Below 5,000 ft by a small margin, but treat it as a no-fire camp regardless — the benches are thin-soiled and there is nothing to burn.
bivy.capacity: Small and rough — a handful of flat spots on benches and slabs near the outlet, two or three tents at most

bivy.name: Williams Lake and the upper Middle Fork meadows below Dutch Miller Gap
bivy.notes: The upper-valley camp of the Middle Fork, and the base for IRON CAP MOUNTAIN's south route. From the Dingford Creek gate it is about seven miles of closed road to the horse camp and roughly seven more of trail up the valley — the last stretch through avalanche slopes, wildflowers and deep bracken fern depending on the season — to the Williams Lake junction. Williams Lake sits about half a mile off the main trail and is genuinely secluded, with a good view across to Little Big Chief. From these meadows the route to Iron Cap climbs toward La Bohn Gap and then takes the ridge, with a bit of exposure but generally easy scrambling to the true summit. Two things to be honest about. First, this is a fourteen-mile approach before any climbing starts, so Iron Cap from here is a three-day objective for most parties. Second, La Bohn Gap is equally reachable from Necklace Valley on the East Fork Foss River off Highway 2, on the north side of the divide — a completely separate drive and a shorter approach to the gap, and the right choice if Iron Cap alone is the objective. Come this way when Big Snow, Burnt Boot or the western side of Chimney Rock and Overcoat are also on the list. The same trail continues over Dutch Miller Gap to the Waptus valley, so the Middle Fork and Cle Elum halves of this zone are linked on foot even though they are hours apart by road. Beyond Camp Pedro the route toward Overcoat and Chimney Rock climbs steeply and brushily into the rocky corridor between the Chief summits and crosses a pass at about 6,140 ft to reach the Overcoat Glacier — long, committing, and the reason the Pete Lake side is the standard for Chimney Rock.
bivy.water: Williams Lake, the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River, and tarns and snowmelt in the meadows toward the gap
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited on the higher benches above 5,000 ft; keep to durable ground and stay off the boggy meadow.
bivy.capacity: Williams Lake holds a small number of quiet sites, a party or two; the heather and huckleberry benches nearer the gap are informal and can absorb a few more

bivy.name: Peggy's Pond and Squaw Lake, Cathedral Pass
bivy.notes: The base for CATHEDRAL ROCK, which sits at the far eastern end of this zone and shares nothing but a wilderness boundary with the Middle Fork peaks. Drive the Cle Elum River road north from Salmon la Sac about twelve miles to the Deception Pass and Tucquala Meadows trailhead at the road end; the road is rough gravel with a creek crossing and wants a bit of clearance, and parking is limited enough that you may walk in from further down. Take the Cathedral Pass trail — not the Deception Pass trail, which leaves the same lot — past Squaw Lake at about 4,800 ft and up easy switchbacks to the pass at roughly 5,600 ft, then the spur west to Peggy's Pond directly beneath the rock. That spur has a short exposed scrambly section that is a genuine obstacle for some parties carrying overnight packs. From the pond the standard southwest face route and the northwest couloir are both short summit days, which is the whole appeal — this is the one peak in the zone with a real climb at the end of a modest approach. The northwest couloir holds snow and is an early-season line; the southwest face is the summer scramble. Hyas Lake, at around 3,550 ft on the Deception Pass trail less than two miles from the same lot, is the low-effort alternative camp with plenty of sites, but it adds 2,000 ft to summit day and is better as a family basecamp than a climbers' one. Honest caveat for 2026: the Deception Pass trail and this whole area were inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer, scheduled to run to the end of October — check before driving out.
bivy.water: Peggy's Pond itself and the snowmelt feeding it; Squaw Lake below. Both reliable through the normal season.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Peggy's Pond carries a reduced group limit — plan on eight rather than twelve, and midweek is the realistic window for a group of that size. Campfires prohibited: the pond is above 5,000 ft and the basin is heavily used and fragile. Camp on the established pads only.
bivy.capacity: Peggy's Pond has roughly four well-levelled bivouac spots plus one on a slight slope — small, and it fills. Squaw Lake lower down has a couple of good sites and is the overflow.

bivy.name: Williams Lake and the upper Middle Fork meadows below Dutch Miller Gap

bivy.name: Peggy's Pond and Squaw Lake, Cathedral Pass

bivy.name: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps

bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead board, filled out and carried. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve including stock. bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites around Pete Lake, enough for a dozen or more parties on a summer weekend; the meadow camps beyond are informal and hold two or three tents each

bivy.name: Park Lakes Basin

bivy.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie

bivy.name: Upper Hardscrabble Lake

bivy.name: Williams Lake and the upper Middle Fork meadows below Dutch Miller Gap

bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited on the higher benches above 5,000 ft; keep to durable ground and stay off the boggy meadow.
bivy.capacity: Williams Lake holds a small number of quiet sites, a party or two; the heather and huckleberry benches nearer the gap are informal and can absorb a few more

bivy.name: Peggy's Pond and Squaw Lake, Cathedral Pass

bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Campfires prohibited: the pond is above 5,000 ft and the basin is heavily used and fragile. Camp on the established pads only.

bivy.name: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps

bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead board, filled out and carried. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve including stock. Campfires are legal at these elevations but the lakeshore is heavily used and a stove is the better manners; no fires above 5,000 ft anywhere in this wilderness.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites around Pete Lake, enough for a dozen or more parties on a summer weekend; the meadow camps beyond are informal and hold two or three tents each

bivy.name: Chimney Glacier hanging basin — the big boulder bivy

From Pete Lake continue to the PCT, turn north, and at the second switchback where the trail starts up toward Waptus Pass leave it westward through open forest, dropping slightly to the North Fork of Lemah Creek at around 3,380 ft. It climbs steeply, roughly 1,400 ft, into the hanging basin below the Chimney Glacier. Aim for the huge boulder near the creek in the middle of the basin. The same basin serves the standard West Face and South Summit line by way of the glacier and the notch. Best from mid-July to mid-September: earlier and the glacier crossing is straightforward but the approach is a snow slog, later and the ice is bare and crevassed. Expect no company. The alternative from the Middle Fork is described under the Dutch Miller Gap entry and is longer, rougher and more committing for the same summit — the Pete Lake side is the right answer unless the Cle Elum roads are closed.

bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Pete Lake trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited — this is well above 5,000 ft in a fragile basin with no wood to spare. Camp on rock or snow, not on the heather.
bivy.capacity: Small. Three or so flat spots around one enormous boulder, including two single-person rectangles tucked under its overhung south side; comfortably two to four climbers, tight beyond that

bivy.name: Escondido Ridge tarns

Honest caveat for 2026: this stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail and its eastern access trails were inside the summer fire closure — verify before committing.

bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Pete Lake trailhead. Group limit twelve. Above 5,000 ft, so campfires are prohibited outright; the bench is exposed and there is nothing to burn anyway.

bivy.name: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps

bivy.name: Chimney Glacier hanging basin — the big boulder bivy

bivy.name: Waptus Lake, with Spade Lake above it

bivy.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie

bivy.name: Upper Hardscrabble Lake

bivy.capacity: Small and rough — a handful of flat spots on benches and slabs near the outlet, two or three tents at most

bivy.capacity: Williams Lake holds a small number of quiet sites, a party or two; the heather and huckleberry benches nearer the gap are informal and can absorb a few more

bivy.name: Williams Lake and the upper Middle Fork meadows below Dutch Miller Gap

bivy.name: Peggy's Pond and Squaw Lake, Cathedral Pass

bivy.name: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps

bivy.name: Park Lakes Basin

bivy.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie

bivy.name: Upper Hardscrabble Lake

bivy.name: Williams Lake and the upper Middle Fork meadows below Dutch Miller Gap

bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited on the higher benches above 5,000 ft; keep to durable ground and stay off the boggy meadow.
bivy.capacity: Williams Lake holds a small number of quiet sites, a party or two; the heather and huckleberry benches nearer the gap are informal and can absorb a few more

bivy.name: Peggy's Pond and Squaw Lake, Cathedral Pass

bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Peggy's Pond carries a reduced group limit — plan on eight rather than twelve, and midweek is the realistic window for a group of that size. Campfires prohibited: the pond is above 5,000 ft and the basin is heavily used and fragile. Camp on the established pads only.

bivy.name: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps

bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead board, filled out and carried. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve including stock. bivy.name: Escondido Ridge tarns

The bench is flat, broad and open, with the whole Snoqualmie crest laid out across the valley: Summit Chief, Chimney Rock, Overcoat, Lemah, Bears Breast and Mount Daniel. Honest caveat for 2026: this stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail and its eastern access trails were inside the summer fire closure — verify before committing.

bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Pete Lake trailhead. Group limit twelve. Above 5,000 ft, so campfires are prohibited outright; the bench is exposed and there is nothing to burn anyway.

The useful camps for that peak are not at the lake but a couple of miles further up the valley, near the bridge over the Waptus River above the lake and near the ford of Chief Creek — call it twelve miles in — and from there the climb is a straight 4,000 ft of off-trail work to the northeast face scramble. Honest caveat for 2026: the Waptus and Spade trails were both inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer — check the status of the closure order before driving to Salmon la Sac.

bivy.name: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps

bivy.name: Waptus Lake, with Spade Lake above it

bivy.capacity: Williams Lake holds a small number of quiet sites, a party or two; the heather and huckleberry benches nearer the gap are informal and can absorb a few more

bivy.name: Williams Lake and the upper Middle Fork meadows below Dutch Miller Gap

bivy.name: Peggy's Pond and Squaw Lake, Cathedral Pass

bivy.name: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps

bivy.name: Chimney Glacier hanging basin — the big boulder bivy

bivy.capacity: Small. Three or so flat spots around one enormous boulder, including two single-person rectangles tucked under its overhung south side; comfortably two to four climbers, tight beyond that

bivy.capacity: Several established sites among the trees, meadows and rolling knolls of the basin; three or four parties fit without being on top of each other

bivy.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie

bivy.name: Waptus Lake, with Spade Lake above it

bivy.name: Park Lakes Basin

bivy.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie

bivy.name: Upper Hardscrabble Lake

bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Below 5,000 ft by a small margin, but treat it as a no-fire camp regardless — the benches are thin-soiled and there is nothing to burn.
bivy.capacity: Small and rough — a handful of flat spots on benches and slabs near the outlet, two or three tents at most

bivy.name: Williams Lake and the upper Middle Fork meadows below Dutch Miller Gap

bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited on the higher benches above 5,000 ft; keep to durable ground and stay off the boggy meadow.
bivy.capacity: Williams Lake holds a small number of quiet sites, a party or two; the heather and huckleberry benches nearer the gap are informal and can absorb a few more

bivy.name: Peggy's Pond and Squaw Lake, Cathedral Pass

Campfires prohibited: the pond is above 5,000 ft and the basin is heavily used and fragile. Camp on the established pads only.

bivy.name: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps

bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead board, filled out and carried. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve including stock. Campfires are legal at these elevations but the lakeshore is heavily used and a stove is the better manners; no fires above 5,000 ft anywhere in this wilderness.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites around Pete Lake, enough for a dozen or more parties on a summer weekend; the meadow camps beyond are informal and hold two or three tents each

bivy.name: Chimney Glacier hanging basin — the big boulder bivy

The alternative from the Middle Fork is described under the Dutch Miller Gap entry and is longer, rougher and more committing for the same summit — the Pete Lake side is the right answer unless the Cle Elum roads are closed.

bivy.capacity: A handful of designated tent spots with a shared cooking area and a backcountry toilet; a second toilet sits at the pass itself

bivy.name: Boundary Camp
bivy.notes: Boundary sits just over Hannegan Pass at the line where Forest Service ground becomes national park, which is exactly why it trips people up: you park under a Northwest Forest Pass and then sleep under an NPS permit. With only three sites it books out on summer weekends, and a party arriving without a reservation has no legal fallback nearby. It is the natural first night for anything heading down the Chilliwack or up onto Copper Ridge. Fire closures in 2026 affected camps and trails on this side of the pass, so check the park's current closure page rather than assuming a reservation implies open ground.
bivy.water: A nearby subalpine stream normally runs through the climbing season, though it is a snowmelt source and thins out late
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, obtained through the park's reservation system and picked up in person at Marblemount. Campfires are not allowed here.
bivy.capacity: Three designated sites, each rated for up to four people, with a pit toilet

bivy.name: Copper Lake Camp, Copper Ridge
bivy.notes: Of the three camps strung along Copper Ridge, this is the one that solves water: the others are drier, and one is normally described as having no water source at all, which forces a long carry from lower down. That makes it the sensible high camp for anyone using the ridge as a high traverse toward the Chilliwack drainage rather than dropping straight into the valley. The ridge is exposed and the sites are small, so a party of more than four has to split across permits. Copper Ridge and the wider Copper Loop were inside the 2026 fire closure footprint, and burned ground stays hazardous for years afterward.
bivy.water: The lake is immediately at hand and reliable all season — a real advantage on this ridge
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, picked up at Marblemount. Food, rubbish and scented items must go in the provided lockers or an approved canister.
bivy.capacity: Designated sites for parties of up to four, with a composting toilet and food-storage lockers

bivy.name: US Cabin Camp, Chilliwack River
bivy.notes: A deep-forest valley camp rather than a climbing bivy, and its value is positional — it is roughly where a party bound for Bear Mountain or the peaks further up the drainage stops before leaving the trail. The lack of a food locker is worth planning around, because the neighbouring camps have them and it is easy to assume continuity. Old-growth valley bottom means it stays cool and damp, so expect wet gear in the morning. The Chilliwack River Trail was among the 2026 closures and its status should be confirmed before a trip is built around it.
bivy.water: The Chilliwack River is a few steps away and runs year round, though it carries glacial silt and needs filtering rather than just treating
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit from Marblemount. Unlike the ridge camps this one has NO food-storage hardware, so bring a canister or be prepared to hang.
bivy.capacity: Four sites, split between a pair near the trail and a pair down by the river, with a pit toilet

bivy.name: Ouzel Lake basin, head of Depot Creek
bivy.notes: For Redoubt and Spickard this is the standard high camp and the reason both peaks are usually done together: the sandy, largely treeless benches near the lake sit within reach of the glacier approaches to each. Getting there involves a steep, brushy climb beside a large waterfall on ground that has at times had fixed line in place, and the condition of that section is variable and should not be counted on. Some parties push higher and bivy nearer the Depot Glacier for an earlier start, trading comfort for time. NOT reachable from the Hannegan Pass trailhead — it must never be treated as an alternative camp on that approach.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet streams are dependable through the season, fed from the glaciers above
bivy.permit: THIS ONE IS DIFFERENT. The approach starts in BRITISH COLUMBIA — up Chilliwack Lake Road and onto the rough Depot Creek spur — and walks south across the international boundary on foot into Washington. There is no port of entry on this route, so the trip raises a genuine customs question in both directions that none of the Hannegan-side approaches do; sort out reporting obligations with the relevant border authorities before going, and carry passports. Once across, the camp is inside North Cascades National Park and a park backcountry permit applies, which is awkward given Marblemount is a long drive away on the other side of the range.
bivy.capacity: Open flat benches with room for several tents; informal, with no built sites, toilet or bear hardware

bivy.name: Basin below the Bear Mountain saddle
bivy.notes: The launching point for the north side of Bear Mountain, reached by leaving the Chilliwack valley trail and following a lightly marked line up the ridge toward treeline and then over into the basin. It is a long way in — most parties treat it as a second or third night rather than something reachable from the road — and the ground above the trail is faint enough that route-finding matters. accounts disagree on how usable the alternative approach from Chilliwack Lake in British Columbia is, with the cross-border stretch reported at times as heavy bushwhacking, so the length of the trail-based approach from Hannegan Pass is the price of certainty.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and tarns in the basin, reliable in early summer and can fail entirely by late season — carry water up if the year has been dry
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for a CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a designated camp, arranged at Marblemount. Zones are quota-limited with their own siting rules, so ask for the zone by name rather than assuming a valley camp reservation covers you.
bivy.capacity: Informal boulder-and-heather sites for a small party; no facilities of any kind

bivy.name: Wing Lake
bivy.notes: This is the working climbers' camp for Black Peak and the natural first night for Corteo as well. From the Rainy Pass west lot the loop trail is followed for a little over a mile, then a right fork leads to Heather Pass; from there a boot path crosses a boulder field and drops to Lewis Lake, and a further climb of about twelve hundred feet up the northwest slope reaches Wing Lake in the cirque under Black Peak. Reckon on four to six hours with a pack, and four to seven more from camp to summit and back. Camping here rather than at Lewis costs an hour on the way in and buys a much shorter summit day, which matters because everything above is talus and heather with route-finding rather than trail. The boundary detail is worth knowing: Black Peak's summit stands on the line between the forest and the national park, but this camp is on the forest side, so a party sleeping here needs no permit even though it is climbing a peak the park shares.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is dependable through the season. Snow patches under Black Peak feed it well into the autumn. Filter or treat.
bivy.permit: None. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, not the national park, so there is no backcountry permit, no quota and nothing to reserve. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass covers parking at Rainy Pass. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine from mid summer onward and at this elevation there is almost nothing to burn anyway, so plan on a stove and check the current order rather than assuming a fire is legal.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established pads in the boulders and heather around the outlet, most taking one or two tents. It is the best ground on this side of the peak and it fills on clear summer weekends and hard in larch season, so have Lewis Lake in mind as the fallback.

bivy.name: Lewis Lake
bivy.notes: Lewis sits in the bowl below Wing, reached by dropping off Heather Pass and picking a way through talus on goat paths around the left-hand shore. Most parties treat it as a waypoint rather than a destination, but it is a genuine camp and a sensible one for a late start, a heavy pack or a party that wants a shorter first day. It is also where the Corteo approach commits: from here the line follows the top of the moraine onto the Lewis Glacier and climbs southeast, bearing left at the top, to a notch on the ridge near seven thousand five hundred feet, then works west along the ridge and downclimbs several hundred feet of dirt or snow into the cirque under Corteo's west face, gaining the southwest ridge at a large notch by an easy gully. Nothing above Lewis is trail. Snow lingers on the traverse out of Heather Pass into early summer and an axe is worth carrying until it has gone.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet run all season. Reliable.
bivy.permit: None — national forest, no permit, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Rainy Pass.
bivy.capacity: A few sites around the shore, fewer and rougher than Wing Lake's. Adequate for a party or two, and the obvious answer when Wing is full or when weather turns on the way up.

bivy.name: Rainy Pass trailhead lots, and the quarter-mile camping closures
bivy.notes: This is the door to Black Peak and Corteo and the reason both are approachable in a weekend. It is also where the Pacific Crest Trail heads north, so the lots serve two entirely different sets of objectives and are busier than their size suggests. The closures above exist because the loop is one of the most walked trails in the state and its meadows were being trampled; they are enforced rather than advisory. Parties commonly sleep in the car here before an early start, and there is a toilet but no water. Everything depends on SR 20 being open — the highway shuts for the winter, usually in late November or early December, and reopens after avalanche control and snow clearing, most often between mid April and early May but occasionally very much later when a hard winter leaves washouts and rockslide damage behind it. Confirm the road is actually open before driving out from either side, and expect construction closures on this stretch in some seasons.
bivy.water: None at the pass. Fill in the valley or plan on filtering from the lakes once you are in.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. The rule that catches people out is a camping closure rather than a permit: no overnight camping within a quarter mile of Lake Ann, Rainy Lake, Heather Pass or Maple Pass, and none anywhere along the Heather-Maple Pass loop trail itself. Walk through to Lewis or Wing and you are legal with no paperwork; stop short of them and you are not.
bivy.capacity: Two large paved lots either side of the highway, with the Maple Pass loop starting from the west side. They fill early on summer and autumn weekends. This is staging and roadside parking, not a campground.

bivy.name: Easy Pass trailhead, SR 20
bivy.notes: This is the only practical trailhead for Mesahchie, Katsuk, Kimtah and Mount Arriva, and it is worth understanding what the walk in costs before committing to it. The trail climbs roughly three thousand feet in a little under four miles, gently through forest at first and then in steep switchbacks up a headwall of loose rock with real exposure to weather; the name is old optimism and nothing about it is easy under a climbing pack. Snow holds on the upper switchbacks and in the basin above into July in an ordinary year and later after a heavy winter, and that traverse is where parties turn around. There is a toilet at the lot and parties routinely sleep in the car here before a pre-dawn start. Dogs may come only as far as the pass, because the top of the pass is the national park boundary.
bivy.water: None at the lot. Granite Creek is crossed on a bridge a few minutes up the trail and is the last easy water low on the approach.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit is needed on the forest side of the pass. THE MOMENT YOU CROSS THE PASS THE RULES CHANGE COMPLETELY — see the Ragged Ridge and Fisher Creek entries below.
bivy.capacity: A small lot with room for roughly ten cars, on a short spur off the highway between mileposts 151 and 152. It is genuinely small and can be full on a good weekend.

bivy.name: Mesahchie basin, below the col
bivy.notes: This is the base for Mesahchie and the usual first night of any Ragged Ridge traverse. From Easy Pass the line goes cross-country west-northwest, sidehilling on heather and tiresome scree at around six thousand eight hundred feet for roughly three hours to reach the basin below Mesahchie Col. It is not a trail and it is not fast — talus, sidehill and sustained scrambling are the whole character of this ridge and parties consistently underestimate the traverse. From camp Mesahchie goes by its south side, Katsuk lies about half a mile further west along the crest by its south spur and east ridge, and Kimtah is beyond that again and is rarely worth a trip on its own. Note that camping is prohibited at Easy Pass itself and in the meadows around it, so this basin or the crest bivy is where the first legal ground is. All of it is inside the park, so leave the dog at home.
bivy.water: Running water in the basin, fed by snow above, and this is what recommends it over the ridge bivy higher up. It is the dependable choice late in a hot summer when the crest has dried out.
bivy.permit: NORTH CASCADES NATIONAL PARK backcountry permit required, without exception. Permits are reserved in advance through the national online reservation system and issued by park staff shortly before the trip, by email or in person at the wilderness desk in Marblemount, with a per-person recreation fee and a small booking fee on top. Camping is in a cross-country zone rather than at a named site, and an approved bear-resistant canister is required wherever there is nothing to hang food from, which up here is everywhere. No campfires; carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: Unimproved ground for a couple of small tents on benches in the basin under Mesahchie and Katsuk. Nothing is built here — no pads, no privy, no fire ring, and there should not be.

bivy.name: Ragged Ridge crest bivy, south of Mesahchie Col
bivy.notes: This is the higher and more committing of the two Ragged Ridge camps, about a mile west-northwest of Easy Pass. Two ways reach it: sidehill west at roughly six thousand eight hundred feet on heather and scree, or climb the grassy slope just past the pass to gain the crest near seven thousand two hundred feet and follow the ridge until the ground steepens toward the 7,690-foot point, where it turns technical. The reward is a start already on the ridge for a long traverse day toward Katsuk and Kimtah; the cost is wind, cold and the water problem. Mount Arriva goes the other way from the pass, southwest, so a party after Arriva alone gains nothing by coming up here. Pitch on gravel rather than on the heather, which is thin and slow to recover, and expect a party of more than two to be split across separate patches of ground.
bivy.water: SEASONAL AND OFTEN GONE. Snow patches supply it early and it is commonly dry by late summer, which is the one reason to prefer the basin below. Coming up here late in the year means carrying water or dropping into the basin to fetch it.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, reserved in advance and issued by park staff before the trip. Cross-country zone camping with an approved bear canister, and no campfires. There is no self-issue option anywhere on this side of the pass — the free trailhead-kiosk permits people are used to on the forest do not exist here.
bivy.capacity: A small high bivy on the south side of the crest, east of the 7,985-foot subpeak. Room for one or two parties on gravel and heather. Exposed, with no shelter of any kind.

bivy.name: Fisher Camp, Fisher Creek basin
bivy.notes: Fisher Camp sits in the forested basin west of and well below Easy Pass, reached by carrying on over the pass and descending into Fisher Creek. It is the comfortable option and it is also the alternative approach to Kimtah that some parties prefer: rather than the long sidehill traverse along the south flank of Ragged Ridge, they drop into the basin, losing something like eighteen hundred feet, and then climb a more direct line straight back up to the crest. Whether that trade is worth it depends on snow on the traverse and on how much the party dislikes scree. Further down the valley the trail passes additional designated camps toward the Thunder Creek junction, which is how a Ragged Ridge trip can be finished as a through-hike rather than an out-and-back. The descent to this camp is real elevation that has to be regained on the way out, and it is the reason a summit-focused party stays high instead.
bivy.water: Fisher Creek, right at the camp, and it runs all season. This is the most reliable water anywhere on the Ragged Ridge side.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required and reserved for this specific named site, not for a zone. Book in advance through the national online system and collect the permit from park staff shortly before the trip. Food must be stored properly; a canister is the simplest answer. No campfires, and no dogs anywhere beyond Easy Pass.
bivy.capacity: Three designated sites — two taking a single tent each and one that will hold about four. A privy is provided. Being a named camp rather than a zone, it is reserved specifically and can simply be full.

bivy.name: Snow Lake Camp

bivy.name: Middle Fork Campground
bivy.notes: The only developed drive-in camping on the Middle Fork road, and the practical roadhead base for every peak in this zone. It sits at about road mile twelve, a few minutes below the Middle Fork trailhead, so a party sleeping here is already at the start of the Preacher Mountain approach and within a short drive of the Garfield pull-outs. The road to it is paved the whole way now, which is a recent change and makes this reachable in any car. Season is roughly mid-May to mid-September; outside those months the gate is shut and the valley has no legal developed option at all. Book ahead, because this is the closest forest campground to Seattle and summer weekends fill months in advance. For Mount Teneriffe parties it is the nearest legal camping of any kind, about twenty minutes' drive from that trailhead.
bivy.water: Potable water is provided from a solar-pumped system, but it has failed for stretches in recent seasons and been shut off mid-summer. Carry enough for the first night rather than counting on the tap. The river runs alongside the campground year-round and can be filtered.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, booked up to six months ahead through the federal reservation system or by phone; the adjacent day-use parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or a small daily fee. No wilderness permit applies at the campground itself. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine through late summer and one is in force at the time of writing, so confirm before planning a fire. A food storage order applies across the whole forest.
bivy.capacity: About 36 tent and trailer units plus a pair of group sites, no hookups, all reservable. Fourteen-day stay limit.

bivy.name: Middle Fork road pull-outs, Taylor River and Dingford Creek
bivy.notes: Worth reading before driving up with a plan to sleep in the back of the car, because the situation has changed and the change is not obvious on the ground. The lower valley is closed to dispersed camping, so the answer there is the campground or nothing. The Taylor River road is gated at the bridge at the end of the drivable road and its old roadbed is now the trail, so there is no driving in to a quieter spot. The upper road toward Dingford Creek is the one stretch still open to roadside camping, and it is currently cut by a washout at about road mile seventeen that closes vehicle access short of the Dingford Creek trailhead at 1,400 ft. That washout matters well beyond camping: with it in place the Mount Price approach and the Treen Peak path both gain several road miles on foot or bike each way, which turns two long days into overnight trips. Beyond the Dingford Creek trailhead the road has been gated to vehicles for years in any case. bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead: fill it in, drop the stub in the box, carry your copy. Northwest Forest Pass to park. bivy.name: Green Ridge Lake
bivy.notes: The staging point for two of this zone's objectives and the one genuinely useful high camp on the north side of the valley. Season is July into October; the approach is snow-free early but the brush stays soaking until the summer settles.

bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit where the boundary is crossed, group size capped at twelve. The start is an unsigned roadside pull-out rather than a developed trailhead, so carry a Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle. The lake sits just below the 4,000 ft campfire line and the ridge camps above it are stoves-only regardless; treat the whole area as no-fire in practice.

bivy.name: Rainy Lake
bivy.notes: Sits directly beneath the exposed south face of Preacher Mountain and is the natural base camp for the Standard Scramble. From the Middle Fork trailhead cross the bridge and follow the Pratt connector west to the junction with the unofficial Rainy Creek path, which the Forest Service abandoned years ago; volunteers keep the brush down in places and much of it is flagged, but it is not maintained tread and route-finding is required, particularly in the lower half. The valley floor here is low enough to be open most of the year, but the lake and the ridge above hold snow into June.
bivy.water: The lake and Rainy Creek are both reliable through the season. Treat.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, group limit twelve. Northwest Forest Pass at the Middle Fork trailhead where the approach begins. The lake is just under the 4,000 ft campfire line, but the sites are small and the ground is thin, so use a stove and expect seasonal bans in late summer.
bivy.capacity: A handful of informal sites around the lake shore. Quiet and rarely busy, since the access path keeps the numbers down.

bivy.name: Garfield Mountain improvised bivouac
bivy.notes: The honest answer for Garfield is that there is no camp, and inventing one would do a party more harm than saying so. There are no trails, no signs and no established approach; you leave the road at a pull-out and go up. Substantial rappels separate some of the summits, so retreat is not always the quick option once committed. The one exception is the East Peak, whose ridge is gained from Green Ridge; a party going that way should use the Green Ridge Lake camp above instead of anything on this face. bivy.permit: No permit for a bivouac on the mountain beyond the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit if your line crosses the boundary, plus a Northwest Forest Pass at whichever pull-out you start from. Note that sleeping at the car is not an option here: the pull-outs at the base of Garfield fall inside the lower-valley dispersed camping closure.
bivy.capacity: Nothing established, and no honest capacity figure to give. Parties sleep where the terrain offers a flat dry patch, a bench in a gully, a ledge system or a heather shoulder, usually one or two people at a time.

bivy.name: Mount Teneriffe and the Mount Si conservation area, no overnight
bivy.notes: Recorded because it is the honest answer rather than a place to sleep. Mount Teneriffe is state conservation land at the very front of the range, reached from its own trailhead at the end of the Mount Si road and not from any of the Middle Fork trailheads that serve the other peaks here, so it has a different land manager, a different pass and different rules. Both the standard trail and the Kamikaze scramble up the southwest ridge are done car-to-car in a day by everyone who climbs them, and there is no camp on the mountain and nothing legal near the trailhead. A party that wants to start from a tent has to drop back to the valley, where the Middle Fork Campground is the nearest developed option, about twenty minutes' drive up the road system. The compensation is season: the lower mountain is snow-free most of the year and this is a genuine winter and shoulder-season objective, though the steep upper section of the Kamikaze line becomes icy and unpleasant once the freeze sets in and the standard trail is the safer choice then.

bivy.permit: A Washington Discover Pass is required in every vehicle at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass is not valid here, which is the commonest mistake parties make arriving from the national forest roads further up the valley, and the fines are real. Camping and campfires are both prohibited, group size is capped at twelve, and the trails are hiking-only.
bivy.capacity: None. Camping is prohibited across the entire conservation area, at any elevation, so there is no legal overnight option anywhere on this mountain.

bivy.name: Middle Fork Campground
bivy.notes: The only developed drive-in camping on the Middle Fork road, and the practical roadhead base for every peak in this zone. It sits at about road mile twelve, a few minutes below the Middle Fork trailhead, so a party sleeping here is already at the start of the Preacher Mountain approach and within a short drive of the Garfield pull-outs. The road to it is paved the whole way now, which is a recent change and makes this reachable in any car. Season is roughly mid-May to mid-September; outside those months the gate is shut and the valley has no legal developed option at all. Book ahead, because this is the closest forest campground to Seattle and summer weekends fill months in advance. For Mount Teneriffe parties it is the nearest legal camping of any kind, about twenty minutes' drive from that trailhead.
bivy.water: Potable water is provided from a solar-pumped system, but it has failed for stretches in recent seasons and been shut off mid-summer. Carry enough for the first night rather than counting on the tap. The river runs alongside the campground year-round and can be filtered.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, booked up to six months ahead through the federal reservation system or by phone; the adjacent day-use parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or a small daily fee. No wilderness permit applies at the campground itself. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine through late summer and one is in force at the time of writing, so confirm before planning a fire. A food storage order applies across the whole forest.
bivy.capacity: About 36 tent and trailer units plus a pair of group sites, no hookups, all reservable. Fourteen-day stay limit.

bivy.name: Middle Fork road pull-outs, Taylor River and Dingford Creek
bivy.notes: Worth reading before driving up with a plan to sleep in the back of the car, because the situation has changed and the change is not obvious on the ground. The lower valley is closed to dispersed camping, so the answer there is the campground or nothing. The Taylor River road is gated at the bridge at the end of the drivable road and its old roadbed is now the trail, so there is no driving in to a quieter spot. The upper road toward Dingford Creek is the one stretch still open to roadside camping, and it is currently cut by a washout at about road mile seventeen that closes vehicle access short of the Dingford Creek trailhead at 1,400 ft. That washout matters well beyond camping: with it in place the Mount Price approach and the Treen Peak path both gain several road miles on foot or bike each way, which turns two long days into overnight trips. Beyond the Dingford Creek trailhead the road has been gated to vehicles for years in any case. Road status in this valley changes year to year, so confirm the current state with the ranger district before committing; a party that discovers the washout at the barricade has lost the day.
bivy.water: The river and its side creeks are within a few minutes of the road the entire length of the valley and run all year. Treat everything; this is a heavily used corridor.
bivy.permit: This is the field that decides whether you can sleep here at all. A forest order closes dispersed camping along the road from the forest boundary up to the confluence of the Taylor and Middle Fork rivers, and along the Taylor River road out to the Snoqualmie Lake trailhead, including a quarter-mile strip on either side. That closure runs through the end of 2026 and covers essentially every pull-out parties used to use, including the ones nearest the Garfield approaches. Above the confluence, on the upper road toward Dingford Creek, roadside camping is not covered by the order. Trailhead parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or the interagency equivalent.
bivy.capacity: Informal gravel pull-outs only, a vehicle or two apiece, nothing signed, levelled or established.

Seasonal fire bans override all of that and are common by August.

bivy.name: Bean Creek Basin meadows
bivy.notes: This is the overnight base for Earl Peak, and it is a contingency rather than the plan — Earl is a straightforward day from the car for most parties, and the reason to sleep here is a late start, a slow party, or a wish to link Earl with Bean Peak and the surrounding scrambles over two days. From the Beverly Creek trailhead at about 3,600 feet, take the right-hand branch at the first junction half a mile in and climb steeply up the Bean Creek valley, crossing the creek to reach the basin at roughly two miles. From the basin the route continues to Earl Pass on the divide between Bean and Standup Creeks at about 6,200 feet, then turns north up the southwest ridge, which carries bits of boot tread most of the way and stays easy scrambling to the summit. The basin is a flower meadow in early July and dry gold by September; mosquitoes are bad from snowmelt through mid-July. The last mile and a half of road to the trailhead is a rough, overgrown one-lane track that punishes a low car.
bivy.water: Bean Creek runs through the basin and is the reason the camp is here, but it is a small east-side creek and by late August only one of the several channels may still be running. The dependable fill is lower down, where the trail crosses Bean Creek at the split with the Earl Peak branch — top off there rather than assuming the basin will provide, and assume nothing at all above the basin, because the climb to Earl Pass and the whole southwest ridge are dry.
bivy.permit: No permit and no quota. Nothing here is inside the Enchantment Permit Area and there is no lottery of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent annual pass is needed to park at the Beverly Creek trailhead. Where a trail from this basin crosses into the Alpine Lakes Wilderness further north, the free self-issue slip from the trailhead box covers it. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet in this national forest, which includes the basin, and the whole valley routinely falls under a total burn ban from midsummer onward. Camp on bare ground or duff, never on the meadow itself.
bivy.capacity: A stand of trees at the edge of the meadow holds four or more multi-tent sites, and there are scattered singles beyond it; two or three parties fit comfortably and it fills on summer weekends. No toilet of any kind.

bivy.name: Beverly Turnpike camps at the Fourth Creek junction
bivy.notes: The best all-round camp on the Beverly Creek side, ringed by the peaks it serves — Iron Peak stands to the southwest, Teanaway Peak to the northwest, and the Bean and Earl ridges close it in to the southeast. It sits two and seven tenths miles up the Beverly Turnpike trail from the Beverly Creek trailhead. For Iron Peak it is the east-side option, which matters because the standard approach from the road end is entirely waterless: a party wanting to sleep out before the scramble is far better off here beside the creek than dry-camped on the saddle. It also links Earl Peak to Iron Peak over two days without returning to the car, and it is the staging point for the Fourth Creek crossing north to Ingalls Creek, which involves fording Ingalls Creek and is genuinely dangerous during June runoff. Ground is forested and level, insects are moderate, and the camp is low enough to be warm at night well into September.
bivy.water: Beverly Creek runs briskly right beside the camp and is the most reliable water anywhere in this group of peaks. That reliability ends abruptly at the junction: the sites up on the saddle where the Fourth Creek and Hardscrabble trails meet are dry, and there is nothing on the climb to Iron Peak's saddle from this side. A small running source sits roughly four tenths of a mile down the Hardscrabble side of that saddle, off-trail, and is worth knowing about if you have committed to the high ground and misjudged.
bivy.permit: No permit, no quota, no lottery. Northwest Forest Pass at the Beverly Creek trailhead. The free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness slip from the trailhead box covers travel where the trails cross the boundary north of here. No campfires above 5,000 feet, and expect a valley-wide burn ban from midsummer; this is dry, brittle east-side timber that has already carried one large fire.
bivy.capacity: A cluster of good sites near the creek holding four or five tents, spread over enough ground that two parties are not on top of each other

bivy.name: Stafford Creek meadow camps below Navaho Pass
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Navaho Peak's south slopes and effectively the only one worth using on that side. From the Stafford Creek trailhead the trail climbs gently for the first mile beside the creek, then steepens as it pulls away from it, crosses a marshy open meadow, and reaches these camps at around five miles. Navaho Pass is another half mile up a bare serpentine slope at about 6,000 feet, and the south slopes above the pass are walking and easy scrambling to the summit. Most parties do the whole thing car to car and the camp is the contingency: a late start, a hot afternoon, or a group that wants the summit at dawn. It is also the hinge of the standard two-day loop that links Navaho Pass with the Bean Creek side and comes out at a different trailhead. The meadow is buggy in early summer and the burn scar in the drainage has changed shade and blowdown patterns, so expect the walking to be rougher than an older description suggests.
bivy.water: The reason this camp exists. Stafford Creek and a side stream come down the rock faces at the meadow edge and run into late summer in most years, and this is the last dependable water before the pass. Above the meadow there is nothing: the final half mile of bare serpentine to Navaho Pass and the whole of the south slopes above it are completely dry, and on a hot east-side day that is four or five hours of climbing on what you carry.
bivy.permit: No permit, no quota, no lottery, and no connection to the Enchantment system. Northwest Forest Pass at the Stafford Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet here and the drainage is normally under a full burn ban by July. The Stafford Creek road and trail were inside the 2025 fire closure and were still subject to repair-work closures afterwards, so this is the site most likely to be legally unreachable on any given date — check before you drive.
bivy.capacity: Established sites in the timber along the edge of a large meadow, with room for several parties; this is a popular long-weekend base camp and can hold a half dozen tents on a summer Saturday

bivy.name: Lake Ann bench and the upper Esmeralda Basin camps
bivy.notes: The Esmeralda-side camp that is not Headlight Basin, and the one that actually serves the two peaks at the head of this valley. Esmeralda Peaks are scrambled directly from the basin on their standard route, and Fortune Peak's standard line goes up the basin and over the pass near Lake Ann before turning up the peak; both are honest day trips from the road end, so this is a place to sleep when the party is slow, the day is short, or you want two summits without driving twice. The trail leaves the road end at about 4,500 feet and climbs gently through meadow, timber and small stream crossings before the ground steepens toward the pass; take the Lake Ann branch to reach the bench and the knoll above it, which has a wide view back down the upper Teanaway. Fortune Peak can also be climbed by its east slope out of Headlight Basin, which is a different camp on the other side of the divide and is described with the Ingalls group rather than here. Mountain goats work this whole area and are bold about salt — keep gear packed and relieve yourself well away from camp.
bivy.water: The bench camp has running water beside it, fed by snowmelt draining the basin, and small streams cross the main basin trail lower down. All of it is snowmelt and all of it fades: reliable through July, marginal in August, and effectively gone by September, when the basin is dry rock and cured grass. There is no water at all on the pass or on either summit.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness above the basin, under the Cle Elum district and entirely outside the Enchantment Permit Area — a free self-issued slip from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use, with no quota, no lottery and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the Esmeralda Basin trailhead. No campfires; this is open subalpine meadow and the ban is both seasonal and permanent by elevation. Camping is prohibited at Ingalls Lake, which is a different basin over the divide, and the designated sites in Headlight Basin are the legal option on that side.
bivy.capacity: Small scattered sites rather than a campground — a bench part way up the Lake Ann branch takes a tent or two, and a knoll on its east side holds several more; nothing here suits a large group

bivy.name: Iron Peak saddle dry camp
bivy.notes: A perch rather than a campsite, and included because Iron Peak's standard approach offers nothing else. The trailhead sits on the North Fork Teanaway Road roughly half a mile above the De Roux campground turn and a mile and a half short of the road end, at about 3,800 feet. The trail climbs a rib at a steady moderate grade with no flat ground and no water until it reaches the saddle, from which the scramble turns west up the ridge to the summit, and most parties continue on to Mount Teanaway from the same saddle. Almost nobody sleeps here and almost nobody needs to — this is a half-day objective for a fit party — but a group that has started late, or one linking Iron Peak with the Beverly Creek peaks over the divide, has this saddle as the only level ground on the route. It is windy, exposed and cold after dark even in August. If there is any choice at all, the creekside camps at the Fourth Creek junction on the other side of the divide are a far better place to spend a night.
bivy.water: None. This is the defining fact about the route and the camp both. The Iron Peak trail passes a steep unnamed creek in the first eighth of a mile from the trailhead and then turns away from it for good; you can hear water in the gullies on either side for half the climb and cannot reach any of it. Carry everything you intend to drink and cook with from the road, and plan on more than feels necessary, because this is a south-facing, sun-hammered hillside.
bivy.permit: No permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at the Iron Peak trailhead. Campfires are prohibited at this elevation and there is nothing here to burn in any case. Pitch on gravel or bare ground; the saddle carries thin meadow that does not recover.
bivy.capacity: A few flat spots at and just below the saddle between Iron Peak and Mount Teanaway; one or two small tents, no shelter, and nothing resembling an established site

bivy.name: Teanaway Community Forest campgrounds — 29 Pines, Teanaway Campground and Indian Camp
bivy.notes: The low-valley drive-in option, on the paved and lower gravel stretches of the Teanaway River Road below the national forest boundary, and the practical answer for a party arriving late from the west side the night before a climb. It is a longer morning drive to the trailheads than the small Forest Service campgrounds higher up — 29 Pines sits at the point where the road turns to dirt, with the Stafford Creek fork about a mile beyond it, Beverly Creek several miles further and the Esmeralda road end roughly ten — but these have far more capacity, they are free, and they do not fill in the same way. Road access has been the weak link: a washout near the end of FS 32 cut vehicle access to the sites at the road end for a period, a bypass has since been built above the damaged section, and both the road and the trailhead have a history of being reachable in one season and not the next. From here the north side route drops to the bergschrund and the south face is reached by downclimbing and a rappel to a pocket glacier and a couloir onto the East Nooksack. Everything about it depends on the approach below being passable, which is the real problem.

bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for the cross-country zone at the head of the Nooksack. Reserved online or issued as a walk-up within 24 hours, collected in person, with per-person and transaction fees. Cross-country rules apply: durable surfaces only, no camping in meadows or within a hundred feet of water, food in an approved canister, and no fires. The lower part of the walk in crosses Mount Baker Wilderness on the forest side, so the parking pass at the road end and the park permit are two separate things you need at once.
bivy.capacity: Flat rock slabs with room for two or three bivy sacks, snow-covered into midsummer; a small party only, and no facilities

bivy.name: Nooksack Cirque river bottom, below the tower
bivy.notes: SAY THIS PLAINLY: there is no real camping in the Nooksack Cirque, and any party heading for Nooksack Tower should expect to improvise a night on gravel or in the trees rather than arrive at a site. The way in is a genuine bushwhack. The spur road dead-ends at Ruth Creek with no bridge, so the trip begins by wading or crossing on whatever log is currently down, and a log that is crossable at dawn can be underwater by afternoon once the day's melt arrives. In early summer Ruth Creek alone can be too high to cross at all, and the North Fork above it is worse. Beyond the creek the route follows two miles of abandoned roadbed, then second growth to the wilderness boundary, then old growth to the river, after which progress depends entirely on whether the gravel bars are exposed or whether you are fighting through riverside brush. Cool weather and low water are what make it work, which is why this valley is best in the autumn — the exact opposite of the season that suits the climbing above. The first ascent party camped near this height on the river before starting up, and little about the ground has become easier since. Treat the water crossings as the crux of the trip, not the climb.

bivy.permit: Split. The lower miles are Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest and then Mount Baker Wilderness, needing only the parking pass and a self-issue wilderness registration. Past the boundary further up the valley it is North Cascades National Park, and a night on that side needs a park backcountry permit for the cross-country zone, arranged in advance or as a walk-up and collected in person before you start. There is no ranger presence out here to sort it out for you, so know which side of the line you intend to sleep on before you leave the road. No fires.
bivy.capacity: Nothing established. Parties make do on gravel bars when the river is low, or on flat ground in the old growth near the point where the route meets the North Fork. One party at a time in practice, and the ground moves year to year.

bivy.name: Necklace Valley — Jade, Emerald and Opal Lakes

On a summer weekend the popular shorelines are full by mid-afternoon.

bivy.name: La Bohn Lakes, La Bohn Gap and the Chain Lakes benches

bivy.name: Tank Lakes basin

bivy.name: Big Heart Lake, with Copper and Little Heart below

bivy.name: Bald Eagle Lake cirque
