bivy.name: Upper Mountaineer Creek bench
bivy.notes: The north-side base for everything on this side of the range: the Sherpa Glacier and Sherpa's north routes, Argonaut's north approaches, and the start of the northeast ridge on Cannon Mountain. Leave the Stuart Lake trail at the first switchback where it begins to climb, roughly half a mile past the Colchuck Lake junction, and follow the creek up on its right for three to four miles on a rough climbers path. The bench at this elevation is the obvious flat ground and everyone stops there. Road access is the seasonal constraint: Forest Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road is gated through winter and typically does not open until well into spring, which shortens the north-side season considerably compared with the Teanaway. Snow lingers in this basin, which is exactly why the couloir routes above are early-season objectives.

bivy.permit: This is the ambiguous one and it matters. The Stuart Lake trailhead sits inside the Enchantment Permit Area, and the Stuart Zone requires an overnight permit from May 15 through October 31, drawn either through the February advance lottery on the federal reservation system or through the daily lottery run from Leavenworth. Where the zone boundary falls in the upper Mountaineer Creek basin above the lakes is not clearly drawn on any public map, and reasonable people read it differently. Do not guess. Call the Wenatchee River Ranger District before the trip, and if you cannot get an answer, carry a Stuart Zone permit. Day use anywhere in the permit area needs only the free self-issued slip at the trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
bivy.capacity: Plenty of good spots spread along the bench near the creek; several parties can spread out without seeing each other

bivy.name: Argonaut north basin bivies, below the Colchuck-Argonaut col

bivy.permit: Approached from the Stuart Lake trailhead, so the same unresolved boundary question applies as at the Mountaineer Creek bench. Assume the Stuart Zone overnight permit is required May 15 to October 31 unless the Wenatchee River Ranger District tells you otherwise. Day climbing needs only the free self-issued wilderness permit. No fires, no dogs.
bivy.capacity: Several small gravel and slab platforms scattered through the upper basin; two or three parties fit if they spread out, and none of the spots is large

bivy.name: Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps

Fire restrictions are common here from midsummer and are taken seriously; this valley is dry and burns. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at Esmeralda the next morning.

Ground near the lakes is soft in places, so use an existing site.

Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.

The payoff is that the East Ridge start is an easy morning from here instead of a pre-dawn thrash. It is also the natural base for the Northeast Couloir on Sherpa Balanced Rock, which is reached by continuing up the basin to the notch east of the balanced block. Ground is a mix of scree and low heather and level spots take some hunting; the basin is open and catches wind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams draining the basin are reliable into midsummer and thin out by September; late-season parties should fill on the way up from Ingalls Creek rather than assume
bivy.permit: Cle Elum Ranger District, Alpine Lakes Wilderness, outside the Enchantment Permit Area. Free self-issued trailhead permit for day and overnight use, no lottery, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at Esmeralda. No campfires at this elevation, and pitch on gravel or bare rock rather than on the meadow.
bivy.capacity: A small number of established spots on gravel and heather benches; two parties is comfortable, three is crowded

bivy.name: Table Rock bivy, upper Sherpa basin
bivy.notes: A large flat block high in the basin below Sherpa's south side, used by parties who want the East Ridge to start within minutes of waking rather than an hour and a half above camp. From here the route climbs a broad gully trending north-northeast to gain the crest east of the balanced rock, then follows blocks and sandy benches west past the block to the summit. It is exposed, windy and cold compared with the basin camp a thousand feet lower, and whether the extra height is worth carrying water up for is a real judgement call rather than an obvious yes. Anyone attempting Sherpa Balanced Rock's Northeast Couloir gets the most from this position, since the couloir tops out close by. Leave no trace of a platform; the rock is bare and the ground around it is fragile.
bivy.water: None dependable. Snow patches persist into midsummer and can be melted, but treat it as a dry bivy and carry water up from the basin below.
bivy.permit: Cle Elum Ranger District, free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, no Enchantment lottery involved. Northwest Forest Pass at Esmeralda if you came over Longs Pass. No fires, and nothing here to build one with.
bivy.capacity: Two to four people on flat rock; this is a perch rather than a campsite, and there is nothing else level nearby

bivy.name: Upper Mountaineer Creek bench
bivy.notes: The north-side base for everything on this side of the range: the Sherpa Glacier and Sherpa's north routes, Argonaut's north approaches, and the start of the northeast ridge on Cannon Mountain. Leave the Stuart Lake trail at the first switchback where it begins to climb, roughly half a mile past the Colchuck Lake junction, and follow the creek up on its right for three to four miles on a rough climbers path. The bench at this elevation is the obvious flat ground and everyone stops there. Road access is the seasonal constraint: Forest Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road is gated through winter and typically does not open until well into spring, which shortens the north-side season considerably compared with the Teanaway. Snow lingers in this basin, which is exactly why the couloir routes above are early-season objectives.
bivy.water: Mountaineer Creek runs beside the camp all season and is easy to draw from where the channel is open; in early season find a spot where the creek is running clear of snow
bivy.permit: This is the ambiguous one and it matters. The Stuart Lake trailhead sits inside the Enchantment Permit Area, and the Stuart Zone requires an overnight permit from May 15 through October 31, drawn either through the February advance lottery on the federal reservation system or through the daily lottery run from Leavenworth. Where the zone boundary falls in the upper Mountaineer Creek basin above the lakes is not clearly drawn on any public map, and reasonable people read it differently. Do not guess. Call the Wenatchee River Ranger District before the trip, and if you cannot get an answer, carry a Stuart Zone permit. Day use anywhere in the permit area needs only the free self-issued slip at the trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
bivy.capacity: Plenty of good spots spread along the bench near the creek; several parties can spread out without seeing each other

bivy.name: Argonaut north basin bivies, below the Colchuck-Argonaut col
bivy.notes: From the bench in Mountaineer Creek the valley forks around 4,800 feet; take the easternmost fork and climb toward the col between Colchuck and Argonaut, and the flat ground in the basin at roughly this height is the high camp for the Northeast Couloir and the Northwest Arete. It puts the foot of the couloir within an easy start, which matters because that line is a snow route best climbed cold and early. The basin is rocky, open and exposed, with no shelter of any kind, so bring a real bivy sack or a tent rather than counting on finding a nook. The travel from the forks up is off-trail on moraine and slabs and takes longer than the distance suggests. Note that this camp serves only Argonaut's north side; the South Face and Southeast Ridge are approached from Ingalls Creek and there is no reasonable way to link the two in a day.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and meltwater off the permanent snow below the col, reliable in early and midsummer and unreliable late; by September expect to melt snow or carry up from the forks lower down
bivy.permit: Approached from the Stuart Lake trailhead, so the same unresolved boundary question applies as at the Mountaineer Creek bench. Assume the Stuart Zone overnight permit is required May 15 to October 31 unless the Wenatchee River Ranger District tells you otherwise. Day climbing needs only the free self-issued wilderness permit. No fires, no dogs.
bivy.capacity: Several small gravel and slab platforms scattered through the upper basin; two or three parties fit if they spread out, and none of the spots is large

bivy.name: Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps
bivy.notes: This is what most parties on Ingalls Peak actually use, because all three Ingalls summits are comfortably a long day from the car and there is no reason to carry a camp. Sleeping on the road puts you at the Esmeralda trailhead in minutes rather than driving up from Cle Elum in the dark. The Ingalls group sits entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, in the Cle Elum Ranger District, so the whole permit problem that dominates the Icicle Creek side simply does not exist here: a free self-issued slip at the trailhead, a parking pass, and you go. Access is by pavement to the end of Teanaway Road and then gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last several miles; the surface is rough enough to want patience in a low car, holds snow into early summer, and washboards badly by August. Beverly is roughly four miles up the gravel and De Roux about eight, with Esmeralda a mile beyond that. If you do want to sleep high for the South Ridge, the designated sites in Headlight Basin are the legal option and camping is prohibited at Ingalls Lake itself; expect the goats there, which are bold, unbothered by people and interested in anything salty, so relieve yourself well away from camp and do not leave sweaty gear out.
bivy.water: No potable water at either campground, so bring what you need. The North Fork Teanaway River runs alongside and is easy to filter from.
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all, and nothing to do with the Enchantment lottery. Both campgrounds charge a modest per-night fee paid on site. Roadside dispersed camping is legal on National Forest ground along Forest Road 9737 but is NOT permitted inside the Teanaway Community Forest lower down the valley, where camping is confined to its designated campgrounds. Fire restrictions are common here from midsummer and are taken seriously; this valley is dry and burns. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at Esmeralda the next morning.
bivy.capacity: Beverly holds around fourteen small tent sites; De Roux is smaller still. Both are first come, first served with no reservations. Dispersed pullouts along the road hold many more parties informally.

bivy.name: Lake Caroline and Little Caroline
bivy.notes: Cashmere Mountain does not belong to the Stuart Lake, Snow Lakes or Teanaway approaches at all; it is climbed from the Eightmile Lake trailhead on its own road off Icicle Creek. The West Ridge goes past Little Eightmile Lake, right at the junction onto the Eightmile to Trout Creek trail, over the ridge and down to Lake Caroline, then two miles on to Windy Pass at around 7,200 feet before turning up the ridge. That is eight or nine miles one way with well over five thousand feet of gain, which is why almost everyone who does not want an enormous day camps at the Caroline lakes. This is also the least visited corner of the permit area, so a party skunked on Colchuck or Core permits can often still get a legal night here, and it is a genuinely good consolation objective rather than a booby prize. Ground near the lakes is soft in places, so use an existing site.
bivy.water: Both lakes are reliable, and the inlet streams run into late summer in most years; treat everything
bivy.permit: Eightmile/Caroline zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through October 31. It comes from the same February advance lottery on the federal reservation system as the rest of the Enchantments, but this is by a wide margin the easiest zone to draw, and walk-up permits at the Leavenworth ranger station are often available for it when every other zone has been gone for months. Outside that window no overnight permit is needed. Day use needs only the free self-issued wilderness slip. A Northwest Forest Pass at the Eightmile Lake trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
bivy.capacity: A number of established sites around the two lakes; the zone quota is small, so it is quiet even at the height of summer

bivy.name: Nada Lake
bivy.notes: The eastern staging camp, five and a half miles and about seventeen hundred feet of gain up the Snow Lakes trail from Icicle Creek Road, and the only road in the region that is open year round rather than gated through winter. It is the base for Cannon Mountain's southeast approach, which continues past Snow Lakes and climbs the peak's south slopes, and it is the first night for anyone reaching Enchantment Peak or Witches Tower from the east rather than over Aasgard Pass. Be clear about the trade: from here the Core basin peaks are a long second day and the shorter approach to both is from Colchuck Lake over Aasgard, so this camp suits a party doing a through-trip or one that drew a Snow permit and nothing better. The trail is hot, exposed and steep on the lower half, hiker only, and holds snow in May, June and again from late September. Cannon can also be climbed from the north out of Mountaineer Creek, which is a different trailhead and a different permit question entirely.
bivy.water: The lake is reliable all season, as is the creek below it; treat it, since the shoreline is heavily used
bivy.permit: Snow zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through October 31, from the February advance lottery on the federal reservation system or from the daily lottery, which is run through a mobile app and demands that you be physically inside a one-mile radius of the ranger station in Leavenworth to apply, for the following day's entry. A Core Enchantment permit is valid in every zone including this one; a Snow permit is not valid in the Core. Outside the season no overnight permit is needed. Day use anywhere in the permit area needs only the free self-issued slip at the trailhead, which is what a party climbing car to car uses and is entirely legal. Northwest Forest Pass at the Snow Lakes trailhead. Dogs are prohibited throughout the permit area and campfires are banned.
bivy.capacity: Many well-established sites along the east shore; the Snow zone quota is larger than most, so it is the easiest of the western zones to draw

bivy.name: Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
bivy.notes: This is the road head for the whole eastern side of the Chelan Mountains crest and the standard place to sleep the night before a long walk in. The drive is the thing people underestimate — it is roughly 38 miles of valley road from the Columbia, most of it paved, and getting here from the west side of the state is the better part of four hours. Cottonwood sits at the end, just short of where the Entiat River trail begins. Camp here and you can be walking at first light with the entire day for the eleven miles to Entiat Meadows or the eight to Fox Camp. Recognise what has happened to this valley: successive fires have run through it and the lower trail corridor is open, burned, dusty and hot, with young growth and standing snags rather than shade. That makes the river the only dependable water for the first several miles and it makes an early start a safety measure rather than a preference. A landslide near the river trailhead currently blocks the normal approach; a temporary high-clearance route has been pushed through the slide, trailers are turned back, and the campground short of it is being used as the turnaround. Confirm before committing to the drive, because there is nothing at the end of this road.
bivy.water: The Entiat River runs beside every one of these campgrounds and is the most reliable water anywhere in the zone. Treat it. Some of the smaller road campgrounds have a hand pump but several have none at all and nothing should be assumed potable.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent recreation pass for the trailhead lot. No permit to camp. Forest-wide Stage 2 fire restrictions have prohibited campfires on all national forest land since early July 2026, including in established rings, and the county has a total outdoor burn ban. All of these campgrounds are inside the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026, and Cottonwood is written off for the remainder of the season.
bivy.capacity: Cottonwood has around two dozen sites; the string of small campgrounds down-valley adds a similar number again

bivy.name: Myrtle Lake and Cow Creek Meadows
bivy.notes: These are the two low staging camps on the Cow Creek branch, taken at mile 3.6 of the Entiat River trail and then a short climb past the lake. They matter for one peak — Fifth of July Mountain — and they are how a party of ordinary fitness splits that approach into two days instead of one brutal one. Myrtle is the easier and more sheltered of the two, a genuinely pleasant first night with water at your feet, and it makes a reasonable objective on its own for anyone acclimatising. Cow Creek Meadows is higher, more open, and puts you closer to the Larch Lakes climb the following morning. Both sit below the worst of the burn, so there is still shade here, which is not true of much of the valley. Season is long by Cascade standards — this is the dry east side and the snow leaves early — but the corresponding cost is heat, and in July and August the walk in from the road is genuinely hot with little cover. Mosquitoes at the meadow are severe through early July. Neither camp is high enough to be a climbing camp; treat them as the first half of the approach.
bivy.water: Myrtle Lake itself, and Cow Creek through the meadows. Both hold water through a normal season. The meadow creek is the last certain water before the climb to the Larch Lakes bench, so fill here rather than counting on anything on the switchbacks.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness — no fee and no quota, but sign in at the trailhead register. Party size limit of twelve. Campfires prohibited under the current forest-wide restrictions and in any case a bad idea in this fuel. Inside the current fire closure order.
bivy.capacity: Several sites scattered along the north and south shores at Myrtle; two good camps at Cow Creek Meadows, one in trees at the edge and one well back into the meadow

bivy.name: Larch Lakes meadow camps
bivy.notes: This is the base camp for Fifth of July Mountain and the only one worth using for it. From the meadow between the two lakes the summit is roughly six miles round trip with modest gain, which makes it a comfortable day out from a camp you have already carried to. The approach is the Cow Creek branch off the Entiat River trail, past Myrtle Lake, then a climb of about 2.6 miles onto the bench that holds the lakes. Total from the road it is a long first day, and most parties break it at Myrtle or Cow Creek Meadows. The name is earned — the larch here turn in the second half of September and October and the camps fill accordingly, which is worth knowing both as an attraction and as a reason to come midweek. Practically, the bench is high enough to be cold and exposed once the weather turns, and there is very little shelter in the meadow itself. The two established sites in the trees at the edge are worth taking over anything in the open. From here the ridge continues toward Cow Creek Pass and a longer loop back to the river, which is the usual way parties link this into a three or four day trip rather than an out-and-back.
bivy.water: Both lakes, and the outlet stream between them. This is dependable all season and is the last water on the way to Fifth of July Mountain — the ridge walk above holds nothing once the last snow patches go, usually by mid-July. Carry the full day's supply from camp.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, self-registration at the trailhead, no fee, party limit of twelve. No campfires under the current forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions. The Larch Lake trails and the connector are named in the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites in the meadow between the lower and upper lakes; comfortable for two or three parties, crowded beyond that in larch season

bivy.name: Snow Brushy Creek junction camps, Entiat River trail
bivy.notes: A working camp rather than a destination, and useful for exactly that reason. It sits roughly where the Snow Brushy Creek trail leaves the Entiat River trail, which is the eastern end of the crossing over Milham Pass toward Emerald Park and the Lake Chelan side. For a party linking Pinnacle Mountain and the Emerald and Saska group into a traverse rather than climbing them out and back from Fox Camp, this is the natural place to break the journey — it is the last camp with easy water on the Entiat side of that pass. It is also the obvious halfway camp for anyone walking the full length of the river trail to Entiat Meadows, which is eleven miles and more than most people want on a first day carrying a climbing pack. Expect burned and open forest for much of the approach; the trees around the junction itself are one of the better remaining patches of shade on the trail. Season here runs long, from roughly June to October, snow being the exception rather than the rule at this elevation, but the exposure and the heat on the walk in are the real constraints.
bivy.water: Snow Brushy Creek at the junction, and the Entiat River a short way off. Both are reliable into late season. This is the last easy water for a party heading up toward Milham Pass, and the climb above it is dry and south-facing.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue at the trailhead register, party limit of twelve. Campfires prohibited forest-wide at present. The Snow Brushy / Emerald Park trail and the Entiat River trail are both named in the current fire closure order.
bivy.capacity: Two or three good sites in the trees near the trail junction; room for a small party, not a group

bivy.name: Entiat Meadows
bivy.notes: The head of the Entiat valley and the reason to walk this trail at all: eleven miles up, entering the glacier drainage with Mount Fernow, Seven Fingered Jack and Mount Maude standing directly above. It serves two peaks. It is the eastern base for Mount Fernow, from which a party crosses toward the Entiat Glacier and takes the east ridge onto the southeast face — a longer and much less travelled line than the Leroy Basin scramble that most people use from the Chiwawa side, and one that should be chosen deliberately rather than by accident. It is also a reasonable if roundabout base for Spectacle Buttes, whose usual approaches leave the same river trail lower down by way of the Ice Creek or Cool Creek trails. Be clear-eyed about the commitment: eleven miles in with a mountaineering load is a full day, the first several miles are burned and hot, and there is no shortening it. The meadow itself is one of the finest places in the eastern Cascades in late July when the flowers are out, and it is high enough and shaded enough to be cold at night even in midsummer. Bring the right shell. The glacier above has retreated substantially and should not be assumed to be where an old map puts it.
bivy.water: The infant Entiat River runs through the meadow directly off the glacier above, so water is abundant, cold and dependable through the whole season. This is the strongest water in the zone. Above the meadows, on the climb toward the glacier and the east ridge, there is nothing until you reach snow, so fill completely at camp.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness — free, self-issued at the trailhead, party size limited to twelve. No campfires under the current forest-wide restrictions; at this elevation in a hanging valley there is little dead wood worth burning anyway. Inside the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026.
bivy.capacity: First camp is a quarter mile into the meadow, tucked into trees on the left; several more sites scattered up-valley. Room for two or three parties spread out.

bivy.name: Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
bivy.notes: The workhorse camp for the Chelan Mountains crest peaks. From the North Fork Entiat trailhead at roughly 3,880 ft the trail runs about eight miles to the Pyramid trail junction, with Fox Camp a quarter mile north of it. Every one of Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain is reachable from here, which is what makes this the single most useful site here — a party that carries in once can pick off several summits over consecutive days rather than repeating the approach. Saska is the shortest of them, essentially a scramble off the trail near where it crosses the south ridge at Saska Pass; Emerald and Cardinal need the higher basin above. Note this is a different spur road and a different trailhead from the Entiat River trail at the end of the valley, and the two are easy to confuse when planning — turn off roughly 35 miles up rather than driving to the road's end. Season is July through early October, though the larch in late September is the standout. The valley is dry and hot low down and the camp is a genuine relief after it.
bivy.water: The North Fork Entiat River is beside the trail for most of the approach and there is water at the camp. It holds through the season in a normal year. Above Fox Camp the Pyramid trail climbs onto drier ground where water becomes intermittent snowmelt only, so this is the last certain fill for parties going high.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue at the trailhead register, party limit of twelve. Northwest Forest Pass at the North Fork Entiat trailhead. No campfires under the current forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions. The North Fork Entiat River and Pyramid trails are both named in the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026.
bivy.capacity: An established backcountry camp with room for a couple of parties; the sites along this trail are described as roomy

bivy.name: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
bivy.notes: The high camp for the crest traverse, about a mile and a half beyond Fox Camp on the Pyramid trail, in the basin that separates Emerald Peak from Saska Peak. This is where a party stages to link Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain in a single push over Milham Pass at about 6,663 ft, which is the classic way to do these four and much the most efficient. From the basin you climb to the upper shelf just below the ridge between Emerald and Saska and pick up the broad gully to the summit. Cardinal is the highest of the group and the furthest, and it is the one that turns a two-day plan into three. The setting is superb and the ground is loose — expect scree and blocky scrambling rather than clean rock, and expect the descents to take longer than the ascents. Season is short at this height in a heavy year, realistically mid-July to early October, and the reason to come late is the larch and the reason not to is the water. Weigh that honestly: an August party that finds the tarns dry has a long, hot walk back down to fix it. Weather moves in from the west with little warning here and the basin is fully exposed.
bivy.water: Snowmelt tarns and rivulets in the basin, and these are the crux of the whole plan. They are dependable in early and mid summer, unreliable by mid-August, and in a dry year they are gone entirely by late August, at which point the nearest certain water is back down at Fox Camp. Do not commit to a high camp here in late season without either confirming water or carrying it up. Milham Pass itself has none.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue, party limit of twelve. Camp on durable ground and well back from the tarns. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions aside, there is no fuel at this elevation and the ground is fragile. Reached only through trails currently inside the fire closure order.
bivy.capacity: A small number of tent-sized spots on benches and moraine in the upper basin; two or three parties at most, and less if you want flat ground

bivy.name: Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
bivy.notes: This is the road head for the whole eastern side of the Chelan Mountains crest and the standard place to sleep the night before a long walk in. Forest-wide Stage 2 fire restrictions have prohibited campfires on all national forest land since early July 2026, including in established rings, and the county has a total outdoor burn ban. All of these campgrounds are inside the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026, and Cottonwood is written off for the remainder of the season.
bivy.capacity: Cottonwood has around two dozen sites; the string of small campgrounds down-valley adds a similar number again

bivy.name: Myrtle Lake and Cow Creek Meadows
bivy.notes: These are the two low staging camps on the Cow Creek branch, taken at mile 3.6 of the Entiat River trail and then a short climb past the lake. They matter for one peak — Fifth of July Mountain — and they are how a party of ordinary fitness splits that approach into two days instead of one brutal one. bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness — no fee and no quota, but sign in at the trailhead register. Party size limit of twelve. Campfires prohibited under the current forest-wide restrictions and in any case a bad idea in this fuel. Inside the current fire closure order.
bivy.capacity: Several sites scattered along the north and south shores at Myrtle; two good camps at Cow Creek Meadows, one in trees at the edge and one well back into the meadow

bivy.name: Larch Lakes meadow camps
bivy.notes: This is the base camp for Fifth of July Mountain and the only one worth using for it. From the meadow between the two lakes the summit is roughly six miles round trip with modest gain, which makes it a comfortable day out from a camp you have already carried to. bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites in the meadow between the lower and upper lakes; comfortable for two or three parties, crowded beyond that in larch season

bivy.name: Snow Brushy Creek junction camps, Entiat River trail
bivy.notes: A working camp rather than a destination, and useful for exactly that reason. It sits roughly where the Snow Brushy Creek trail leaves the Entiat River trail, which is the eastern end of the crossing over Milham Pass toward Emerald Park and the Lake Chelan side. For a party linking Pinnacle Mountain and the Emerald and Saska group into a traverse rather than climbing them out and back from Fox Camp, this is the natural place to break the journey — it is the last camp with easy water on the Entiat side of that pass. bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue at the trailhead register, party limit of twelve. Campfires prohibited forest-wide at present. The Snow Brushy / Emerald Park trail and the Entiat River trail are both named in the current fire closure order.
bivy.capacity: Two or three good sites in the trees near the trail junction; room for a small party, not a group

bivy.name: Entiat Meadows

Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
bivy.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
bivy.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
bivy.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

bivy.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — WEST side
bivy.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
bivy.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
bivy.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

bivy.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — WEST side
bivy.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
bivy.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
bivy.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
bivy.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen

bivy.name: Upper Silver Star Creek basin camp — EAST side, Silver Star only
bivy.notes: SERVES THE EAST AND NORTH APPROACH up Silver Star Creek, which reaches the glacier near its toe rather than crossing Burgundy Col — it is no use for the Wine Spires on the west side. It is the better choice under spring snow cover, when the drainage skis or snowshoes well and the col approach is a loose, avalanche-prone mess. Later in the summer the same ground turns brushy, and the scree and talus above make it less appealing than the shorter western approach.
bivy.water: Reliable through the climbing season from the creek and from meltwater draining the glacier, and typically abundant under spring snow — a marked contrast to the col.
bivy.permit: None. Same National Forest, non-wilderness status; no permit and no reservation, though the pullout is still gated by the seasonal highway closure.
bivy.capacity: Open alpine benches with room for several tents; sites are unimproved and parties spread out

bivy.name: Lower Silver Star Creek basin — EAST side, Silver Star only
bivy.notes: The drainage levels out near a cascade at about this height, roughly two miles up from the highway, and it is where many parties cross to the west side before continuing. It works as a low, sheltered camp for a ski approach or for a party that started late, but it leaves a long day to the summit. On the east approach it is a waypoint more often than a destination, with most parties pushing on to the upper basin.
bivy.water: Silver Star Creek runs here through the season, so water is not a planning constraint at this elevation
bivy.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside wilderness; standard dispersed-camping rules apply.
bivy.capacity: Informal; flat ground on either side of the drainage, several parties

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
bivy.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
bivy.water: Developed campground with potable water when open; Early Winters Creek runs alongside
bivy.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
bivy.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

bivy.name: Colonial Creek South Campground, Diablo Lake
bivy.notes: The practical staging ground for the whole west end of the corridor: directly under Colonial Peak and a short drive from the Pyramid Lake and Thunder Creek trailheads. Because it lies west of the usual winter gate at the Ross Dam trailhead, a handful of walk-in sites normally stay reachable through winter with no services and no fee — though a gate moved down to Newhalem would cut that off. Treat serviced opening and closing dates as approximate; they shift with snow and staffing. Arriving late on a summer Friday without a reservation is a poor plan.
bivy.water: Potable tap water during the serviced season; no supply in winter, when Thunder Arm and the creek are the only sources and need treating
bivy.permit: National Park Service, Ross Lake NRA. Fee campground, reservations through Recreation.gov for most of the season plus some first-come sites. No backcountry permit to sleep here — but one IS needed the moment you move uphill onto Colonial, Pyramid or Snowfield.
bivy.capacity: Large road campground, roughly 90-100 numbered sites including walk-in tent sites and a group site; a smaller north loop sits across the highway

bivy.name: Colonial Basin bench camps, below the Pyramid-Colonial col
bivy.notes: The standard first-night camp for Snowfield, Neve and Colonial, reached by a steep sustained climb from the Pyramid Lake trailhead with no easy water for much of it. Early in the season the ground is still under snow and flat bivy platforms are easier to find than proper tent pitches; by late summer the basin rim dries to sand and polished rock and the tent sites improve. accounts disagree on exactly where the best camp sits — some parties stop on the bench near 5,400 ft, others push over the col into the basin — and both are defensible depending on snow cover and how far you want to carry water. Camp on rock or snow rather than the thin heather.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and small tarns; reliable in early summer, patchy to absent by late August in a dry year, so plan to carry up from lower on the trail
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required — a cross-country zone reached by the Pyramid Lake and Pyramid Peak trails, with permits from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center or the park's online system.
bivy.capacity: Several small parties; a scatter of flat gravel and slab platforms rather than a defined number of sites

bivy.name: Neve-Colonial col high bivy
bivy.notes: Parties heading for Snowfield sometimes push past the basin and sleep at the pass above the Colonial Glacier to shorten summit day and get onto the Neve Glacier early. The trade is weather: this notch funnels wind badly and a night here can be miserable or unsafe in anything but settled conditions, so it suits a stable forecast and a party willing to retreat downhill. Snow cover varies enormously through the season, which changes both whether you can melt water and whether the ground under you is snow or bare rock. Sleeping on the glacier itself is a separate decision with crevasse-hazard implications — scout the site in daylight.
bivy.water: Melted snow only, and that assumes snow is still present at the col; there is no running water
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, same cross-country zone as the basin camps below.
bivy.capacity: One to two small parties on flat snow or a cleared rock platform; genuinely exposed and not somewhere to spread out

bivy.name: Cosho Camp, Fisher Creek
bivy.notes: This forested camp on the north side of Fisher Creek is the usual base for Cosho Peak and the eastern end of Ragged Ridge, reached over Easy Pass from the SR 20 trailhead and then down roughly 1,400 ft of switchbacks to the valley. It is an easy first day from the car, which is why parties use it despite the elevation given back on the descent. Easy Pass sits well east of the winter gate, so this approach exists only while SR 20 is open across the pass — typically late spring through the first serious storms of autumn.
bivy.water: Fisher Creek runs right there and is reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required — a DESIGNATED camp assigned by night, not a first-come dispersed site, so a walk-up can be refused if it is already booked. Have a fallback.
bivy.capacity: Small designated backcountry camp, on the order of one to three parties

bivy.name: Devils Park Shelter, Jackita Ridge trail
bivy.notes: The obvious overnight stop for Crater Mountain and the eastern approaches, about eight miles in from Canyon Creek up a long hot climb through McMillan Park. The shelter is unmaintained and its condition is reported inconsistently year to year, so carry a tent and treat the roof as a bad-weather bonus rather than the plan. Access is seasonal at both ends: SR 20's winter closure puts the Canyon Creek trailhead behind a gate, and the Canyon Creek bridge on the Jackita Ridge trail has been reported out — check current Forest Service conditions, because the ford is dangerous in spring and early-summer runoff.
bivy.water: A stream just east of the shelter is normally flowing well; it can drop off late in a dry summer, and the ridge above Devils Park is dry, so fill here
bivy.permit: US Forest Service, Okanogan-Wenatchee — Pasayten Wilderness. NO reservation and NO fee: free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park at Canyon Creek. This is the sharpest contrast with the Park Service side of the same corridor.
bivy.capacity: An old log shelter with a few rough bunks, plus open meadow camping for several parties immediately around it

bivy.name: Jerry Lakes basin, Jack Mountain south side
bivy.notes: Reached by leaving the Crater Mountain trail and travelling several miles cross-country, this basin is the usual high camp for the south face of Jack Mountain. It is a long committing day from the Canyon Creek trailhead and route-finding on the approach is the crux for many parties, so budget for arriving late. An unplanned bivy on this mountain is common enough that carrying emergency shelter is a reasonable default rather than a precaution. The trailhead is behind the SR 20 winter gate, which closes this approach entirely for roughly half the year.
bivy.water: The lakes themselves plus inlet streams; reliable but standing water, so filter or treat
bivy.permit: CONTESTED BY LOCATION, and this is the one to get right. The administrative boundary runs through the Jack Mountain massif: ground east of the Little Jack ridge crest is Pasayten Wilderness under the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, needing only the free self-issue permit, while ground west of the crest falls in Ross Lake NRA and requires a National Park Service backcountry permit. Jerry Lakes sit on the Forest Service side of that divide — but if your route wanders west you have changed agencies. Carry both or confirm against the boundary before you go.

bivy.capacity: Small designated backcountry camp, on the order of one to three parties

bivy.name: Devils Park Shelter, Jackita Ridge trail
bivy.notes: The obvious overnight stop for Crater Mountain and the eastern approaches, about eight miles in from Canyon Creek up a long hot climb through McMillan Park. The shelter is unmaintained and its condition is reported inconsistently year to year, so carry a tent and treat the roof as a bad-weather bonus rather than the plan. Access is seasonal at both ends: SR 20's winter closure puts the Canyon Creek trailhead behind a gate, and the Canyon Creek bridge on the Jackita Ridge trail has been reported out — check current Forest Service conditions, because the ford is dangerous in spring and early-summer runoff.
bivy.water: A stream just east of the shelter is normally flowing well; it can drop off late in a dry summer, and the ridge above Devils Park is dry, so fill here
bivy.permit: US Forest Service, Okanogan-Wenatchee — Pasayten Wilderness. NO reservation and NO fee: free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park at Canyon Creek. This is the sharpest contrast with the Park Service side of the same corridor.
bivy.capacity: An old log shelter with a few rough bunks, plus open meadow camping for several parties immediately around it

bivy.name: Jerry Lakes basin, Jack Mountain south side
bivy.notes: Reached by leaving the Crater Mountain trail and travelling several miles cross-country, this basin is the usual high camp for the south face of Jack Mountain. It is a long committing day from the Canyon Creek trailhead and route-finding on the approach is the crux for many parties, so budget for arriving late. An unplanned bivy on this mountain is common enough that carrying emergency shelter is a reasonable default rather than a precaution. The trailhead is behind the SR 20 winter gate, which closes this approach entirely for roughly half the year.
bivy.water: The lakes themselves plus inlet streams; reliable but standing water, so filter or treat
bivy.permit: CONTESTED BY LOCATION, and this is the one to get right. The administrative boundary runs through the Jack Mountain massif: ground east of the Little Jack ridge crest is Pasayten Wilderness under the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, needing only the free self-issue permit, while ground west of the crest falls in Ross Lake NRA and requires a National Park Service backcountry permit. Jerry Lakes sit on the Forest Service side of that divide — but if your route wanders west you have changed agencies. Carry both or confirm against the boundary before you go.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed; a few flat spots at the lakes and a hidden pocket among the trees, enough for one or two parties

bivy.name: Source Lake basin, Alpental valley
bivy.notes: The honest finding for this zone is that all three peaks are day climbs from the Alpental lot at about 3,100 ft, and almost nobody camps for them — a full car-to-car day on Chair Peak's Northeast Buttress runs 10-12 hours, The Tooth is shorter, and Guye Peak's west face is barely an approach at all. Separately for Guye Peak: the old walking approach through the Alpental Community Club's private roads has been closed to climbers, so plan the talus approach from public ground.
bivy.water: Reliable in summer: the lake and the South Fork Snoqualmie headwater creeks run all season. In winter the whole basin is snow-covered and you melt.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Snow Lake trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to Oct 31. Parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass, or a day fee; a Washington Discover Pass is NOT valid. Ski season changes this: on weekends and holidays the Alpental lots are run by the ski area under a paid permit, free for carpools of 3+ and for season-pass holders. No Sno-Park permit applies at Alpental.
bivy.capacity: Informal — a handful of small tent spots on durable ground; no established or designated sites

bivy.name: Snow Lake designated campsites
bivy.notes: The busiest destination in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, and a lake basin rather than a climbers' camp, so expect company. It sits north of the divide from the Alpental valley, which means using it as a base for Chair Peak involves crossing the 4,400 ft saddle and dropping to the lake, then reversing that in the morning. For The Tooth and Guye Peak it is the wrong side of the ridge entirely. Its real value to a climbing party is as a legal, established place to sleep when the weather turns or a descent runs late.
bivy.water: The lake is reliable water through summer; treat it. Under snow in winter.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead in season. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of the lake, group size is capped at 12, and campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft in the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest — so stoves only. Same trailhead parking rules as Source Lake.
bivy.capacity: Multiple designated sites around the lake; heavily used and often full on summer weekends

bivy.name: Chair Peak basin snow camp
bivy.notes: Parties climbing Chair Peak's north face or Northeast Buttress in winter sometimes carry up and camp in the basin near the Thumb Tack, which removes the last stretch of approach from a long summit day. Whether that is a good trade is genuinely contested: it shortens the morning but puts you sleeping under loaded avalanche slopes, and most parties instead take a 5 a.m. start from the car and accept the full approach. The elevation given is approximate for the gearing-up basin and will shift with where the snowpack lets you build a platform. Treat this as a conditions-dependent choice, not a standing campsite.
bivy.water: None running. Melt snow — this is a winter and spring option and there is no reliable liquid source in the basin.
bivy.permit: No self-issue wilderness permit is required outside roughly May 15 to Oct 31, but wilderness rules still apply and parking is governed by the ski area's winter permit scheme on peak days. Check the Alpental parking rules for the current season before counting on a spot.
bivy.capacity: Snow camp for one or two tents; no ground sites, entirely dependent on snowpack

bivy.name: Denny Creek Campground, I-90 exit 47
bivy.notes: The nearest developed campground to the Alpental trailhead, roughly a twenty-minute drive back down I-90 and then three miles up the Denny Creek road. The sensible answer for a party arriving late the night before a Tooth or Chair Peak day, since it needs no wilderness permit and no early-morning decisions. Sites go quickly on summer weekends; book ahead rather than driving up hoping. In winter this option disappears entirely and you are back to sleeping in the valley towns or driving up in the dark.
bivy.water: Potable water provided during the operating season.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, reserved through recreation.gov up to six months ahead; a small number of first-come sites. No wilderness permit needed, and no trailhead pass required to sleep here. Seasonal — closed outside the summer months, so it is not an option for a winter climb.
bivy.capacity: About 33 sites, most reservable, including electric and double sites plus one group site

bivy.name: Tinkham Campground, I-90 exit 42
bivy.notes: Further down the valley than Denny Creek, about 1.5 miles in on Forest Road 55 from exit 42, and the usual fallback when Denny Creek is booked out. The extra driving costs perhaps fifteen minutes on the approach next morning, which matters little against a ten-hour climbing day. Like every developed site on this stretch of I-90 it is a summer-only option. It sits well below the pass, low in the South Fork valley.
bivy.water: Water availability here varies by year and is not guaranteed — confirm before relying on it and carry enough for the night otherwise.
bivy.permit: Campground fee via recreation.gov; seasonal operation only, closed outside the summer months. No wilderness permit or trailhead pass involved.
bivy.capacity: Small forested Forest Service campground, reservable sites

bivy.capacity: Small forested Forest Service campground, reservable sites

bivy.water: Better than anywhere else on this side. A creek fed by a lingering snowfield runs at the upper camp through most of the season, and there are ponds along the divide that are worth treating and not drinking untreated. Water gets scarce once the snowfield goes.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit and no climbing permit. The access road is gated seasonally, closed from the start of November until the second week of July for wildlife, which is the single biggest planning constraint on this side of the mountain. Party size 12, no campfires, pack out all waste.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites in the meadows near the head of the divide; pick rocky ground rather than heather, which recovers slowly here

bivy.name: Skyline Divide crest camps
bivy.notes: The other approach to Hadley Peak, from the west along the divide and over Chowder Ridge. The road in has been the problem for years rather than the trail: flood damage at around mile three has left the trailhead inaccessible to vehicles for extended periods with no firm repair date, and the trail has been listed as closed on that account, so this is the first thing to confirm and not an afterthought. When it goes, the crest is easy walking with big views and the last three quarters of a mile up to Chowder Ridge is talus with one steeper step before you top out west of the Hadley Glacier. Camping on the open crest means taking whatever weather arrives off the mountain, and the exposure is the reason parties often drop into the basin instead.
bivy.water: None at the trailhead and none along the trail after early summer, when the snow patches below the crest are gone. Carry everything or plan the trip around a lingering snowfield you have confirmed is still there.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. A recreation pass is required at the trailhead. No campfires anywhere, party size capped at 12, all waste packed out. There is no permit or quota for camping, but the meadows are heavily used and heavily damaged, so camp on bare ground.
bivy.capacity: Several exposed sites along the open crest of the divide once the trail tops out; popular and visible, with no screening from wind or weather

bivy.name: Deadhorse Creek basin, below Chowder Ridge
bivy.notes: The basin sits between Skyline Divide and Cougar Divide, just short of the climb onto Chowder Ridge, and it solves the problem both crest camps have: it has water and it has shelter. A party approaching Hadley from either road can drop into it, sleep out of the wind, and take the ridge in the morning with full bottles. Summit day from here is short by any standard on this mountain. It is subalpine meadow and creek terrain, so camp on durable ground well back from the water. Season is the same as everything else on the north side, mid-August into early October, held back at the front end by mosquitoes and by the road gate on the Cougar Divide side and at the back end by the first real snow.
bivy.water: The most reliable water on the Hadley approach — the creek runs from snowmelt above the basin and holds up later than anything on the ridge crests. Treat it. This is the reason to camp here rather than higher.
bivy.permit: Mount Baker Wilderness, no overnight permit required. Recreation pass at whichever trailhead you start from. Party size 12, campfires prohibited, human waste and everything else packed out — there are no toilets on either divide.
bivy.capacity: Scattered informal sites in the basin between the two divides; sheltered, low use, no facilities of any kind

bivy.name: Lower Blum Lake
bivy.notes: This is the base camp for both peaks and effectively the only one. Getting here is the whole difficulty of the trip: leave trail 606 a short distance past the Baker River suspension bridge, before Blum Creek, and find the faint path that works away from the creek through old timber. The first section is genuine devil's club, fern and deadfall bushwhacking, and the path comes and goes; above that it settles into a steep, tiring forest ridge, then an ascending traverse along the south side of that ridge into the lake basin. Five hours from the car is a good day, and parties routinely take longer. For Mount Blum, the south ridge and southeast slopes go from here up through gullies and snow to the east ridge. For Hagan, climb southeast from the lower lake to about 5,600 ft on the east-west ridge, then traverse south toward the pass below the Hagan peaks. Best from mid-July into September; earlier and the traverse to the lakes is a snow slope with a long runout, later and the water thins. There is no shelter of any kind and no cell coverage.
bivy.water: The lake itself, and a small outlet stream. Treat everything. This is the first reliable water since the river, four thousand feet below
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, required year-round for any overnight stay. The Blum cross-country zone is not one of the reservable zones, so it is walk-up only through the wilderness information center near Marblemount. No campfires anywhere in the zone. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground, never in the meadow, and keep a hundred feet back from the water. Human waste goes in a cathole or, on snow and glacier, in a blue bag carried out. Bear canisters are the sensible answer where the heather gives you nothing to hang from, and can be borrowed in person at the permit office
bivy.capacity: Two or three small tents on heather shelves and gravel near the outlet; the basin is tight and the park caps this cross-country zone at six people and two parties at a time

bivy.name: Middle Blum Lake
bivy.notes: A few hundred yards and a hundred feet of gain above the lower lake, and the more common choice for parties who want to shorten summit day on Blum. The ground is heather and slab, so tent sites are where the rock is, not where the flat grass is. It holds snow later than the lower lake and it catches more wind, which is a fair trade for mosquitoes in July. From here the line to Blum's summit continues past the upper tarn and into the gullies below the east ridge, and the Hagan traverse also starts from this shelf. Nothing about the position changes the approach problem — you still spend a full day getting up from the river.
bivy.water: Lake water. Treat it
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades National Park backcountry permit and the same Blum zone rules as the lower lake — walk-up only, six people, no fires, durable surfaces, hundred-foot setback from water
bivy.capacity: One or two tents on the benches above the shore; smaller and more exposed than the lower lake

bivy.name: Upper Blum tarn, southeast of the main lakes
bivy.notes: The highest practical ground on the Blum side, on the way from the main lakes toward the gullies and snow slopes leading to Blum's east ridge. It buys perhaps an hour on summit day and costs an extra 700 ft of carrying at the end of an already brutal approach day, so most parties leave it to those going on to Hagan or continuing the traverse east. Exposed to weather from every direction. In a low-snow year the tarn is dry and this stops being an option at all.
bivy.water: The tarn, when it is out; it is snow-covered well into summer and may be a snowpatch rather than water in early season. Carry from the lakes below if in doubt
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, Blum cross-country zone, walk-up only. No fires. Because this sits above the meadow line, expect to be camping on snow or bare rock, which is what the zone rules ask for anyway
bivy.capacity: One or two tents at most, on rock and gravel; there is no established site here, only ground that happens to work

bivy.name: South Hagan bench
bivy.notes: Open benches on the south side of Hagan Mountain, reached from the Blum Lakes by climbing to the ridge crest near 5,600 ft and traversing south. This is where parties stage for Hagan's south slopes: from the bench, talus and a scree couloir lead to the southwest end of the Hagan crags, and slabs on the south side give the final scramble to the summit. It is also the natural stop for anyone continuing east toward Hidden Lake and Bacon. The bench is comfortable and the position is superb, but it is fully exposed and the water is seasonal, which is the reason most parties still base at the lakes and do Hagan in a long day.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and small pools that shrink through the season; late summer parties should plan to carry water up from the Blum Lakes or from Hidden Lake below
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit. This ground sits on the boundary between the Blum and Bacon Peak cross-country zones, so confirm which zone your permit is written for when you pick it up. Six-person party limit either way, no fires, no camping in meadow
bivy.capacity: Two tents on heather and gravel benches; informal, with no fixed site

bivy.name: Hidden Lake, below the Blum-Hagan divide
bivy.notes: A small lake in the saddle country between Hagan and Bacon, reached from the Blum Lakes by crossing the ridge southeast of them and dropping to it. It matters here as the reliable water on Hagan's far side and as the standard second night for parties traversing east. It is a considerable drop below the Hagan bench, so it is a poor choice if Hagan is your only objective — you give back four hundred feet you will re-climb in the morning. Reaching it involves snow into midsummer and steep heather afterwards. Do not treat this as an approach camp for Bacon Peak from the Baker River side; the practical way to Bacon is from a different road entirely.
bivy.water: The lake. Treat it. Reliable all season, which is not true of the benches above
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit. This lake sits toward the Bacon Peak side of the divide, so check which cross-country zone the ranger writes your permit for. No fires, six-person limit, camp a hundred feet back from the water
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents on the flats near the shore

bivy.name: Sulphide Camp, end of the Baker River trail
bivy.notes: This is the only designated, built camp anywhere near this trailhead: flat sites and a toilet at the end of trail 606, a couple of easy valley miles past the suspension bridge. IT IS NOT ON THE WAY TO BLUM OR HAGAN. The climbers' path for both peaks leaves the trail near Blum Creek, well before this, and heading up-valley to Sulphide takes you in the wrong direction. It is listed because it is the legal, comfortable option for a party that arrives late, wants a short first evening, or is waiting out weather at the bottom, and because low-elevation valley ground here is otherwise wet, brushy and off-limits. Elevation is valley-bottom, only a little above the trailhead.
bivy.water: Sulphide Creek and the Baker River, both close by. Treat the water; the river runs silty in high melt
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for a designated camp, which is a different reservation than a cross-country zone — book it or ask for it at the permit office rather than assuming a zone permit covers it. No fires
bivy.capacity: Two established sites and a backcountry toilet; a small party each

bivy.name: Blum Creek spur ridge, forest bivy
bivy.notes: THERE IS NO ESTABLISHED CAMP ON THIS APPROACH, said plainly rather than recommending a place that does not exist. The 4,000 ft of steep forest between the Baker River and the Blum Lakes has no benches worth the name, no water on the crest and no clearings; parties who run out of daylight here flatten a spot among the trees and move on at first light. The right plan is to start early and reach the lakes in one push. Keep it in mind only as what you will actually do if the bushwhacking at the bottom eats more of the day than you expected, which it often does in wet conditions, or if somebody in the party is struggling with the load.
bivy.water: None dependable. Blum Creek is below the path and hard to reach from the ridge; carry what you need from the river or push on to the lakes
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit if you sleep here — the park boundary sits close to the river crossing, so assume the whole climb is inside the park and ask at the permit office where the line actually falls before you plan on it. No fires

bivy.capacity: One tent, found rather than chosen; the ridge is steep, timbered and littered with deadfall, and genuinely flat ground is rare

bivy.name: Lunch Counter
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for the South Climb and effectively the only sheltered ground on the route, a wide rubble bench under Suksdorf Ridge about four miles and 3,700 ft above Cold Springs. It sits anywhere from roughly 9,200 to 9,400 ft because the bench is long and people camp at both ends rather than at one spot. The rock walls left by earlier parties are the whole reason to camp here — wind funnels across the bench and an unprotected tent takes a beating — so plan on repairing a wall rather than finding a perfect one. The summit ridge east of here forms the Yakama Nation boundary; the South Climb stays on Forest Service ground, but do not descend or traverse east off the standard line.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and seasonal. Running meltwater usually appears at the upper end of the bench through early and mid summer, but it is not dependable — in a thin snow year or by late season the bench can be dry, so carry a stove and fuel to melt snow.
bivy.permit: Cascade Volcano Pass (Mt. Adams Climbing Pass) required — this camp is above the 7,000 ft threshold that triggers it between May 1 and Sept 30. Bought through recreation.gov, valid for a single climbing trip; carry it and leave a copy in the windshield. Parking at the South Climb trailhead needs a recreation pass, and the climbing pass parking stub satisfies that within Mt. Adams Wilderness in season. Outside that window or below 7,000 ft, a free self-issued wilderness permit is what applies. Human waste must be packed out in the supplied bags.
bivy.capacity: Large — dozens of parties on summer weekends, spread across a broad bench; scores of pre-built rock windbreaks, though the best-sheltered ones fill first

bivy.name: Cold Springs / South Climb trailhead
bivy.notes: Most South Climb parties sleep here the night before, either to acclimatise a little or to get an alpine start without carrying a camp to the Lunch Counter. Facilities are primitive — a vault toilet, no piped water, no developed fee sites. Access is FR 80 to FR 8040 and then FR 8040-500, roughly eight miles of washboarded and rutted gravel with the last three miles steep, narrow and switchbacked; ordinary cars get up it at low speed but a low-slung vehicle can bottom out, and RVs and trailers should not attempt it. The road generally opens around mid-May and is usually clear of snow by the start of July, so early-season parties should expect to park lower and walk.
bivy.water: Unreliable. Treat this as a dry camp and arrive with water. Small springs and Morrison Creek near the road can be running early in the season and gone by late summer.
bivy.permit: A recreation pass is required to park — Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass, or a day pass; a valid Mt. Adams Climbing Pass parking stub also works between May 1 and Sept 30. Camping here is below the 7,000 ft climbing-pass threshold, so a free self-issued wilderness permit covers you unless you go above that line. Waste bags are usually stocked at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Small — a handful of primitive sites plus overflow in the parking area; fills on summer weekends

bivy.name: Morrison Creek Campground
bivy.notes: The fallback camp when the upper road defeats a vehicle or when Cold Springs is full, about three miles below the South Climb trailhead on the same road. The 2012 Cascade Creek fire burned through here, so shade is patchy and there is standing dead timber to consider when choosing a tent spot in wind. Camping here means driving or walking the last steep section to the trailhead in the morning, which costs about an hour but keeps the option open when the road is rough.
bivy.water: Morrison Creek runs beside the camp but is seasonal and can be low or dry by late summer; treat what you take and do not count on it in August or September.
bivy.permit: No climbing pass needed at this elevation — it sits well below the 7,000 ft line. A free self-issued wilderness permit covers travel into Mt. Adams Wilderness from here, and a recreation pass applies at the trailheads above.
bivy.capacity: Small — a handful of primitive sites, several strung along the creek

bivy.name: High Camp (Adams Creek Meadows)
bivy.notes: The base for the north side, reached by the Killen Creek trail from about 4,600 ft to the PCT and then a boot path up to the meadows below the Adams Glacier. Roughly four miles and 2,300 ft of gain, an easy carry compared with the Lunch Counter, and it puts you directly under the glacier's icefall. There is no shelter from wind other than what the rock benches give you, and afternoon weather rolls in fast off the north face. Snow lingers here into July in a heavy year, which affects both the boot track and where you can pitch.
bivy.water: Generally reliable through summer. Meltwater streams from the Adams Glacier snout and small tarns feed the meadows, and Killen Creek runs lower on the approach; filter everything, and expect surface streams to shrink late in a dry season.
bivy.permit: Free self-issued wilderness permit at the Killen Creek trailhead. Note the elevation carefully — at about 6,900 ft this camp sits just under the 7,000 ft threshold, so the camp itself does not require a Cascade Volcano Pass, but any climbing above that line between May 1 and Sept 30 does, so a party heading for the Adams Glacier or North Ridge needs one. Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent for trailhead parking. Camp on durable ground and well back from water — this is fragile subalpine meadow.
bivy.capacity: Moderate — open meadow and bench terrain with many dispersed spots; busy in wildflower season but rarely crowded by alpine standards

bivy.name: Adams Glacier moraine bivy
bivy.notes: Parties attacking the Adams Glacier sometimes move above High Camp onto the moraines below the icefall to shorten summit day, with usable ground reported roughly between 7,100 and 7,700 ft depending on which rib and how the moraine has changed. Exact spots shift year to year as the glacier retreats and the moraine slumps, so treat any elevation given for it as approximate and be prepared to camp lower. It is exposed, rockfall from the moraine walls is a real consideration in warm weather, and there is no shelter at all — the trade is a shorter and colder-snow start onto the glacier. Whether the extra carry beats simply starting early from High Camp is argued both ways.
bivy.water: Meltwater from the glacier snout and moraine pools during the day, freezing overnight; workable in warm conditions but not a certainty. Most parties melt snow here rather than depend on running water.
bivy.permit: Cascade Volcano Pass (Mt. Adams Climbing Pass) required — above 7,000 ft, May 1 through Sept 30, single trip, from recreation.gov. Outside that window a free self-issued wilderness permit applies instead. Pack out all human waste.
bivy.capacity: Very small — a few flat gravel or snow platforms for one or two tents; you may have to build a platform

The road generally opens around mid-May and is usually clear of snow by the start of July, so early-season parties should expect to park lower and walk.
bivy.water: Unreliable. Treat this as a dry camp and arrive with water. Small springs and Morrison Creek near the road can be running early in the season and gone by late summer.
bivy.permit: A recreation pass is required to park — Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass, or a day pass; a valid Mt. Adams Climbing Pass parking stub also works between May 1 and Sept 30. Camping here is below the 7,000 ft climbing-pass threshold, so a free self-issued wilderness permit covers you unless you go above that line. Waste bags are usually stocked at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Small — a handful of primitive sites plus overflow in the parking area; fills on summer weekends

bivy.name: Morrison Creek Campground
bivy.notes: The fallback camp when the upper road defeats a vehicle or when Cold Springs is full, about three miles below the South Climb trailhead on the same road. The 2012 Cascade Creek fire burned through here, so shade is patchy and there is standing dead timber to consider when choosing a tent spot in wind. Camping here means driving or walking the last steep section to the trailhead in the morning, which costs about an hour but keeps the option open when the road is rough.

bivy.permit: No climbing pass needed at this elevation — it sits well below the 7,000 ft line. A free self-issued wilderness permit covers travel into Mt. Adams Wilderness from here, and a recreation pass applies at the trailheads above.
bivy.capacity: Small — a handful of primitive sites, several strung along the creek

bivy.name: High Camp (Adams Creek Meadows)
bivy.notes: The base for the north side, reached by the Killen Creek trail from about 4,600 ft to the PCT and then a boot path up to the meadows below the Adams Glacier. Roughly four miles and 2,300 ft of gain, an easy carry compared with the Lunch Counter, and it puts you directly under the glacier's icefall. There is no shelter from wind other than what the rock benches give you, and afternoon weather rolls in fast off the north face. Snow lingers here into July in a heavy year, which affects both the boot track and where you can pitch.

Note the elevation carefully — at about 6,900 ft this camp sits just under the 7,000 ft threshold, so the camp itself does not require a Cascade Volcano Pass, but any climbing above that line between May 1 and Sept 30 does, so a party heading for the Adams Glacier or North Ridge needs one. bivy.capacity: Moderate — open meadow and bench terrain with many dispersed spots; busy in wildflower season but rarely crowded by alpine standards

bivy.name: Adams Glacier moraine bivy
bivy.notes: Parties attacking the Adams Glacier sometimes move above High Camp onto the moraines below the icefall to shorten summit day, with usable ground reported roughly between 7,100 and 7,700 ft depending on which rib and how the moraine has changed. Exact spots shift year to year as the glacier retreats and the moraine slumps, so treat any elevation given for it as approximate and be prepared to camp lower. It is exposed, rockfall from the moraine walls is a real consideration in warm weather, and there is no shelter at all — the trade is a shorter and colder-snow start onto the glacier. Whether the extra carry beats simply starting early from High Camp is argued both ways.
bivy.water: Meltwater from the glacier snout and moraine pools during the day, freezing overnight; workable in warm conditions but not a certainty. Most parties melt snow here rather than depend on running water.
bivy.permit: Cascade Volcano Pass (Mt. Adams Climbing Pass) required — above 7,000 ft, May 1 through Sept 30, single trip, from recreation.gov. Outside that window a free self-issued wilderness permit applies instead. Pack out all human waste.
bivy.capacity: Very small — a few flat gravel or snow platforms for one or two tents; you may have to build a platform

bivy.name: Lunch Counter
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for the South Climb and effectively the only sheltered ground on the route, a wide rubble bench under Suksdorf Ridge about four miles and 3,700 ft above Cold Springs. Its height is given anywhere from roughly 9,200 to 9,400 ft because the bench is long and people camp at both ends rather than at one spot. The rock walls left by earlier parties are the whole reason to camp here — wind funnels across the bench and an unprotected tent takes a beating — so plan on repairing a wall rather than finding a perfect one. The summit ridge east of here forms the Yakama Nation boundary; the South Climb stays on Forest Service ground, but do not descend or traverse east off the standard line.

bivy.permit: Cascade Volcano Pass (Mt. Adams Climbing Pass) required — this camp is above the 7,000 ft threshold that triggers it between May 1 and Sept 30. Bought through recreation.gov, valid for a single climbing trip; carry it and leave a copy in the windshield. Parking at the South Climb trailhead needs a recreation pass, and the climbing pass parking stub satisfies that within Mt. Adams Wilderness in season. Outside that window or below 7,000 ft, a free self-issued wilderness permit is what applies. Human waste must be packed out in the supplied bags.
bivy.capacity: Large — dozens of parties on summer weekends, spread across a broad bench; scores of pre-built rock windbreaks, though the best-sheltered ones fill first
