Later in the season the ice recedes, the slab runoff dries up, and the whole plan depends on melting snow instead. Check that there is still snow or ice water before relying on this camp in August or September.
bivy.water: Running water at the edge of the glacier and on the glacial slabs below the col in season. This is meltwater, so it flows on warm afternoons and can vanish on a cold morning or after the snow has gone
bivy.permit: National forest wilderness. Dispersed camping is legal with no overnight permit currently required, party size limited to twelve. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than on the thin heather, and pack out everything including waste. Campfires are inappropriate at this elevation and are usually prohibited under late season fire restrictions. A Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass is needed at the forest service trailheads on the southeast side.
bivy.capacity: Two or three small tents on gravel benches and slabs; exposed and windy

bivy.name: South Twin Sister summit bivies
bivy.notes: The highest summit in the range, somewhere between about six thousand nine hundred and seven thousand feet depending on which survey you believe, and the classic place to split the north to south traverse into two days. There are a number of flat gravel and rubble bivy spots scattered among the summit blocks, built up by parties over the years, and the view across to Mount Baker at dawn is the reason people do it. It is entirely waterless. The dunite the range is made of is dense and unfractured and sheds or swallows water rather than holding it, so there are no springs on the crest and no tarns near the summit; whatever you drink here you carried or melted. Exposed to everything, with no wind shelter beyond the blocks themselves. Reasonable from July into September once the snow has consolidated. Do not plan on finding snow to melt in a dry late summer.
bivy.water: None. Melt snow if there is any, otherwise carry every litre from Orsino Creek, the glacier margin or Green Creek
bivy.permit: National forest wilderness, dispersed camping legal, no overnight permit currently required, party size limit twelve. No fires. The whole approach to this summit crosses private timberland where the current landowner permit applies, so the camp itself is legal while the walk to it may not be without the right paperwork.
bivy.capacity: Several small hand-built gravel platforms among the summit blocks; one or two tents plus tarps or bags

bivy.name: Green Creek cirque dispersed camp
bivy.notes: This basin under the Green Creek glacier is ringed by Skookum, Little Sister and Cinderella and sits directly below the south end of the traverse, which makes it the natural base for all three of those summits and for the circuit that links them to South Twin. It is reached by branching off the Elbow Lake trail at a switchback onto a blazed climbers path, then working up into the cirque. There are no developed campsites; parties use sandy patches beneath protecting boulders and small flat spots in the heather, and the area holds a wilderness feel that low impact camping is the only way to keep. The springs here are worth planning around, because once you are on the crest above there is nothing. Getting into the basin involves a long loose talus slope where most of what you stand on moves, which is slow and hazardous when wet. Midsummer through early autumn; early season snow makes the approach faster but the river crossing more dangerous.
bivy.water: Two springs of running water in the basin, plus Green Creek lower down. The most dependable water anywhere on the southeast side of the range and the reason this basin is used at all
bivy.permit: National forest, largely within the wilderness unit. Dispersed camping legal, no overnight permit currently required, party size limit twelve, no developed sites and no facilities. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed at the trailhead. Fire restrictions are common from midsummer. Access from this side does not cross the private timberland, but it does require fording the Middle Fork Nooksack, and the roads serving the trailhead have their own closures.
bivy.capacity: Small dispersed sites, sandy patches under boulders; two or three parties spread out

bivy.name: Elbow Lake hiker camps
bivy.notes: These are the only established campsites anywhere near this range, reached by a spur off the main trail to the east shore of the lake. They are not on the direct line to any of these five summits, sitting on the divide east of the crest rather than under it, so treat them as a legal and comfortable staging camp on public ground rather than as a climbing basecamp. They are most useful for a party coming in from the south with an awkward road situation, or for anyone who wants a settled night before or after a long day on the ridge. The lake is buggy in early summer and the surrounding ground is boggy in places. Because the road access on both ends of this trail has been unreliable and at least one vehicle closure has been in force recently, check the current status of the forest roads and of the river ford before planning a trip around this camp.
bivy.water: The lake, filtered. Reliable all season, though shallow and warm by late summer
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, within or adjoining the wilderness unit. No overnight permit currently required, party size limit twelve, Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass at the trailhead. Fires may be restricted or banned in late summer. Access is the problem rather than the permit: there is no bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack at the northern trailhead and has not been for decades, so that side requires a ford that is not safe at high flow, and the southern road approach has been subject to a vehicle closure part way in. Confirm both roads and the crossing before committing.
bivy.capacity: Two established hiker sites on the east shore

bivy.name: Camp Mystery — the last water below Marmot Pass
bivy.notes: The standard base for Buckhorn Mountain, sitting at 4.6 miles and about 5,400 ft on the Upper Big Quilcene trail, roughly half a mile and 500 ft below Marmot Pass. From here the summit day is short: over the pass at 5,950 ft, then a rough open boot path climbing about a mile and 900 ft to the 6,996 ft southwest summit. Camping here rather than at the pass costs you the sunset and the view and buys you water, tree cover and shelter from wind, which on this crest is not a small trade. Below it, Shelter Rock Camp at 2.6 miles and about 3,600 ft is the wet-weather fallback if you start late. The season is roughly late June through October; snow lingers in the upper basin into early summer and the trail above camp is exposed once it leaves the trees.
bivy.water: The reason to stop here. A stream runs through camp and is the LAST RELIABLE WATER on the whole approach — everything above is dry ground. Fill for the summit day here, not at the pass.
bivy.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. No advance permit and no fee to camp — sign the free self-issued register at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park. Group limit is twelve. OPEN FIRES ARE PROHIBITED above 3,500 ft, which includes this camp, so bring a stove and do not gather wood.
bivy.capacity: A scatter of established sites among the firs, perhaps eight to ten tents spread out along the trail; busy but rarely truly full

bivy.name: Marmot Pass — high dry bivy on the crest
bivy.notes: The obvious camp for anyone whose objective is Buckhorn Mountain and who is willing to haul water, because the summit path leaves directly from the pass and a party sleeping here is on top for sunrise with an hour of walking. It is also the hinge of this whole zone: the trail carries on over the pass and drops 1.7 miles down to Boulder Shelter, which is how a Quilcene-side party reaches the Warrior and Inner Constance country without driving around to the Dungeness. The cost of camping this high is real — the pass is a wind funnel with no tree cover, weather arrives with no warning off the Dungeness side, and the meadows here are fragile enough that you should use an existing pad rather than making a new one. Snow-free from roughly early July; a spring ascent on skis or snowshoes is common but then the pass is a genuine winter camp.
bivy.water: NONE. This is a dry camp and it is the single most common mistake made here — late-season accounts describe not a puddle or a patch of snow anywhere near the pass. Carry everything up from Camp Mystery, which is the last source half a mile below.
bivy.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. Free self-registration at the trailhead, Northwest Forest Pass to park, group limit twelve, no fires at this elevation. No quota and no reservation.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small hardened pads and windbreaks in the meadow and just over the far side; two or three parties before it feels crowded

bivy.name: Buckhorn Lake — the base for Mount Worthington
bivy.notes: Mount Worthington has no maintained trail to its summit and no route that anyone would call standard, so the camp does most of the work. Buckhorn Lake sits about half a mile off the Tubal Cain trail on a spur leaving at roughly five and a half to six miles, and from it the usual line crosses the outlet, works around the south end of the lake on a discontinuous path through moderate brush, climbs south into an open basin near 5,260 ft, and then heads up to the saddle between Worthington and Iron Mountain — the 6,938 ft summit is off-trail scrambling and routefinding from there. Camping lower at the old mine workings adds several hundred feet and a couple of miles to the morning; camping higher is not really an option, since above the lake there is neither water nor level ground until the ridge. Scope the descent line on the walk in, because it is much harder to identify from above. Best from July into October once the brush is dry and the basin has melted out.
bivy.water: Reliable at the lake all season. It is a shallow forested tarn rather than running water, so filter it, and there is nothing above once you start up toward the saddle.
bivy.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. Free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass required to park at the Tubal Cain trailhead. Group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft. No quota, no reservation, no bear canister requirement on this side of the divide — though the mine area sees enough traffic that hanging or canistering food is sensible anyway.
bivy.capacity: Modest, three or four small sites in dark timber at the lake; the Tubal Cain mine area lower down holds more parties if this is taken

bivy.name: Camp Windy, below Mount Townsend
bivy.notes: The only real camp on Mount Townsend, sitting somewhere around 5,200 ft at roughly two and a half to three miles up the trail — published elevations for it vary by about a hundred feet, which is fair given it is a spread of sites rather than a point. Townsend is a walk-up by its standard trail and most parties do it as a day hike, so the case for camping is weather, an early start for the view east over Puget Sound, or linking it with the Silver Lakes basin. The switchbacks above camp reach the Silver Lakes junction near 5,500 ft at about three miles, and those lakes at roughly 5,400 ft are the quieter alternative if Camp Windy is full — but they sit in a side valley and add distance to the summit rather than saving any. Above camp the trail breaks out onto open, wind-scoured slopes to the 6,280 ft south summit; the name of the camp is not decorative, and a tent pitched carelessly here will not survive the night.
bivy.water: Windy Lake, a shallow tarn just off the trail below camp, is the water source and holds through the season, but it is a still pool rather than a stream — treat it. There is nothing above camp on the way to the summit.
bivy.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. Free self-registration at the Mount Townsend trailhead. Accounts disagree about whether a parking pass is enforced at this particular trailhead, so carry a Northwest Forest Pass rather than find out. Group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft, no quota and no advance booking.
bivy.capacity: Several established sites with plenty of flat ground; comfortably takes four or five parties, and it is popular with families

bivy.name: Boulder Shelter — the last camp outside the national park
bivy.notes: The working base for Warrior Peak, and the cheapest night in this zone by a wide margin because nothing has to be booked. It sits at about 4,950 ft and roughly 6.3 miles from the Upper Dungeness trailhead at 2,500 ft, past Camp Handy at 3,100 ft — an easy valley walk on maintained trail, which is why this and not the Dosewallips is how people actually get into this country. It is also 1.7 miles below Marmot Pass, so a Quilcene-side party can traverse in over the pass. For the Warrior Peak southeast summit the day runs south two-plus miles on the Dungeness trail, then up the prominent couloir north-northeast to a saddle near 7,000 ft; the couloir holds snow into late season and turns icy in cold weather, and the first twenty to fifty feet of rock above it is genuinely poor, low fifth class, and wants a rope. Camping higher in the cirque below the summit shortens that considerably and several parties recommend it, but it is a dry, unestablished bivy and you carry water for it. Best from July into September.
bivy.water: A stream runs by the site and is dependable. This is the last water you can rely on without a park permit, and it is worth topping off here whichever direction you are heading.
bivy.permit: THIS IS THE JURISDICTION LINE AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL FACT IN THIS ZONE. Boulder Shelter is in the Buckhorn Wilderness on national forest ground: free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass to park, group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft, NO reservation, NO quota and NO bear canister requirement. Walk a couple of miles further toward Home Lake and you cross into Olympic National Park, where every one of those rules changes. Dogs are legal up to the boundary and illegal past it.
bivy.capacity: Established sites around a three-sided wooden shelter plus the boulders it is named for; several parties fit, and it is quiet by Olympic standards

bivy.name: Home Lake, below Constance Pass — inside the park, and reached from the north
bivy.notes: The high camp for both Warrior Peak and the northwest side of Inner Constance, and the natural next step up from Boulder Shelter once you want to be closer to the peaks. Reach it from the UPPER DUNGENESS trailhead by way of Camp Handy and Boulder Shelter — the approach from the Dosewallips over Constance Pass is technically the same lake but adds the long closed-road walk on that side and is not how anyone sensibly gets here. Do not confuse this basin with Lake Constance: they sit on opposite flanks of the massif, the twenty-person quota that governs Lake Constance does not apply here, and neither camp substitutes for the other. From Home Lake the usual line for Inner Constance works up the northwest side toward the 7,670 ft summit on loose alpine rock; the northeast summit by way of Crystal Pass at the head of Avalanche Canyon is a different climb from a different camp altogether. Camping lower at Boulder Shelter saves you the permit and the canister at the cost of two miles and 400 ft each way on summit morning, which on a long alpine day is a real price. Snow-free from roughly July; the basin is exposed and holds weather off Constance Pass.
bivy.water: The lake, reliable through the season. It is the last dependable water before Constance Pass and before anything you climb from here, and the slopes above hold no running water once the snow has gone.
bivy.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK, and everything changes at the boundary sign about a mile below the lake. An overnight wilderness permit is mandatory and is reserved in advance through the federal recreation booking site; the summer season runs roughly mid-May to mid-October with reservations opening in the spring. BEAR CANISTERS ARE REQUIRED — hangs and wires are not accepted, and free loaners can be collected from the park wilderness office. No fires at this elevation. Dogs are prohibited. None of this applies at Boulder Shelter two miles back down the trail, and confusing the two is the standard way to arrive here without a legal place to sleep.
bivy.capacity: A few small sites in an open subalpine basin; the park sets a maximum party size for the area, so check what your permit allows before assuming a big group fits

bivy.capacity: Several established sites with plenty of flat ground; comfortably takes four or five parties, and it is popular with families

bivy.name: Boulder Shelter — the last camp outside the national park
bivy.notes: The working base for Warrior Peak, and the cheapest night in this zone by a wide margin because nothing has to be booked. It sits at about 4,950 ft and roughly 6.3 miles from the Upper Dungeness trailhead at 2,500 ft, past Camp Handy at 3,100 ft — an easy valley walk on maintained trail, which is why this and not the Dosewallips is how people actually get into this country. It is also 1.7 miles below Marmot Pass, so a Quilcene-side party can traverse in over the pass. For the Warrior Peak southeast summit the day runs south two-plus miles on the Dungeness trail, then up the prominent couloir north-northeast to a saddle near 7,000 ft; the couloir holds snow into late season and turns icy in cold weather, and the first twenty to fifty feet of rock above it is genuinely poor, low fifth class, and wants a rope. Camping higher in the cirque below the summit shortens that considerably and several parties recommend it, but it is a dry, unestablished bivy and you carry water for it. Best from July into September.
bivy.water: A stream runs by the site and is dependable. This is the last water you can rely on without a park permit, and it is worth topping off here whichever direction you are heading.
bivy.permit: THIS IS THE JURISDICTION LINE AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL FACT IN THIS ZONE. Boulder Shelter is in the Buckhorn Wilderness on national forest ground: free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass to park, group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft, NO reservation, NO quota and NO bear canister requirement. Walk a couple of miles further toward Home Lake and you cross into Olympic National Park, where every one of those rules changes. Dogs are legal up to the boundary and illegal past it.
bivy.capacity: Established sites around a three-sided wooden shelter plus the boulders it is named for; several parties fit, and it is quiet by Olympic standards

bivy.name: Home Lake, below Constance Pass — inside the park, and reached from the north
bivy.notes: The high camp for both Warrior Peak and the northwest side of Inner Constance, and the natural next step up from Boulder Shelter once you want to be closer to the peaks. Reach it from the UPPER DUNGENESS trailhead by way of Camp Handy and Boulder Shelter — the approach from the Dosewallips over Constance Pass is technically the same lake but adds the long closed-road walk on that side and is not how anyone sensibly gets here. Do not confuse this basin with Lake Constance: they sit on opposite flanks of the massif, the twenty-person quota that governs Lake Constance does not apply here, and neither camp substitutes for the other. From Home Lake the usual line for Inner Constance works up the northwest side toward the 7,670 ft summit on loose alpine rock; the northeast summit by way of Crystal Pass at the head of Avalanche Canyon is a different climb from a different camp altogether. Camping lower at Boulder Shelter saves you the permit and the canister at the cost of two miles and 400 ft each way on summit morning, which on a long alpine day is a real price. Snow-free from roughly July; the basin is exposed and holds weather off Constance Pass.
bivy.water: The lake, reliable through the season. It is the last dependable water before Constance Pass and before anything you climb from here, and the slopes above hold no running water once the snow has gone.
bivy.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK, and everything changes at the boundary sign about a mile below the lake. An overnight wilderness permit is mandatory and is reserved in advance through the federal recreation booking site; the summer season runs roughly mid-May to mid-October with reservations opening in the spring. BEAR CANISTERS ARE REQUIRED — hangs and wires are not accepted, and free loaners can be collected from the park wilderness office. No fires at this elevation. Dogs are prohibited. None of this applies at Boulder Shelter two miles back down the trail, and confusing the two is the standard way to arrive here without a legal place to sleep.
bivy.capacity: A few small sites in an open subalpine basin; the park sets a maximum party size for the area, so check what your permit allows before assuming a big group fits

bivy.name: Sloan Peak high camp — heather benches above Cougar Creek
bivy.notes: Camps here sit on open heather with the Sloan Glacier and the start of the corkscrew ledge system directly above, which makes for a short summit morning. Lower bivy pockets exist around 3,500 ft where the trail eases off, and some parties stop there when the river ford has eaten the day. EVERYTHING ABOVE THE TRAILHEAD DEPENDS ON THE NORTH FORK SAUK FORD, which is the genuine crux of the trip: it has no bridge, runs fast and thigh-deep or worse in snowmelt, and log jams that worked one season are gone the next. Camp on bare ground or snow rather than the meadow turf, which is thin and slow to recover.
bivy.water: Cougar Creek below the benches and snowmelt runnels near camp are reliable into midsummer; by late August the higher pockets can dry and parties may need to descend or melt snow
bivy.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead box; no reservation or quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group size limited to 12.
bivy.capacity: Small, scattered pockets — a few tents on heather and gravel benches; no single site holds a large party

bivy.name: Vesper Creek basin and Lake Elan, beyond Headlee Pass
bivy.notes: The working base camp for Vesper Peak's north side and for Sperry, and it puts Morning Star within reach along the ridge. Getting here means the Sunrise Mine trail's ford of the South Fork Stillaguamish, then the switchbacked chute below Headlee Pass at roughly 4,700 ft, which is loose and known for rockfall — parties should not stack up in it. Snow lingers in the chute and on the pass long after the valley is clear, and it is the section most likely to turn an overnight around. Camp on the durable benches rather than the meadow closest to the water. No elevation is recorded; none was confidently sourced.
bivy.water: Reliable — the basin outlet stream runs all season and the lake itself is a backup, though it holds ice and snow cover well into July
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest but OUTSIDE any wilderness — no permit of any kind to camp. Northwest Forest Pass required at the Sunrise Mine trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Several tents — grassy benches above the stream just past the pass, plus more spread around the lake basin

bivy.name: Foggy Lake, Gothic Basin
bivy.notes: From here both Del Campo and Gothic go as short snow-and-scramble outings, which is why parties carry in rather than push either from the road. The approach leaves Barlow Pass on the old road grade before turning up a steep, rocky climbers' trail with slabby sections that are unpleasant when wet. The basin is bare rock and thin alpine soil with almost nothing to bury waste in, so pack it out. Whether the basin is a July trip or an August one moves year to year with the snowpack.
bivy.water: The lake is the water source and is dependable, but it is frequently frozen or snow-covered into July, so early-season parties should expect to melt or find running melt below the outlet
bivy.permit: National forest land, NOT wilderness — no camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. Campfires are prohibited in the basin.
bivy.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the south shore and on the bench toward the base of Gothic; the basin absorbs a fair number of parties but fills on good weekends

bivy.name: Monte Cristo townsite, walk-in from Barlow Pass
bivy.notes: Reaching it is a flat four-mile walk on the old road and rail grade from the Barlow Pass gate, which makes it an easy place to stage a long approach without a real backpacking day. Climbers use it mainly as a jumping-off point deeper into the Monte Cristo group rather than for Vesper or Sloan. Barlow Pass itself is the usual car-bivy for early starts on Gothic Basin, though it is a parking area rather than a campground — no water, no facilities, and it fills. The site is historic mining ground with old debris and open workings, so wander off the beaten paths carefully.
bivy.water: Creek and river water is plentiful and must NOT be treated as ordinary backcountry water. This drainage carries arsenic and other heavy metals from the mining era at levels above drinking-water standards, and filtering, boiling and tablets do none of them any good — those methods address organisms, not dissolved metals. Carry what you need for the road walk, or draw from tributaries well above the old workings rather than from the valley bottom.
bivy.permit: Outside designated wilderness at the townsite itself; no camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Barlow Pass. The peaks above, including the Columbia Glacier group, sit in the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness where the free self-issue permit applies.
bivy.capacity: Small — roughly half a dozen developed sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet, plus scattered backcountry spots along the way in

bivy.name: Bedal Campground, Mountain Loop Highway
bivy.notes: The closest road camp to the Sloan Peak and Bedal Creek trailheads, and the standard place to sleep the night before a Sloan attempt since the useful start time is well before dawn. It sits on the UNPAVED stretch of the loop, so access depends entirely on whether the seasonal gate between Barlow Pass and the Bedal area is open — the road normally closes around early November and reopens in the second half of May, with the exact date set by snow and washout repairs. Coming from Granite Falls when that gate is shut means the long drive around through Darrington. Check the Darrington district's road status, because the gate has opened as late as Memorial Day in heavy years.
bivy.water: No treated drinking water at the sites — bring your own or filter from the adjacent river
bivy.permit: Developed fee campground on national forest land; the per-night fee covers it and no pass or permit is needed to occupy a site. Nothing here is inside wilderness.
bivy.capacity: Around 20 developed sites with tables, tent pads, fire rings and vault toilets; fee campground, typically open late spring to fall

bivy.name: Verlot corridor campgrounds — Turlo, Verlot and Gold Basin
bivy.notes: These sit on the paved lower half of the loop and stay reachable when the gravel section above Barlow Pass is gated shut, which makes them the fallback base for Vesper, Morning Star, Sperry and the Big Four side of the valley. They are closer to the Sunrise Mine and Big Four trailheads than anything up-valley, at the cost of being low, wooded and busy with general campers rather than climbers. Weekend availability is genuinely tight in midsummer, so a reservation is worth having. Dispersed roadside pullouts along the corridor need no permit but are increasingly signed and patrolled.
bivy.water: Verlot and Gold Basin generally have drinking water in season; the Stillaguamish runs alongside as a backup
bivy.permit: Developed fee campgrounds, no permit. None are in wilderness. A Northwest Forest Pass is what you need for the trailheads up the road, not for the sites themselves.
bivy.capacity: Large by the standards of this valley — dozens of developed sites across the three, tables, toilets, some with potable water; fee sites, reservable in part

bivy.name: Artist Point and the Heather Meadows road end
bivy.notes: The obvious place to sleep is, plainly, the one place you cannot. Table Mountain is a short, steep switchbacked climb from the Artist Point lot and is usually done in an hour or two; Mount Herman goes from the Bagley Lakes trailhead across from the ski area, past the lakes and up towards Herman Saddle, leaving the trail at the last switchback for the ridge between Mazama Dome and the summit; Mount Ann leaves the Lake Ann trail at the Austin Pass trailhead a little below Artist Point and is a much bigger day, around ten and a half miles with four thousand feet of gain, ending in a genuine scramble. All three are car-to-car objectives for a fit party. THE SEASONAL GATE IS THE PLANNING CONSTRAINT: the last stretch of highway above Heather Meadows to Artist Point is narrow, steeply banked and closed to vehicles every winter, typically shutting somewhere between mid-October and the start of November with the first real snow and not reopening until the plows get through, which in a heavy year is well into July. The highway is kept open to Heather Meadows through the winter for the ski area, so a closed gate costs you the top two and a half miles rather than the whole road. Parties arriving before the gate opens are walking or skinning that section with the peaks still under snow, which changes all three from scrambles into snow climbs.
bivy.water: None. There is no potable water anywhere along this stretch of road or on the trails above it, and every lake and stream on the Chain Lakes circuit has to be treated.
bivy.permit: A recreation pass must be displayed at Artist Point and at the Bagley Lakes trailhead; the state parks pass is not valid at these Forest Service sites. There is a self-issue wilderness register near the trailhead. The camping rules here are the strict part and they are easy to fall foul of: camping is prohibited on Table Mountain from mid-May to mid-November, prohibited at the Bagley Lakes trailhead over the same window, and prohibited within a mile of the Chain Lakes trail junction on the Ptarmigan Ridge side. Camping outside that window, in deep winter, is legal on Table Mountain. Party size in the wilderness is capped at twelve, campfires are prohibited outright and only carry-in stoves are allowed, and dogs must be leashed through the developed area.
bivy.capacity: A large paved turnaround at Artist Point and a second big lot at Heather Meadows below it; parking for many vehicles, and NO legal camping at either. Treat this as a start line rather than a site.

bivy.name: Silver Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground to the Heather Meadows end of the highway, roughly fourteen miles east of Glacier on the west side of the road just after the river crossing, and about eight miles below the Heather Meadows lots. This is the practical answer for a party that drives up the night before a scramble on Table Mountain, Mount Herman or Mount Ann and wants to be at the trailhead early without sleeping in a day-use car park. It is emphatically staging rather than plan: you are three thousand feet below the objectives and the drive up in the morning takes twenty minutes. Because there are no reservations it is a gamble on a Friday evening in July and August, and the fallback is the campground further down the valley. It stays open later into the autumn than the road to Artist Point does, which matters for anyone climbing these peaks in October.
bivy.water: Piped water at the campground during the operating season, and the river alongside. Confirm the water is turned on if you are arriving at the shoulders of the season.
bivy.permit: A campground fee is charged per night and paid on site; this is a fee campground rather than a pass site, so a recreation pass does not cover the overnight. Fires are allowed in the provided rings unless a county or forest-wide burn ban is in force, which through a dry August is common. Standard national forest food-storage sense applies — black bears work this valley.
bivy.capacity: About twenty sites in forest beside the North Fork Nooksack, with vault toilets and drinking water in season; first come, first served, and it fills on summer weekends

bivy.name: Douglas Fir Campground
bivy.notes: Two and a half miles east of Glacier, low in the valley and a long way below anything you would climb — but it is the campground that serves BOTH halves of this zone, because the Canyon Creek Road turning is only a couple of miles back down the highway. A party bound for Bearpaw Mountain has a rough, slow forest road ahead of them in the morning and this is the sensible place to be the night before; a party bound for Heather Meadows has a longer drive up than they would from the higher campground but a guaranteed bed. Being at a thousand feet in dense timber it is warm, damp and mosquito-prone in early summer, and it gives you no acclimatisation and no view. The upside is that it is open when the high country is not, and that it is the only bookable option on this side of the mountain.
bivy.water: Piped water in season plus the river. Treat river water.
bivy.permit: Per-night campground fee, bookable ahead through the national reservation system, so unlike the higher campground you can arrive at ten at night and know you have a site. Campfire rings are provided and are subject to seasonal burn bans. A recreation pass does not cover camping here.
bivy.capacity: Around thirty sites in old growth beside the North Fork Nooksack, with vault toilets and seasonal drinking water; reservable in advance, which is the reason to choose it over the campground higher up

bivy.name: Mazama Lake designated sites, Chain Lakes
bivy.notes: The nearest legal backcountry camping to the Heather Meadows peaks and the only overnight option in the immediate basin, in the string of subalpine lakes that the Chain Lakes trail drops into on the far side of Herman Saddle. From Artist Point the circuit is around six miles with roughly seventeen hundred feet of gain and loss, and the lakes sit a bit under halfway round. For Mount Herman this is genuinely useful: the saddle is on the route, so a party that camps here is above the trailhead with a very short morning to the south ridge. For Table Mountain it is a detour rather than an approach, and the reason to know about it is the ban on camping on Table Mountain itself through the summer. Snow lingers in the basin into mid-August in a heavy year, which is worth knowing before committing to a site that may be under a drift. Trekking poles earn their weight on the snow traverses. Table Mountain is a short, steep switchbacked climb from the Artist Point lot and is usually done in an hour or two; Mount Herman goes from the Bagley Lakes trailhead across from the ski area, past the lakes and up towards Herman Saddle, leaving the trail at the last switchback for the ridge between Mazama Dome and the summit; Mount Ann leaves the Lake Ann trail at the Austin Pass trailhead a little below Artist Point and is a much bigger day, around ten and a half miles with four thousand feet of gain, ending in a genuine scramble. All three are car-to-car objectives for a fit party. THE SEASONAL GATE IS THE PLANNING CONSTRAINT: the last stretch of highway above Heather Meadows to Artist Point is narrow, steeply banked and closed to vehicles every winter, typically shutting somewhere between mid-October and the start of November with the first real snow and not reopening until the plows get through, which in a heavy year is well into July. The highway is kept open to Heather Meadows through the winter for the ski area, so a closed gate costs you the top two and a half miles rather than the whole road. Parties arriving before the gate opens are walking or skinning that section with the peaks still under snow, which changes all three from scrambles into snow climbs.
bivy.water: None. There is no potable water anywhere along this stretch of road or on the trails above it, and every lake and stream on the Chain Lakes circuit has to be treated.
bivy.permit: A recreation pass must be displayed at Artist Point and at the Bagley Lakes trailhead; the state parks pass is not valid at these Forest Service sites. There is a self-issue wilderness register near the trailhead. The camping rules here are the strict part and they are easy to fall foul of: camping is prohibited on Table Mountain from mid-May to mid-November, prohibited at the Bagley Lakes trailhead over the same window, and prohibited within a mile of the Chain Lakes trail junction on the Ptarmigan Ridge side. Camping outside that window, in deep winter, is legal on Table Mountain. Party size in the wilderness is capped at twelve, campfires are prohibited outright and only carry-in stoves are allowed, and dogs must be leashed through the developed area.
bivy.capacity: A large paved turnaround at Artist Point and a second big lot at Heather Meadows below it; parking for many vehicles, and NO legal camping at either. Treat this as a start line rather than a site.

bivy.name: Silver Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground to the Heather Meadows end of the highway, roughly fourteen miles east of Glacier on the west side of the road just after the river crossing, and about eight miles below the Heather Meadows lots. This is the practical answer for a party that drives up the night before a scramble on Table Mountain, Mount Herman or Mount Ann and wants to be at the trailhead early without sleeping in a day-use car park. It is emphatically staging rather than plan: you are three thousand feet below the objectives and the drive up in the morning takes twenty minutes. Because there are no reservations it is a gamble on a Friday evening in July and August, and the fallback is the campground further down the valley. It stays open later into the autumn than the road to Artist Point does, which matters for anyone climbing these peaks in October.
bivy.water: Piped water at the campground during the operating season, and the river alongside. Confirm the water is turned on if you are arriving at the shoulders of the season.
bivy.permit: A campground fee is charged per night and paid on site; this is a fee campground rather than a pass site, so a recreation pass does not cover the overnight. Fires are allowed in the provided rings unless a county or forest-wide burn ban is in force, which through a dry August is common. Standard national forest food-storage sense applies — black bears work this valley.
bivy.capacity: About twenty sites in forest beside the North Fork Nooksack, with vault toilets and drinking water in season; first come, first served, and it fills on summer weekends

bivy.name: Douglas Fir Campground
bivy.notes: Two and a half miles east of Glacier, low in the valley and a long way below anything you would climb — but it is the campground that serves BOTH halves of this zone, because the Canyon Creek Road turning is only a couple of miles back down the highway. A party bound for Bearpaw Mountain has a rough, slow forest road ahead of them in the morning and this is the sensible place to be the night before; a party bound for Heather Meadows has a longer drive up than they would from the higher campground but a guaranteed bed. Being at a thousand feet in dense timber it is warm, damp and mosquito-prone in early summer, and it gives you no acclimatisation and no view. The upside is that it is open when the high country is not, and that it is the only bookable option on this side of the mountain.
bivy.water: Piped water in season plus the river. Treat river water.
bivy.permit: Per-night campground fee, bookable ahead through the national reservation system, so unlike the higher campground you can arrive at ten at night and know you have a site. Campfire rings are provided and are subject to seasonal burn bans. A recreation pass does not cover camping here.
bivy.capacity: Around thirty sites in old growth beside the North Fork Nooksack, with vault toilets and seasonal drinking water; reservable in advance, which is the reason to choose it over the campground higher up

bivy.name: Mazama Lake designated sites, Chain Lakes
bivy.notes: The nearest legal backcountry camping to the Heather Meadows peaks and the only overnight option in the immediate basin, in the string of subalpine lakes that the Chain Lakes trail drops into on the far side of Herman Saddle. From Artist Point the circuit is around six miles with roughly seventeen hundred feet of gain and loss, and the lakes sit a bit under halfway round. For Mount Herman this is genuinely useful: the saddle is on the route, so a party that camps here is above the trailhead with a very short morning to the south ridge. For Table Mountain it is a detour rather than an approach, and the reason to know about it is the ban on camping on Table Mountain itself through the summer. Snow lingers in the basin into mid-August in a heavy year, which is worth knowing before committing to a site that may be under a drift. Trekking poles earn their weight on the snow traverses. This is a busy, family-friendly circuit and the sites go early on a summer weekend, so arrive with a plan for finding all four taken.
bivy.water: The lakes, and they are reliable all season. There is no potable water anywhere on the circuit, so treat everything.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit is required or issued. Recreation pass on the vehicle at whichever of the four trailheads you start from. CAMPING IS RESTRICTED TO THE MARKED SITES — the meadows here are heather over thin soil and the designation exists because they were being destroyed. No campfires at all, carry-in stoves only. Party size twelve. Food must go in a bear-resistant canister or be hung at least ten feet up and four feet out from the trunk and branches; there is no hardware provided.
bivy.capacity: Four designated sites marked by posts with a tent symbol, and a backcountry toilet. First come, first served, with no reservations and no permit to obtain — which means four parties get in and the fifth has nowhere legal to go.

bivy.name: Hayes Lake designated sites, Chain Lakes
bivy.notes: The upper pair of the Chain Lakes camps, a short distance on from the lower lake and a little higher, closer to the climb back up to Herman Saddle. For a party that has come over from the Artist Point side and intends to finish the circuit in the morning this is the better position, and it catches the evening light on Baker; for a party using the basin as a base for Mount Herman it is marginally further from the saddle than the lower lake and marginally more exposed to weather coming across the ridge. Elevation is not stated because the usable ground spreads across the shore rather than sitting at one identifiable point. Everything the basin holds is heavily used — camp on the marked pads, keep well back from the shoreline, and do not add a ninth site because the eight are taken. The right answer when they are full is to walk out; the trailhead is not far and the road is paved.
bivy.water: The lake, treated. Iceberg Lake nearby holds floating ice well into summer and is the colder and less pleasant draw of the two.
bivy.permit: Mount Baker Wilderness, same rules as the sister camp: no overnight permit, recreation pass at the trailhead, camping only at the marked sites, no fires of any kind, party limit twelve, food canistered or hung with no provided hardware. Nothing here is reservable, so the eight sites across both lakes are the entire legal capacity of the basin on any given night.
bivy.capacity: Four designated sites marked with posts, slightly more open and more exposed than the lower lake, with a pit toilet on the stretch between Iceberg Lake and here

bivy.name: Bearpaw Lake
bivy.notes: The base for Bearpaw Mountain and the only camping anywhere near its own line. Canyon Creek Road leaves the Mount Baker Highway about two miles east of Glacier and runs north for a long, slow fourteen miles or so of alternating tarmac and serious potholes before a signed spur climbs right to the lake trailhead; the last couple of miles are single lane with brush closing in that will mark a car. From the trailhead it is roughly a mile to the lake, short but steep. The peak's easiest line is a class three scramble from the southwest, following the timbered ridge east of the lake, with a direct variation onto the steeper part of the ridge that gives a narrow and locally exposed scramble. ROAD ACCESS IS THE FIRST THING TO CHECK AND NOT AN AFTERTHOUGHT: Canyon Creek Road has been closed at around mile four by a landslide carrying large timber and debris, with more downed trees below the block, which cuts off the lake spur and the road end entirely. When that closure is in force there is no alternative approach to this peak, only a very long road walk. Snow lies on this ground into July in most years.
bivy.water: The lake, at camp. Treat it. This is the only water on the peak's own approach and there is nothing on the ridge above.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, OUTSIDE any designated wilderness — this ground sits west of the Mount Baker Wilderness boundary, so there is no self-issue permit and no wilderness party limit here, and the twelve-person rule and blanket fire ban that govern the Heather Meadows half of this zone do not automatically apply. What does apply is a recreation pass at the trailhead, and whatever county or forest-wide burn ban is in force, which through a dry summer is usually a total one. Pack out everything including human waste; there is no toilet.
bivy.capacity: A few rough informal sites at a small lake in the trees; low use, no facilities, no toilet and nothing built

bivy.name: Excelsior ridge camps and the high spring, Canyon Creek Road end
bivy.notes: This is the established high camping on the Canyon Creek road system, at the far end of the same road that serves Bearpaw, and it is listed with the caveat that IT IS NOT ON BEARPAW'S OWN ROUTE. Bearpaw is the prominent summit standing to the west, seen across the drainage from the pass and the ridge, and reaching it from here means dropping and re-climbing rather than walking a connecting line. Its value is as the answer to what a party does when the day goes wrong or when they want two objectives out of one long, slow drive: legal, watered, established camping at the road end of a road most people will only want to drive once. The trail leaves the road end, meets a junction in less than a mile with the Canyon Ridge trail going left, reaches the small lakes just beyond and then climbs through forest and into open meadow towards the pass. The same landslide closure that gates the Bearpaw spur gates this trailhead as well; the alternative is to walk up from the highway instead, which is a far bigger day. Meadows here are at their best in July and August and again for autumn colour in September and October.
bivy.water: A spring about half a mile short of Excelsior Pass is the best and most dependable water in this high country and is the reason the camps are where they are. The lakes lower down at the trailhead end are shallow and warm late in the season. Treat everything, and fill at the spring rather than counting on anything on the crest.
bivy.permit: The ridge camps sit inside the Mount Baker Wilderness, which the High Divide trail enters at the pass — so from there on it is party size twelve, no campfires of any kind, carry-in stoves only, camp on durable ground and pack out all waste including human waste. A recreation pass is required at the trailhead and there is a self-issue register. The ground below the pass around the lakes is outside the wilderness and less strictly governed, but the burn bans still apply.
bivy.capacity: Scattered informal sites on the ridge running south from Excelsior Peak and along the High Divide, plus a cluster near the spring; a handful of small parties, spread out, with no built sites and no toilet

bivy.name: Watson Lakes designated camps
bivy.notes: The substance of this zone and the best camping anywhere near these three peaks. It is a genuinely short walk — about two miles from the road end, through forest to a meadow junction, over a saddle at around 4,700 ft and down to the pair of lakes at 4,400 ft — which makes it the rare alpine camp in the North Cascades that costs a heavy pack almost nothing. Mount Watson rises straight above: from the lakes the line works up the north side, traverses to the large col near 5,900 ft between the East Peak and the jumbled western summits, then takes heather and treed slopes west to the basin under the true summit, a heather and dirt gully on the south side of the summit block, and a short exposed class two to three ridge to the top where many parties want a fixed line. For Bacon Peak this is the staging night rather than the base, since the summit is a long way east across the massif. The lakes are notoriously buggy through midsummer and hold snow into early season. Everything here is heavily used and the designation exists because it was being trampled.
bivy.water: The lakes and a nearby stream, reliable through the season. There is no potable water on the road or the trail, so treat everything.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, inside the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness, which the trail enters at the saddle before dropping to the lakes. No overnight permit is required or issued. A recreation pass must be displayed at the trailhead, and between December and April a state Sno-Park permit is required at the Anderson Creek Sno-Park instead. CAMPING IS ALLOWED ONLY IN THE DESIGNATED SITES and campfires are prohibited outright — carry a stove. Standard wilderness rules otherwise: keep the party small, camp on rock or bare ground rather than in the heather, pack out everything, and secure food overnight since there is no hardware provided.
bivy.capacity: Designated sites at the two lakes, first come first served with no reservations, plus a backcountry toilet. Flat ground is mostly rock outcrop along the shoreline; the upper lake takes the larger share of parties.

bivy.name: Lower Anderson Lake
bivy.notes: Half a mile down from the second trail junction and a hundred feet above the Watson Lakes, and the more useful of the two basins for anyone climbing rather than hiking, because BACON PEAK'S APPROACH RUNS DIRECTLY ABOVE IT. From the saddle about 1.4 miles up the Watson Lakes trail a boot path climbs south onto the ridge high above this lake and opens into the meadows that lead east across the massif toward the Bacon summits, so a party camped here is on the line rather than beside it. It also solves the problem the designated sites create — when the four-and-four at the Watson Lakes are taken there is nowhere legal to squeeze in, and this basin is the fallback. Anderson Butte, a former lookout site with a long view over Baker Lake and across to Baker and Shuksan, is a short spur off the same trail junction and is worth the twenty minutes on an evening you are not going anywhere. Bugs are as bad here as at the lakes over the saddle.
bivy.water: The lake, treated. Dependable all season.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. This lake sits on the trail before it crosses into the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness, so the strict designated-site rule that governs the lakes beyond the saddle does not apply in the same way here — but the campfire ban, the small-party expectation and the pack-it-all-out rule should be treated as applying regardless, because the ground is identical and equally fragile. Recreation pass at the trailhead; Sno-Park permit instead from December through April. No permit is issued for an overnight and none is needed.
bivy.capacity: A small number of informal sites at the lake with a backcountry privy; quieter than the sister lakes over the saddle and usually the one with space left

bivy.name: Anderson Creek road end, Watson Lakes trailhead
bivy.notes: This is the road rather than a campsite, because on this side of the massif the road decides what the trip is. It is a rare thing in this range — a driveable gravel road that delivers you to 4,200 ft, within two miles of an alpine lake basin — and it is why the Anderson and Watson Lakes are the substance of this zone rather than a footnote. THE ROAD IS THE PROBLEM AS OF 2026: an atmospheric river in December 2025 cut a washout in FS 1107 at around mile three to four, well below the road end, and that failure has closed the trailhead and the Sno-Park with no quick fix. When it is in force the whole approach becomes four or five miles of road walking with 1,500 ft of gain before the trail even starts, which turns a comfortable overnight on Mount Watson into a serious two-day trip and puts Bacon Peak out of reach for most parties from this side. Confirm the road with the ranger district before driving out, and if it is open, sleeping in the lot the night before is a normal and sensible way to save the morning. The road holds snow late and is not usually driveable to the end until well into the season.
bivy.water: None at the road end. Carry what you need for the evening; the first water is at the lakes, which are close enough that most parties simply walk in.
bivy.permit: Recreation pass required, and a state Sno-Park permit instead from December through April. This is national forest outside the wilderness boundary, so a night in the lot or a pullout is generally tolerated, but never in a way that narrows the road or blocks a turning place. The wilderness rules start at the saddle above.
bivy.capacity: A modest gravel lot at the road end with room for perhaps a dozen vehicles and a few flat spots to sleep beside them; no facilities, and it fills on summer weekends

bivy.name: Northeast Bacon camp, above the glacier
bivy.notes: The high camp for Bacon Peak from the Anderson Creek road, and the reason the peak is a two-day trip rather than an epic. It is reached by leaving the Watson Lakes trail at the saddle, climbing the ridge above Lower Anderson Lake, and working east through meadows and moraine across the massif — a long undulating traverse rather than a climb, and the part of the day that eats the time. From camp the summit is a short ascent to the southeast, and it is possible to reach the top without crossing glaciers at all, which is what makes this a scramble for a competent party rather than a rope-up. Immediately north the ground falls away past post-glacial moraine to the saddle above the green lake below the glacier, and that is the line onward for anyone continuing east or north across the range. It is a fully exposed shelf with nothing to shelter behind and the weather here comes across from Baker with no warning. The season is roughly mid-July into September; earlier and the traverse is a long snow slope, later and the water is gone.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier melt near camp through most of the season, and tarns in the moraine below. Late in a dry summer expect to be melting snow. Treat anything you find, and do not count on liquid water in early season when the whole shelf is still covered.
bivy.permit: This camp sits on the boundary country between the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness and North Cascades National Park, and which one it falls in decides whether you need a permit at all. Ask specifically when you plan the trip: the Forest Service side needs no overnight permit, while the park side needs a backcountry permit written for the correct cross-country zone. No campfires on either side of the line. Camp on snow, rock or gravel and never on the heather, keep well back from water, and pack out all waste — on snow and glacier that means blue bags carried out.
bivy.capacity: Open ground for a couple of small parties on gravel, rock and heather about half a mile northeast of the summit; informal, with nothing built and no toilet

bivy.name: Upper Diobsud Lakes
bivy.notes: The highest comfortable camp on the massif and the natural pivot for anyone crossing it, in the upper Diobsud Creek basin on the far side of Bacon Peak from the Anderson Creek road. It is the camp a party reaches at the end of a long traverse day, and the one they leave from for the summit, for the ground east toward Berdeen, or for the long line north over the divide toward Hagan and Blum. What sets it apart from every other high site here is that it has water at six thousand feet, which nothing on the connecting ridges does. It is alpine meadow, so the heather is the thing to protect and the tent goes on rock. Snow covers this basin well into July and the lakes can still be part frozen at the start of the season. There is no shelter, no cell coverage, and no quick way down from here in any direction.
bivy.water: The lakes, dependable and right at camp — the best water this high anywhere on the massif. Treat it.
bivy.permit: This basin lies on the North Cascades National Park side of the divide, so a park backcountry permit for the correct cross-country zone is required for an overnight, collected in person at the wilderness information center. No campfires. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than in the meadow, keep a hundred feet back from the water, and carry out human waste in a blue bag from snow and glacier ground. The party limit in a park cross-country zone is small — confirm the number when you collect the permit rather than assuming a Forest Service twelve.
bivy.capacity: Room for a small party or two on alpine meadow and heather benches beside the upper pair of lakes; established by use rather than designation, with no facilities

bivy.name: Berdeen Lake benches
bivy.notes: The camp for Berdeen Peak and the substance of the Bacon Creek side of this zone. The documented approach starts at the Bacon Creek road end at valley-bottom elevation, scrambles up Porkbelly Ridge, crosses the east side of the peak around 6,400 ft and drops to camp above the lake — a very big first day with four thousand feet of gain, much of it trackless. The lake sits in a deep cirque a little over a mile east of Hagan Mountain and drains east over an enormous waterfall into a tributary of Bacon Creek, which is the geography that settles the argument about which road it belongs to: it faces Bacon Creek, not Baker Lake. It can be reached from the Blum Lakes over the divide to the northwest, but that is a traverse variation for a party already committed to a long trip, not an approach. From camp Berdeen Peak's east ridge is the way up, and the ground south and west continues onto the Bacon massif. Season is roughly mid-July into September, held back at the front by snow on the ridge and at the back by short days on a route with no trail.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet streams, fed off the glaciers above and reliable all season. Treat it. This is the first dependable water since the valley bottom, over four thousand feet below.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, required for any overnight and written for a cross-country zone rather than a designated camp — a different thing to ask for, and it must be collected in person at the wilderness information center, which is a long way round on the far side of the range from the Anderson Creek trailheads. No campfires anywhere in the zone. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and never in the meadow, keep a hundred feet back from the water, and carry out human waste. A bear canister is the sensible answer where the heather gives you nothing to hang from; they can usually be borrowed at the permit office.
bivy.capacity: A handful of tent-sized spots on benches above the lake shore; the basin is large but the flat, durable ground is limited, and this is a cross-country zone with a small party cap rather than an established campground

bivy.name: Bacon Creek road end and Porkbelly Ridge
bivy.notes: THERE IS NO ESTABLISHED CAMPING ON THIS APPROACH and the honest answer is to start early and reach the lake basin in one push. The road leaves the highway a few miles east of Marblemount and runs up the valley to a road end around 850 ft, from which Porkbelly Ridge is climbed trackless — steep timber, deadfall and brush with better travel once the ridge crest establishes itself, and no benches, clearings or water worth the name in four thousand feet. THE ROAD IS THE FIRST PROBLEM: it carries very large potholes over long stretches, a bridge on the main road beyond one of the side creeks has been out, and the spurs off it are variously blocked by missing bridges, washouts and downed timber, so how far a vehicle gets is a live question that changes year to year and adds miles at the bottom when it goes against you. A party that runs out of daylight on the ridge flattens a spot among the trees and moves at first light; that is the realistic use of this camp, not a plan. The same road end is the start for the Diobsud Creek side of Bacon Peak, which is climbed on a longer line past Salvation Peak with a glacier saddle camp around 6,250 ft — a spring and early summer objective needing snow travel gear, and a different proposition entirely from the summer scramble off the Anderson Creek road.
bivy.water: The creek near the road end, treated. Above it there is nothing dependable until the lake basin high on the ridge, so fill everything before you start climbing.
bivy.permit: The road end and the lower part of the ridge are Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, where a night in a pullout is generally tolerated and no permit is issued. The ground higher up crosses into North Cascades National Park, so if you sleep anywhere above the lower ridge you need a park backcountry permit for the cross-country zone. The boundary is not marked on the ground on this ridge, so ask at the permit office where it falls before planning a bivy rather than deciding on the hill. No campfires above the road, and total burn bans are common on this side through a dry August.
bivy.capacity: Rough parking at the road end and whatever flat ground you can find in the timber; one party, found rather than chosen. There is no camp here, and that is worth saying plainly.

bivy.name: Watson Lakes designated camps
bivy.notes: The substance of this zone and the best camping anywhere near these three peaks. It is a genuinely short walk — about two miles from the road end, through forest to a meadow junction, over a saddle at around 4,700 ft and down to the pair of lakes at 4,400 ft — which makes it the rare alpine camp in the North Cascades that costs a heavy pack almost nothing. Mount Watson rises straight above: from the lakes the line works up the north side, traverses to the large col near 5,900 ft between the East Peak and the jumbled western summits, then takes heather and treed slopes west to the basin under the true summit, a heather and dirt gully on the south side of the summit block, and a short exposed class two to three ridge to the top where many parties want a fixed line. bivy.water: The lakes and a nearby stream, reliable through the season. There is no potable water on the road or the trail, so treat everything.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, inside the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness, which the trail enters at the saddle before dropping to the lakes. No overnight permit is required or issued. A recreation pass must be displayed at the trailhead, and between December and April a state Sno-Park permit is required at the Anderson Creek Sno-Park instead. CAMPING IS ALLOWED ONLY IN THE DESIGNATED SITES and campfires are prohibited outright — carry a stove. Standard wilderness rules otherwise: keep the party small, camp on rock or bare ground rather than in the heather, pack out everything, and secure food overnight since there is no hardware provided.
bivy.capacity: Designated sites at the two lakes, first come first served with no reservations, plus a backcountry toilet. Flat ground is mostly rock outcrop along the shoreline; the upper lake takes the larger share of parties.

bivy.name: Lower Anderson Lake
bivy.notes: Half a mile down from the second trail junction and a hundred feet above the Watson Lakes, and the more useful of the two basins for anyone climbing rather than hiking, because BACON PEAK'S APPROACH RUNS DIRECTLY ABOVE IT. From the saddle about 1.4 miles up the Watson Lakes trail a boot path climbs south onto the ridge high above this lake and opens into the meadows that lead east across the massif toward the Bacon summits, so a party camped here is on the line rather than beside it. It also solves the problem the designated sites create — when the four-and-four at the Watson Lakes are taken there is nowhere legal to squeeze in, and this basin is the fallback. Anderson Butte, a former lookout site with a long view over Baker Lake and across to Baker and Shuksan, is a short spur off the same trail junction and is worth the twenty minutes on an evening you are not going anywhere. Bugs are as bad here as at the lakes over the saddle.
bivy.water: The lake, treated. Dependable all season.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. This lake sits on the trail before it crosses into the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness, so the strict designated-site rule that governs the lakes beyond the saddle does not apply in the same way here — but the campfire ban, the small-party expectation and the pack-it-all-out rule should be treated as applying regardless, because the ground is identical and equally fragile. Recreation pass at the trailhead; Sno-Park permit instead from December through April. No permit is issued for an overnight and none is needed.
bivy.capacity: A small number of informal sites at the lake with a backcountry privy; quieter than the sister lakes over the saddle and usually the one with space left

bivy.name: Anderson Creek road end, Watson Lakes trailhead
bivy.notes: This is the road rather than a campsite, because on this side of the massif the road decides what the trip is. It is a rare thing in this range — a driveable gravel road that delivers you to 4,200 ft, within two miles of an alpine lake basin — and it is why the Anderson and Watson Lakes are the substance of this zone rather than a footnote. THE ROAD IS THE PROBLEM AS OF 2026: an atmospheric river in December 2025 cut a washout in FS 1107 at around mile three to four, well below the road end, and that failure has closed the trailhead and the Sno-Park with no quick fix. When it is in force the whole approach becomes four or five miles of road walking with 1,500 ft of gain before the trail even starts, which turns a comfortable overnight on Mount Watson into a serious two-day trip and puts Bacon Peak out of reach for most parties from this side. Confirm the road with the ranger district before driving out, and if it is open, sleeping in the lot the night before is a normal and sensible way to save the morning. The road holds snow late and is not usually driveable to the end until well into the season.
bivy.water: None at the road end. Carry what you need for the evening; the first water is at the lakes, which are close enough that most parties simply walk in.
bivy.permit: Recreation pass required, and a state Sno-Park permit instead from December through April. This is national forest outside the wilderness boundary, so a night in the lot or a pullout is generally tolerated, but never in a way that narrows the road or blocks a turning place. The wilderness rules start at the saddle above.
bivy.capacity: A modest gravel lot at the road end with room for perhaps a dozen vehicles and a few flat spots to sleep beside them; no facilities, and it fills on summer weekends

bivy.name: Northeast Bacon camp, above the glacier
bivy.notes: The high camp for Bacon Peak from the Anderson Creek road, and the reason the peak is a two-day trip rather than an epic. It is reached by leaving the Watson Lakes trail at the saddle, climbing the ridge above Lower Anderson Lake, and working east through meadows and moraine across the massif — a long undulating traverse rather than a climb, and the part of the day that eats the time. bivy.name: Upper Diobsud Lakes

bivy.name: Berdeen Lake benches

bivy.capacity: A handful of tent-sized spots on benches above the lake shore; the basin is large but the flat, durable ground is limited, and this is a cross-country zone with a small party cap rather than an established campground

bivy.name: Bacon Creek road end and Porkbelly Ridge
bivy.notes: THERE IS NO ESTABLISHED CAMPING ON THIS APPROACH and the honest answer is to start early and reach the lake basin in one push. The road leaves the highway a few miles east of Marblemount and runs up the valley to a road end around 850 ft, from which Porkbelly Ridge is climbed trackless — steep timber, deadfall and brush with better travel once the ridge crest establishes itself, and no benches, clearings or water worth the name in four thousand feet. THE ROAD IS THE FIRST PROBLEM: it carries very large potholes over long stretches, a bridge on the main road beyond one of the side creeks has been out, and the spurs off it are variously blocked by missing bridges, washouts and downed timber, so how far a vehicle gets is a live question that changes year to year and adds miles at the bottom when it goes against you. A party that runs out of daylight on the ridge flattens a spot among the trees and moves at first light; that is the realistic use of this camp, not a plan. bivy.permit: The road end and the lower part of the ridge are Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, where a night in a pullout is generally tolerated and no permit is issued. The ground higher up crosses into North Cascades National Park, so if you sleep anywhere above the lower ridge you need a park backcountry permit for the cross-country zone. The boundary is not marked on the ground on this ridge, so ask at the permit office where it falls before planning a bivy rather than deciding on the hill. No campfires above the road, and total burn bans are common on this side through a dry August.
bivy.capacity: Rough parking at the road end and whatever flat ground you can find in the timber; one party, found rather than chosen. There is no camp here, and that is worth saying plainly.

bivy.name: Watson Lakes designated camps
bivy.notes: The substance of this zone and the best camping anywhere near these three peaks. It is a genuinely short walk — about two miles from the road end, through forest to a meadow junction, over a saddle at around 4,700 ft and down to the pair of lakes at 4,400 ft — which makes it the rare alpine camp in the North Cascades that costs a heavy pack almost nothing. For Bacon Peak this is the staging night rather than the base, since the summit is a long way east across the massif. bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, inside the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness, which the trail enters at the saddle before dropping to the lakes. No overnight permit is required or issued. bivy.capacity: Designated sites at the two lakes, first come first served with no reservations, plus a backcountry toilet. Flat ground is mostly rock outcrop along the shoreline; the upper lake takes the larger share of parties.

bivy.name: Lower Anderson Lake
bivy.notes: Half a mile down from the second trail junction and a hundred feet above the Watson Lakes, and the more useful of the two basins for anyone climbing rather than hiking, because BACON PEAK'S APPROACH RUNS DIRECTLY ABOVE IT. From the saddle about 1.4 miles up the Watson Lakes trail a boot path climbs south onto the ridge high above this lake and opens into the meadows that lead east across the massif toward the Bacon summits, so a party camped here is on the line rather than beside it. Bugs are as bad here as at the lakes over the saddle.
bivy.water: The lake, treated. Dependable all season.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. This lake sits on the trail before it crosses into the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness, so the strict designated-site rule that governs the lakes beyond the saddle does not apply in the same way here — but the campfire ban, the small-party expectation and the pack-it-all-out rule should be treated as applying regardless, because the ground is identical and equally fragile. bivy.capacity: A small number of informal sites at the lake with a backcountry privy; quieter than the sister lakes over the saddle and usually the one with space left

bivy.name: Anderson Creek road end, Watson Lakes trailhead
bivy.notes: This is the road rather than a campsite, because on this side of the massif the road decides what the trip is. bivy.permit: Recreation pass required, and a state Sno-Park permit instead from December through April. This is national forest outside the wilderness boundary, so a night in the lot or a pullout is generally tolerated, but never in a way that narrows the road or blocks a turning place. The wilderness rules start at the saddle above.
bivy.capacity: A modest gravel lot at the road end with room for perhaps a dozen vehicles and a few flat spots to sleep beside them; no facilities, and it fills on summer weekends
