bivy.name: Camp Muir
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for the Disappointment Cleaver, Ingraham Direct and Gibraltar routes, reached by the roughly 4,500 ft slog up the Muir Snowfield from Paradise. The Public Shelter is first-come and cannot be reserved, so treat it as a bonus rather than a plan and carry a tent regardless; it has been closed for maintenance in past seasons and its status is worth re-checking each year. Weather is the main hazard to the camp itself, and the snowfield below is notorious for whiteout navigation, so record your descent bearings before you need them. The Paradise road is plowed year-round, so unlike the north-side camps this one is not gated by a seasonal road closure.
bivy.water: No running water and no reliable melt stream. Every party must carry a stove and fuel and melt snow; snow is normally available on the Cowlitz year-round, but late in a dry season the cleanest snow can be a walk from the tent platforms
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit required for any overnight, obtained through Recreation.gov with roughly two-thirds reservable in advance and about one-third held for walk-ups within a day of departure. Separately, anyone travelling on glaciers, going above high camp or attempting the summit owes the climbing cost recovery fee, paid on Pay.gov before arriving; the amount is revised periodically, so confirm it at booking. Walking to Camp Muir and back as a day trip needs neither. In-person registration at a ranger station is still required on or before the climb date.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 25-35 tent parties on the Cowlitz Glacier snow platforms in a normal season, plus the 1921 stone Public Shelter which sleeps on the order of 15-20 on its bunks; permits are issued against a party quota rather than numbered pads, so the practical ceiling moves with snow cover

bivy.name: Ingraham Flats
bivy.notes: About a thousand feet above Camp Muir past Cathedral Gap, this bench shortens summit day meaningfully and is the usual overflow when the Muir quota is full. The trade is real: less acclimatisation, a colder and more exposed camp, and objective exposure to icefall off the Ingraham headwall above, which is why parties argue about whether the higher start is worth it. Whether it is sound in a given week is conditions-dependent and worth asking the climbing rangers rather than deciding from a published description. Sites are dug into snow, so bring a shovel and expect to build your own platform and walls.
bivy.water: Snow only, melted on a stove. There is no liquid water source at this elevation
bivy.permit: Same Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit as Camp Muir, issued for a specific camp — a permit written for Camp Muir does not authorise a night here. The climbing cost recovery fee applies to everyone camping here, since reaching it means crossing the Cowlitz Glacier and going above Camp Muir.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties, typically under ten tents; the usable flat ground shifts year to year as the Ingraham Glacier changes and crevasses open across the bench

bivy.name: Camp Schurman
bivy.notes: The high camp for the Emmons-Winthrop, the standard north-side route, approached from the White River Campground through Glacier Basin and up the Inter Glacier. There is an NPS ranger hut with an emergency radio on its exterior and toilet facilities, but the hut is staff quarters and not a shelter climbers can sleep in, so a tent is mandatory. Access is gated by the White River Road, which typically does not open until late June, and by the Inter Glacier, which is small but crevassed enough that roping up is a judgement call that changes through the season. Late in a dry summer the Inter Glacier turns to bare ice and rubble.
bivy.water: Snow to melt in most conditions, and the camp generally has adequate clean snow through the season. Some parties find running meltwater near camp late in summer, but it is seasonal and should not be counted on when planning fuel
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit required, same reservation and walk-up split as the rest of the park's climbing camps, with in-person registration before the climb. The climbing cost recovery fee applies to anyone continuing onto the Emmons or Winthrop glaciers or attempting the summit; walking to Camp Schurman as a day trip without going higher does not trigger it.
bivy.capacity: Considerably smaller than Camp Muir, on the order of a dozen tent sites on the snow and rock around Steamboat Prow; the quota fills quickly on good-weather weekends

bivy.name: Thumb Rock
bivy.notes: The standard and effectively only bivouac on Liberty Ridge, a notch of snow and rock partway up the ridge on the Carbon Glacier side. It is exposed to rockfall from Thumb Rock itself and from the bands above, and a fatal rockfall struck tents here in 2019, so site selection within the notch and the timing of your arrival matter more than comfort. Warm afternoons that prevent an overnight freeze are the usual trigger, and the park service advises against the route when the freezing level on the mountain is high. The approach from the Carbon River or Mowich side is long and its own seasonal problem, since those roads open on different schedules and can be closed by washouts or fire.
bivy.water: Snow only. There is no water and no shelter, so carry all fuel for the bivouac and for summit day
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit required for the overnight, plus the climbing cost recovery fee, which is unavoidable on this route. Registration is in person at a ranger station and climbing rangers will discuss current route conditions at that point, which on Liberty Ridge is worth treating as part of the planning rather than a formality.
bivy.capacity: Very limited, realistically two to four small tents; parties have ended up stacking tents in a vertical line on the slope when the site is busy, which is not a safe arrangement

bivy.name: White River Campground
bivy.notes: The roadhead camp for the Emmons-Winthrop, five miles up White River Road off Highway 410, and the Glacier Basin trail to Camp Schurman starts here. Being the highest of the park's drive-in campgrounds it is normally the last to open, around late June, and the first to close in September, so early-season parties often sleep outside the park. Its availability is not guaranteed year to year — it has been listed closed for fire activity — so confirm status before driving in. A reasonable place to sort gear and get a short night before an early start up the Inter Glacier.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground when it is open for the season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed, but this is inside Mount Rainier National Park so park entrance applies, and the park has operated timed-entry reservations for corridor access in recent summers. Recent NPS listings show it as first-come rather than reservable, which contradicts several third-party campground sites still advertising reservations, so check the current NPS page before relying on either. A camping permit here does not cover the mountain: the wilderness permit and the climbing fee are separate.
bivy.capacity: 88 individual drive-in sites with flush toilets and fire grates; RV length is limited to about 27 ft

bivy.name: Cougar Rock Campground

Because the Nisqually entrance road is kept open through the year, it is the least season-gated approach on the mountain, though the campground itself runs roughly late May to late September. It sits low and forested at just over 3,000 ft, which makes for comfortable sleeping but no acclimatisation value whatsoever. Book early, since it is one of only two campgrounds in the park taking reservations and fills on summer weekends.
bivy.water: Potable water available at the campground during the operating season
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park entrance applies, and the park has used timed-entry reservations for the Nisqually/Paradise corridor in recent summers, which can affect what time you can drive up on summit morning. Campsites are reservable through Recreation.gov and required during the peak midsummer window. This covers the campground only and is unrelated to the wilderness permit and climbing fee.

bivy.name: Bathtub Lakes basin, east of Mount Pilchuck
bivy.notes: This is the only real camp on Pilchuck and it serves the east side rather than the standard route. It is reached from below, from the Bear Lake and Pinnacle Lake trailhead on a spur road off the loop east of Verlot, then up past the lower lake and into the gulch above — a loose, brushy, steep piece of ground with vegetation-pulling and poor rock that is the genuine difficulty of the East Ridge, not the ridge itself. Camping in the basin splits that so the gulch is climbed fresh. It has no bearing on the standard summit trail, which leaves the end of the Mount Pilchuck road on the other side of the mountain and is a straightforward day hike to the restored summit lookout with no camping along it and none needed. Treat this as a plan for the east side and as a contingency for anyone who commits to the gulch late and would rather not descend it in the dark.
bivy.water: The lakes and their outlets, dependable through the season and needing treatment. This is a wet basin, which is the whole reason it works as a camp.
bivy.permit: The summit and upper mountain are a STATE CONSERVATION AREA rather than national forest, but this basin and the approach to it are forest land and no camping permit applies. The parking requirement at the trailheads on this mountain is the FEDERAL pass — a state Discover Pass is not valid at them, which catches people out because of the state park name. No fires on the state land above, and fire bans are routine below in late summer.
bivy.capacity: Informal sites among the small lakes and benches of the basin; a few parties, nothing developed

bivy.name: Found Lake and the Kindy Ridge saddle
bivy.notes: The first useful camp on the eastern approach and the one most parties reach on a late start. From where road 1570 becomes impassable you walk the blocked, overgrown roadbed for roughly three miles, crossing several creeks and two large washouts that are genuinely awkward when snowmelt is high, then take a steep climbers' path off it at about 2,300 feet. That path leads up toward this lake, and the junction where the Found Lake line and the Snowking line split is in the saddle above at about 4,800 feet. Stopping here splits an approach that otherwise routinely takes two days and sometimes three. It is low, forested and buggy in early summer, and it is a long way still from any summit, so treat it as a staging camp rather than a base.
bivy.water: The lake, dependable through the season, and the first certain water after the long walk up the old logging road. The saddle above it is dry.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue wilderness permit from the register. Forest Service road 1570 has no developed trailhead, so a vehicle pass is not normally required there, unlike the Slide Lake trail on the other side of the massif; confirm with the district before relying on that. Practical bear precautions are a hang or a canister rather than a requirement here, since this is not park ground.
bivy.capacity: A few rough spots by the lake, party-sized. Nothing established, no toilet, no platforms.

bivy.name: Kindy Ridge crest camps
bivy.notes: The Kindy Ridge crest, also described as the northeast ridge, is a long undulating plod rather than a climb, and the honest description of camping on it is that parties stop where the day ends. There are quite a few workable spots and no established ones. This matters most for anyone linking the peaks rather than climbing one: the high route around the headwaters of Kindy Creek runs along this ground and Mutchler is often called the best vantage point on the whole traverse. Weather is the risk that makes a crest camp expensive here, since the ridge is exposed for miles with no shelter and the retreat is back down the same slow ground. Season is roughly July into September, earlier if you want continuous snow to travel on and later if you want the cornices gone.
bivy.water: Conditions-dependent and the thing to plan around. Early in the season there are snow patches and runnels most of the way along; by late summer whole sections of the crest are dry and the reliable water is back down at the lakes. Carry from the last certain source rather than expecting to find one.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground, keep off the heather where you can, and pack out human waste — there is no toilet anywhere in this zone. Stoves only up here.
bivy.capacity: Scattered heather benches and gravel flats along the crest rather than any one site, party-sized, spread over several miles of ridge. No facilities of any kind.

bivy.name: Head of Kindy Creek and the Kindy-Buck Creek pass
bivy.notes: THE GROUND THAT PUTS MOUNT BUCKINDY IN RANGE. Buckindy's standard route is a class 4 scramble on the north slopes, with glaciers on the north and east flanks, and the parties who climb it are camping either in the basins at the head of Kindy Creek or at the pass between the Kindy and Buck Creek drainages. Coming in from road 1570 this is a second or third night out, well beyond the Cyclone Lake ground. There is a second way in from the south, over Green Mountain and the Horse Lake saddle from the Suiattle side, with camps on the divide and in the basins on the way, but that country has its own long road problems and is not the approach this zone is built around. Nothing here is a site in any developed sense: it is remote, lightly visited ground where the answer to where you sleep is wherever the light runs out, and a party should carry the fuel to melt snow and the tolerance for a dry, windy night.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small basin streams, generally running through midsummer and thinning badly after that. There is ice on Buckindy's north and east flanks, so late in the season the water that is left is glacier outflow rather than clean snowmelt.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on durable ground, pack out human waste, no fires. There is no quota and no reservation anywhere in this zone, so the constraint on a trip here is the approach rather than the paperwork.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on snow, moraine or heather at the passes and in the basins beneath them. Nothing built, no toilet.

bivy.name: Slide Lake
bivy.notes: The western gateway, and by a long way the easiest walking: about 2.5 miles round trip and 300 feet of gain to a lake formed when a landslide dammed the creek. For a climber it is a staging camp rather than an objective, since Snowking's west side and the lakes beyond are hours further on. Getting to the trailhead is the part to plan: from Darrington it is 16 miles north on the highway and then 20.5 miles up Illabot Creek Road, a long remote road with blind curves through the middle section and a small rock slide around mile 13.8 that can stop a low-clearance vehicle. Illabot Creek Road and the Cascade River Road have both been closed by washouts in the past and both are subject to seasonal closure, so confirm the road before committing to a trip that depends on it. The trail itself carries significant blowdown and boulder fields.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet. Reliable, though the exposed lakebed in late summer is slick and muddy and the shallow edges are not pleasant to draw from.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit at the register, which is passed at about 0.9 miles where the boundary is marked. THIS IS THE ONLY OFFICIAL TRAILHEAD IN THE ZONE and so realistically the only place a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is needed on the vehicle. Camp back from the shore, stove rather than fire.
bivy.capacity: Several rough sites, with the last good ones at about 1.25 miles where the well-beaten path ends. Parking at the trailhead takes roughly eight vehicles, which is a fair measure of how busy it gets.
